summary: TruLens 2.16 This release adds new evaluation metrics and Jury reliability metadata, improves handling of unparsable judge scores, and fixes cost accounting, batch evaluation, and OpenTelemetry tracing. Breaking changes and compatibility Streamlit-in-Snowflake dashboard support has been removed. ( #2784 ) All packages now require Python 3.10 or later. The test matrix now includes Python 3.14. ( #2896 ) New features Added a deterministic conversation_repetition metric. ( #2898 ) Added a requirement satisfaction metric. ( #2910 ) Added Jury.repeated and reliability metadata on every Jury result. ( #2854 ) Client hooks now adopt inherited W3C trace context. ( #2829 ) Fixes Evaluation scores and metrics Improved handling of unparsable judge responses: Excluded the parse-failure sentinel from score normalization, groundedness, and answerability scores. ( #2833 , #2834 , #2864 ) Dropped jurors whose judges returned no parsable score and excluded unparsable scores from per-item averages. ( #2837 , #2917 ) Excluded unparsable scores from BatchEvaluator aggregation, leaderboard averages, and compare_runs . ( #2866 , #2905 , #2939 ) Guardrails now reject unparsable and non-finite scores. ( #2902 ) Validated structured-output scores against the configured scale and corrected chain-of-thought context relevance scoring to use the requested scale. ( #2836 , #2860 ) Added response labeling to the agreement judge prompt. ( #2835 ) Added validation for retrieval relevance score lengths. ( #2853 ) Deduplicated ideal DCG by golden chunk text in ndcg_at_k . ( #2857 ) Skipped non-finite predictions during few-shot selection. ( #2852 ) Preserved min_score_val , max_score_val , and temperature in Metric.with_arguments . ( #2922 ) Fixed a pandas 3 get_group error when there is a single evaluation root. ( #2937 ) Corrected the llm_provider module import in jury.py . ( #2869 ) Batch evaluation and core behavior Read batch column mappings from the original row and preserved results when output column names collide. ( #2845 , #2844 ) Kept BatchEvaluator independent of the optional feedback package. ( #2901 ) Treated missing DataFrame cells as None and preserved columns in empty batch DataFrames. ( #2942 , #2946 ) Preserved retrieval order in context_filter results. ( #2932 ) Added a warning when TruSession is re-created with different settings. ( #2944 ) Cost accounting and reporting Prevented nested cost scopes from leaking callbacks into their parent scope. ( #2872 ) Fixed double-counting of evaluation spend in eval_cost . ( #2873 ) OpenAI cost tracking now adds per-call token and cost deltas rather than cumulative totals. ( #2855 ) Google provider cost accounting now includes thinking tokens and can price responses without constructing a client. ( #2861 ) LiteLLM cost tracking now accumulates across calls instead of retaining only the last call's cost. ( #2862 ) Anthropic now returns None for unknown model costs instead of reporting zero. ( #2856 ) Included child-span costs in OpenTelemetry leaderboard and trend calculations. ( #2912 ) Averaged per-input evaluation scores in the OpenTelemetry records view. ( #2909 ) Fixed handling of Postgres Decimal latency values in app metric trends. ( #2930 ) OpenTelemetry and client hooks Prevented generator span context from remaining active in the caller between chunks. ( #2914 ) Resolved default argument values when mapping instrument attributes. ( #2916 ) Client hooks now prioritize the traces-specific OTLP protocol setting. ( #2920 ) Added tracing for async methods wrapped in synchronous decorators. ( #2934 ) Prevented class methods from being re-wrapped for every new recorder. ( #2928 ) Provider and integration compatibility Bedrock now explicitly reports that response_format is not honored. ( #2795 ) LangChain now maps role="system" messages to SystemMessage rather than AIMessage . ( #2859 ) Added Claude 5 model support to the Anthropic provider. ( #2948 ) Documentation Documented UNPARSABLE_SCOR

summary: SSTIM Workbench , previously developed as BSC Lab, is the open reference environment for SSTIM , the Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary developed through the W3C Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary Community Group . It has two integrated layers: a precision multi-engine audiovisual stimulation application, and a knowledge layer over the SSTIM ontology. This release freezes SSTIM 0.20.0, published at https://w3id.org/sstim under CC BY 4.0: 18 modules holding 182 OWL classes and 371 properties labelled in English, and 645 SKOS concepts in English, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish, with SHACL validation shapes, four conformance profiles (Kernel, Core, Core Plus, Full), qualified evidence assessments, exposure and ecosystem term modules, and 110 verified external mappings to Wikidata, MeSH, UBERON and SNOMED CT alongside term reuse from BFO, COB, IAO, OBI, PROV-O and W3C ORG. Every mapping is dereferenced at the authority that mints its identifier and carries dated provenance and the reason for its predicate. The version IRI https://w3id.org/sstim/0.20.0 resolves to the frozen artifacts this archive contains. The archive is the whole repository at its release tag: the ontology sources and their frozen snapshot, the Svelte application (Graph Navigator, SPARQL interface, Patch Studio, four selectable audio engines), the validation and release tooling, and the documentation and architecture decision records. Its public reference data include nine published sensory stimulation protocols, from the 40 Hz auditory response of 1981 to a randomized home-use trial of 2022, each encoded from its paper, citing it, and asserting no effect. Licensing is per artifact class, and the three licences above are not alternatives. Each governs a different part of this archive: Apache-2.0 the software, build tooling and JSON contracts; CC BY 4.0 the ontology, vocabulary, public RDF data and documentation; CC0 1.0 the synthetic reference audio. A file carrying its own notice is governed by that notice, and LICENSING.md in the archive is the scope matrix. Scope. Sensory stimulation spans self-directed practice through regulated clinical intervention, and SSTIM describes that whole range: electroconvulsive therapy, interventional neurostimulation and preclinical study designs are published terms. The Workbench itself is general wellness software rather than a medical device, and carries no diagnostic or treatment claim; that is a statement about this implementation, not about the field. Community Group work is not a W3C Recommendation and is not W3C-endorsed technology. Ecosystem fixtures in the release are synthetic; real live-only agent records are kept outside this archive by design. The Workbench's stakeholder directory does list real companies, laboratories, people and projects of the field, each from a public source: it is a listing of relevance, not an agent record, and an entry removed on request is absent from later releases only. Each tagged release is archived here for citation.

summary: How much classical information can a noisy optical channel carry when both signal energy and preshared entanglement are limited? This work gives an exact capacity frontier for this joint resource problem. It allows one to determine the best asymptotic communication rate, price the benefit of additional entanglement, and distinguish the effect of tolerating errors from that of changing how entanglement is supplied. Exact capacity under two resource constraints The setting is any fixed bosonic Gaussian channel \(\Phi\) with finitely many input and output modes. Signal energy is measured by a positive quadratic Hamiltonian \(H_G=\tfrac12 R^{\mathsf T}GR\), with \(G>0\) and ground energy \(E_0\); \(R\) collects the canonical quadratures. The budgets satisfy \(E\ge E_0\) and \(P\ge0\). For an \(n\)-use code, the mean total signal energy is at most \(nE\), while the same initially shared maximally entangled state has Schmidt rank \(K_n\) satisfying \(\log K_n\le nP\). Thus \(P\) is a strictly supplied entanglement rate. Encoders may be arbitrary joint quantum operations, and decoding may be collective. The classical capacity is \[ C(E,P)=\max_{\substack{U\ge V\;\mathrm{physical}\\ \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(GU)\le E,\;S_G(V)\le P}}\bigl[S_G(\Phi U)+S_G(V)-S_G(\Phi^c V)\bigr]. \] Here \(V\) is a Gaussian seed covariance, \(U\) is the average-input covariance, and \(U-V\) is the displacement-modulation covariance. A covariance is physical when \(V+i\Omega/2\ge0\), where \(\Omega\) is the canonical commutation matrix and the vacuum covariance is \(I/2\). The notation \(S_G\) denotes Gaussian von Neumann entropy, and \(\Phi^c\) is the full complementary channel, including any environment purification. All logarithms are natural, so rates are in nats per channel use. This formula replaces optimization over arbitrary quantum block codes by a finite-dimensional covariance optimization. It supplies both an achievable rate and a converse against non-Gaussian, correlated encodings. At \(P=0\), it also determines the unassisted capacity of general fixed finite-mode Gaussian channels, including channels without a passive decomposition into independent modes. The reduction specifies the exact capacity value; it does not require a closed-form optimizer for every device. Energy and strict entanglement supply respond differently to errors For a fixed allowed average error \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), the exact capacity under the mean-energy constraint is \[ C_\varepsilon(E,P)=C\!\left(E_0+\frac{E-E_0}{1-\varepsilon},\,P\right). \] Allowing failure rescales the mean energy above the ground state, but leaves the strict initial entanglement budget unchanged. The proof uses an exponential strong converse for codes whose inputs obey a hard total-energy cutoff. In a different model, where a readable flag permits random entanglement supply constrained only on average, the work establishes an achievable bound and a strict small-supply advantage for thermal attenuation at positive energy and fixed nonzero error. That comparison identifies the operational importance of the supply rule; it is not a complete capacity characterization of the flagged model. The communication value of entanglement For a thermal attenuator, let \(0<\eta<1\) be the transmissivity, \(b>0\) the output mean photon number for vacuum input, and \(N\) the input mean photon number. Write its capacity as \(C_N(P)\), and define \(g(N)=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N\). The gain from entanglement obeys the sharp bound \[ 0\le C_N(P)-C_N(0)\le\frac{\eta}{1+b}\,P. \] For every fixed \(N>0\), the coefficient \(\eta/(1+b)\) is attained as the initial right derivative at \(P=0\). In the low-photon limit, the stronger resource law is \[ C_N(P)-C_N(0)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}\min\{P,g(N)\}+O(N),\qquad N\downarrow0. \] The remainder is uniform over \(P\ge0\) at fixed \(\eta\) and positive \(b\). Noise therefore determines the conversion efficiency, while \(g(N)\sim N\log(1/N)\) sets the entanglement scale

summary: This replication package contains the data, analysis code, and documentation accompanying “Impact Pathways of a Jurisdictional Approach to Slowing Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon” by Jill L. Caviglia-Harris, Thales A. P. West, Daniel W. Harris, Erin O. Sills, and Katrina Mullan. The study evaluates the effects of Brazil’s Priority List on deforestation across 772 municipalities in the nine states of the Brazilian Legal Amazon from 2000 to 2024. The analyses examine overall policy effects, differences across land-tenure categories, and spillovers to neighboring municipalities. The accompanying README describes the package contents, software requirements, and instructions for reproducing the results.
tags: Brazilian Amazon; deforestation; Priority List; jurisdictional approaches; environmental policy; land tenure; policy evaluation; difference-in-differences; spatial spillovers; replication data and code.

summary: This record contains the pair-level summaries, model-level matrices and analysis scripts for the manuscript Static Embeddings Are Poor Cross-Architecture Proxies: A Metric-Sensitive Reassessment . The archive covers 231 static pairs from 22 language models, a 153-pair multi-family static-to-contextual set from 18 models (Qwen 7, Gemma 4, SmolLM 4, Phi 3), and 91 layer-wise pairs from 14 models. The balanced set is analyzed with angular and Euclidean RDMs; the angular metric is primary. The archive includes the 22 x 22 Mantel, CKA, distance-correlation and Gromov-Wasserstein matrices, the 13 x 13 legacy proxy matrices, the 14 x 14 layer-wise Mantel and Procrustes matrices, the 153-pair extension table, the crossed random-effects inputs and outputs, and the scripts that reproduce them. Raw model weights, token-level distance matrices and cached hidden states are not included. The Procrustes values are shared-token subspace statistics, not full-width alignment. The static and multi-family sets are Qwen-heavy; the manuscript reports family-specific correlations and does not claim a uniform within-family effect. Code is released under GPL-3.0-or-later. Data and derived tables are released under CC BY 4.0. See README.md and PROVENANCE.md for file mapping, reproduction instructions and caveats.
title: Code and derived data for: Static Embeddings Are Poor Cross-Architecture Proxies: A Contextual Reassessment

summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Here we provide the first systematic, scale-resolved quantification of Greenland Ice Sheet mass change structure recoverable from its SSH fingerprint when ice loss geometry varies. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.
title: Neural Operators Reveal Scale-Dependent Limits on Recovering Greenland Ice Loss from Sea Level Fingerprints

summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. summary: This release contains 345 computed metamer mismatch bodies with their defining inputs and validation records. It also contains the software that computes and validates them. A metamer mismatch body describes how objects that match in color under one illuminant can differ in color under another. The collection covers six observer models and 38 illuminant pairs, each pairing D65 with a second illuminant. The wavelength spacings are 1, 2, 5 and 10 nm. The target colors are defined by flat reflectances from 10% to 90%. The manifest lists the combinations included. Each dataset contains five files. One is a generators file that defines the color mechanisms and the target color. The others hold the boundary vertices, the triangular faces, a summary and a validation certificate. The vertices and faces are CSV files. The method computes the exact body for the discretized problem. Coordinates are stored as floating-point numbers. Reflectances are bounded between 0 and 1 without additional smoothness constraints. The software includes MATLAB and CUDA sources, CIE input tables and a Slurm workflow for running the computations on an HPC cluster. Documentation covers configuration, a small worked example and recovery from interrupted jobs. Validation records describe file integrity, volume consistency and reflectance feasibility checks. The manifest and certificates report the validation coverage and numerical tolerances for each dataset. README.md describes each file and its license.
title: Exact Discrete Metamer Mismatch Bodies from Zonotope Tiling

summary: AUTONOMOUS MICROROBOTIC NAVIGATION FOR AGING MICROENVIRONMENT MAPS AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Institute XXVI | Flagship 01 What if a mobile microscale instrument could choose where to measure an aging-associated tissue environment, yet remain honest about the regions it cannot reach and the biological changes it might cause while observing? This prospective English research monograph develops an evidence-constrained framework connecting externally actuated microrobotic navigation, spatial phenotypes of cellular aging, and information-theoretic active learning. Its central hypothesis is deliberately falsifiable: under matched sampling budgets and strict disturbance limits, a pre-registered active route must reduce reconstruction error in independently withheld regions compared with optimized fixed-grid, passive-imaging, and random-navigation methods. Attractive trajectories, single-marker fluorescence, and confident maps are not accepted as substitutes for valid biological ground truth. The work is organized around a five-layer scientific architecture: three-dimensional phantom truth, traceable robot localization, safety-constrained acquisition, biological noninterference, and blinded cross-batch or cross-laboratory transfer. It includes 30 domain-qualified mathematical derivations, 82 research chapters, 410 separately paginated studies, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence register makes explicit what external research supports and what remains untested. The accompanying Excel workbook connects Gates, equations, chapter pages, and evidence sources. The proposed studies are limited to engineered hydrogel phantoms and carefully bounded ex-vivo research. This book does not report newly conducted experiments, clinically approved autonomous nanorobots, human diagnosis, demonstrated rejuvenation, or lifespan extension. Its enduring aim is to leave future investigators a rigorous, revisable set of research questions, including the possibility that simpler instruments may prove scientifically superior. Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI White Rainbow Scientific Library | October 2026

summary: HHT is an open-source, local-first iOS application designed for personal mobility tracking and travel behavior research. It records location data in the background, reconstructs daily travel activities into visits, trips, transportation modes, and trip chains. It allows users to review and correct inferred travel records. The application supports exporting structured mobility datasets in CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, and SQLite formats, with a Python loader for further analysis. By combining automated GPS-based travel detection with user-controlled data management, HHT aims to lower the technical and financial barriers to collecting travel behavior data. Its broader vision is to provide researchers, educational institutions, and resource-constrained communities with an accessible and adaptable alternative to proprietary travel survey technologies, while preserving individual control over sensitive location information. Documentation: https://zhanchaoyang.com/HHT-app/docs/

summary: This dataset provides monthly global ocean mixed layer depth (MLD) estimates at 1° spatial resolution from January 1982 to December 2023, developed using SJTU-ViT, a Vision Transformer-based reconstruction model. It contains 504 monthly fields on a regular latitude–longitude grid, with valid coverage defined by a fixed RECCAP2 open-ocean mask. The target MLD is defined by a potential density increase of 0.03 kg m⁻³ relative to 10 m. MLD estimates are expressed in metres, positive downward from the sea surface, with a lower bound of 10 m. Data are provided in NetCDF-4 format, accompanied by a README describing the variables, coordinates, MLD definition, masking, and data access.
title: A monthly 1° global ocean mixed layer depth dataset for 1982–2023 developed with SJTU-ViT

summary: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. These limitations are especially critical in domains such as insurance, where KPIs, regulatory constraints, and legacy relational systems demand high precision. We introduce a multi-agent, persona-driven NL2SQL framework that combines (1) domain relevance detection, (2) schema-grounded knowledge construction, (3) KPI-aware SQL synthesis, (4) syntax-level self-repair using sqlite execution feedback, and (5) semantic consistency checking via SQL-to-NL reverse engineering. Our system significantly reduces query hallucination and improves semantic fidelity compared to direct LLM prompting. Evaluated on 60 queries (50 from a HuggingFace text-to-SQL dataset and 10 custom domain queries), the system achieves 90% correctness using Mistral across seven coordinated LLM calls showing that this approach can substantially increase the reliability of NL2SQL pipelines in high-stakes environments.
title: NL2SQL with Iterative Self-Refinement

summary: Code, independent checks and the record of the Anaxia engine for the paper Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic by Deep Bhattacharjee and Ushashi Bhattacharya. The paper determines, for the heterotic string with the standard embedding on the one-parameter family of quintic threefolds, which vibration modes become which families of charged particles. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. The invariant deformation pairs each family with exactly one partner, so that the mass matrix has determinant psi^70, full rank away from the Fermat point and rank 51 there, where the masses are given in closed form by the Gamma function. The Geometric Selection Conjecture is shown to be equivalent to the existence of one viable vacuum fixed by mirror symmetry, and no smooth quintic and no free quotient of one carries three families. The existence of a viable vacuum is open. The archive holds 64 independent checks: a C program for the labels, the couplings allowed by the group and the mass map, a C++ expansion of the Hessian over its 120 permutations, Python checks of the socle, the Hessian, the intersection form of the Fermat quintic and the Gamma values, a Julia check of the Hodge norms, a Macaulay2 computation of the Jacobian ring at two rational values of the modulus with the socle functional on all 3876 monomials of degree fifteen, and 11 Lean 4 theorems on the counts and the arithmetic of the Hessian, each axiom-free or depending on propext only. code/run_checks.sh runs them all. code/bllm/ holds the failure, change and retry record of the four targets on the Anaxia engine (release 3.0.5, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23469389).
title: Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic: code, checks and engine record

( #2937 ) Corrected the llm_provider module import in jury.py . ( #2869 ) Batch evaluation and core behavior Read batch column mappings from the original row and preserved results when output column names collide. ( #2845 , #2844 ) Kept BatchEvaluator independent of the optional feedback package. ( #2901 ) Treated missing DataFrame cells as None and preserved columns in empty batch DataFrames. ( #2942 , #2946 ) Preserved retrieval order in context_filter results. ( #2932 ) Added a warning when TruSession is re-created with different settings. ( #2944 ) Cost accounting and reporting Prevented nested cost scopes from leaking callbacks into their parent scope. ( #2872 ) Fixed double-counting of evaluation spend in eval_cost . ( #2873 ) OpenAI cost tracking now adds per-call token and cost deltas rather than cumulative totals. ( #2855 ) Google provider cost accounting now includes thinking tokens and can price responses without constructing a client. ( #2795 ) LangChain now maps role="system" messages to SystemMessage rather than AIMessage . ( #2859 ) Added Claude 5 model support to the Anthropic provider. summary: SSTIM Workbench , previously developed as BSC Lab, is the open reference environment for SSTIM , the Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary developed through the W3C Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary Community Group . It has two integrated layers: a precision multi-engine audiovisual stimulation application, and a knowledge layer over the SSTIM ontology. This release freezes SSTIM 0.20.0, published at https://w3id.org/sstim under CC BY 4.0: 18 modules holding 182 OWL classes and 371 properties labelled in English, and 645 SKOS concepts in English, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish, with SHACL validation shapes, four conformance profiles (Kernel, Core, Core Plus, Full), qualified evidence assessments, exposure and ecosystem term modules, and 110 verified external mappings to Wikidata, MeSH, UBERON and SNOMED CT alongside term reuse from BFO, COB, IAO, OBI, PROV-O and W3C ORG. Every mapping is dereferenced at the authority that mints its identifier and carries dated provenance and the reason for its predicate. The version IRI https://w3id.org/sstim/0.20.0 resolves to the frozen artifacts this archive contains. The archive is the whole repository at its release tag: the ontology sources and their frozen snapshot, the Svelte application (Graph Navigator, SPARQL interface, Patch Studio, four selectable audio engines), the validation and release tooling, and the documentation and architecture decision records. Its public reference data include nine published sensory stimulation protocols, from the 40 Hz auditory response of 1981 to a randomized home-use trial of 2022, each encoded from its paper, citing it, and asserting no effect. Licensing is per artifact class, and the three licences above are not alternatives. Each governs a different part of this archive: Apache-2.0 the software, build tooling and JSON contracts; CC BY 4.0 the ontology, vocabulary, public RDF data and documentation; CC0 1.0 the synthetic reference audio. A file carrying its own notice is governed by that notice, and LICENSING.md in the archive is the scope matrix. Scope. Sensory stimulation spans self-directed practice through regulated clinical intervention, and SSTIM describes that whole range: electroconvulsive therapy, interventional neurostimulation and preclinical study designs are published terms. The Workbench itself is general wellness software rather than a medical device, and carries no diagnostic or treatment claim; that is a statement about this implementation, not about the field. Community Group work is not a W3C Recommendation and is not W3C-endorsed technology. Ecosystem fixtures in the release are synthetic; real live-only agent records are kept outside this archive by design. The Workbench's stakeholder directory does list real companies, laboratories, people and projects of the field, each from a public source: it is a listing of relevance, not an agent record, and an entry removed on request is absent from later releases only. Each tagged release is archived here for citation.
title: SSTIM Workbench: Open Sensory Stimulation Platform and SSTIM Ontology

summary: This record contains the pair-level summaries, model-level matrices and analysis scripts for the manuscript Static Embeddings Are Poor Cross-Architecture Proxies: A Metric-Sensitive Reassessment . The archive covers 231 static pairs from 22 language models, a 153-pair multi-family static-to-contextual set from 18 models (Qwen 7, Gemma 4, SmolLM 4, Phi 3), and 91 layer-wise pairs from 14 models. The balanced set is analyzed with angular and Euclidean RDMs; the angular metric is primary. The archive includes the 22 x 22 Mantel, CKA, distance-correlation and Gromov-Wasserstein matrices, the 13 x 13 legacy proxy matrices, the 14 x 14 layer-wise Mantel and Procrustes matrices, the 153-pair extension table, the crossed random-effects inputs and outputs, and the scripts that reproduce them. Raw model weights, token-level distance matrices and cached hidden states are not included. The Procrustes values are shared-token subspace statistics, not full-width alignment. The static and multi-family sets are Qwen-heavy; the manuscript reports family-specific correlations and does not claim a uniform within-family effect. Code is released under GPL-3.0-or-later. Data and derived tables are released under CC BY 4.0. See README.md and PROVENANCE.md for file mapping, reproduction instructions and caveats.
title: Code and derived data for: Static Embeddings Are Poor Cross-Architecture Proxies: A Contextual Reassessment

summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Here we provide the first systematic, scale-resolved quantification of Greenland Ice Sheet mass change structure recoverable from its SSH fingerprint when ice loss geometry varies. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.
title: Neural Operators Reveal Scale-Dependent Limits on Recovering Greenland Ice Loss from Sea Level Fingerprints

summary: This release contains 345 computed metamer mismatch bodies with their defining inputs and validation records. It also contains the software that computes and validates them. A metamer mismatch body describes how objects that match in color under one illuminant can differ in color under another. The collection covers six observer models and 38 illuminant pairs, each pairing D65 with a second illuminant. The wavelength spacings are 1, 2, 5 and 10 nm. The target colors are defined by flat reflectances from 10% to 90%. The manifest lists the combinations included. Each dataset contains five files. One is a generators file that defines the color mechanisms and the target color. The others hold the boundary vertices, the triangular faces, a summary and a validation certificate. The vertices and faces are CSV files. The method computes the exact body for the discretized problem. Coordinates are stored as floating-point numbers. Reflectances are bounded between 0 and 1 without additional smoothness constraints. The software includes MATLAB and CUDA sources, CIE input tables and a Slurm workflow for running the computations on an HPC cluster. Documentation covers configuration, a small worked example and recovery from interrupted jobs. Validation records describe file integrity, volume consistency and reflectance feasibility checks. The manifest and certificates report the validation coverage and numerical tolerances for each dataset. README.md describes each file and its license.
title: Exact Discrete Metamer Mismatch Bodies from Zonotope Tiling

summary: AUTONOMOUS MICROROBOTIC NAVIGATION FOR AGING MICROENVIRONMENT MAPS AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Institute XXVI | Flagship 01 What if a mobile microscale instrument could choose where to measure an aging-associated tissue environment, yet remain honest about the regions it cannot reach and the biological changes it might cause while observing? This prospective English research monograph develops an evidence-constrained framework connecting externally actuated microrobotic navigation, spatial phenotypes of cellular aging, and information-theoretic active learning. Its central hypothesis is deliberately falsifiable: under matched sampling budgets and strict disturbance limits, a pre-registered active route must reduce reconstruction error in independently withheld regions compared with optimized fixed-grid, passive-imaging, and random-navigation methods. Attractive trajectories, single-marker fluorescence, and confident maps are not accepted as substitutes for valid biological ground truth. The work is organized around a five-layer scientific architecture: three-dimensional phantom truth, traceable robot localization, safety-constrained acquisition, biological noninterference, and blinded cross-batch or cross-laboratory transfer. It includes 30 domain-qualified mathematical derivations, 82 research chapters, 410 separately paginated studies, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence register makes explicit what external research supports and what remains untested. The accompanying Excel workbook connects Gates, equations, chapter pages, and evidence sources. The proposed studies are limited to engineered hydrogel phantoms and carefully bounded ex-vivo research. This book does not report newly conducted experiments, clinically approved autonomous nanorobots, human diagnosis, demonstrated rejuvenation, or lifespan extension. Its enduring aim is to leave future investigators a rigorous, revisable set of research questions, including the possibility that simpler instruments may prove scientifically superior. Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI White Rainbow Scientific Library | October 2026

summary: HHT is an open-source, local-first iOS application designed for personal mobility tracking and travel behavior research. It records location data in the background, reconstructs daily travel activities into visits, trips, transportation modes, and trip chains. It allows users to review and correct inferred travel records. The application supports exporting structured mobility datasets in CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, and SQLite formats, with a Python loader for further analysis. By combining automated GPS-based travel detection with user-controlled data management, HHT aims to lower the technical and financial barriers to collecting travel behavior data. Its broader vision is to provide researchers, educational institutions, and resource-constrained communities with an accessible and adaptable alternative to proprietary travel survey technologies, while preserving individual control over sensitive location information. Documentation: https://zhanchaoyang.com/HHT-app/docs/
title: HHT: An Open-Source, Privacy-First Travel Diary for Mobility Research

summary: This dataset provides monthly global ocean mixed layer depth (MLD) estimates at 1° spatial resolution from January 1982 to December 2023, developed using SJTU-ViT, a Vision Transformer-based reconstruction model. It contains 504 monthly fields on a regular latitude–longitude grid, with valid coverage defined by a fixed RECCAP2 open-ocean mask. The target MLD is defined by a potential density increase of 0.03 kg m⁻³ relative to 10 m. MLD estimates are expressed in metres, positive downward from the sea surface, with a lower bound of 10 m. Data are provided in NetCDF-4 format, accompanied by a README describing the variables, coordinates, MLD definition, masking, and data access.
title: A monthly 1° global ocean mixed layer depth dataset for 1982–2023 developed with SJTU-ViT

summary: Assembly traces can support explicit probabilistic inference without being treated as recovered program meaning. Active Assembly Theory and Practice makes that distinction executable: transparent x86-64 fixtures are decoded with Capstone, traced under bounded Unicorn emulation, and mapped to typed observations that distinguish missing, unseen, and unsupported evidence. Two Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) specifications define passive-phase and prospective sensor models whose tensors drive real pymdp execution. A native categorical Julia/RxInfer companion consumes the passive model's same parameters (Friedman 2026; Heins et al. 2022; Bagaev et al. 2023). The sensor Agent selects an action before fixture evidence is acquired. Independent finite calculations check beliefs and policy scores; native smoothing uses the same parameters and first-observation convention. Every inference comparator and fitted diagnostic also consumes an upstream-parsed numeric GNN specification, with source-bound runtime instances and rendered model graphs. A corpus of 10 authored fixtures supports complete-fixture exclusion diagnostics. At the fixed informative likelihood, the memoryless decoder outperforms the temporal filter; temporal advantages appear under synthetic observation ambiguity. Designed category ambiguity remains a visible failure case. The separate Gaussian and categorical Bethe free-energy diagnostics are not compared numerically with policy expected free energy. The quotient benchmark contains 64 transformation-family identifiers and 4096 rows, with 16 families held out from model fitting. The co-primary portfolio includes an interpretable classifier, a temporal probabilistic model, a fixed one-layer tanh recurrent classifier, and surface baselines; the temporal endpoint reaches balanced accuracy 0.775 and macro-F1 0.772 on this frozen bounded benchmark. Held-out identifiers share authored template lineages with the fitting data. Family-resampling intervals and conditional randomization diagnostics therefore describe this finite inventory; the retrospective protocol correction withholds superiority claims. A complementary pinned static-only corpus supplies 5 licensed source projects and 100 source-contract rows, including 40 lexical witnesses, 40 contract-directed near misses, and 20 identity controls. The corpus establishes provenance and coverage; it does not execute arbitrary external binaries or support application-effectiveness claims. Selected normalized machine-state relations are checked by Python, native execution, and a bounded Lean fragment. Exact finite sensing certificates and source-bound reader artifacts make assumptions and failures inspectable. Independent physical replication remains unearned. The contribution is a reproducible substrate for testing assembly-to-inference mechanisms, with explicit limits on semantics, statistical generalization, and external validity.
title: Active Assembly Theory and Practice

Two Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) specifications define passive-phase and prospective sensor models whose tensors drive real pymdp execution. A native categorical Julia/RxInfer companion consumes the passive model's same parameters (Friedman 2026; Heins et al. 2022; Bagaev et al. 2023). The sensor Agent selects an action before fixture evidence is acquired. Independent finite calculations check beliefs and policy scores; native smoothing uses the same parameters and first-observation convention. Every inference comparator and fitted diagnostic also consumes an upstream-parsed numeric GNN specification, with source-bound runtime instances and rendered model graphs. A corpus of 10 authored fixtures supports complete-fixture exclusion diagnostics. At the fixed informative likelihood, the memoryless decoder outperforms the temporal filter; temporal advantages appear under synthetic observation ambiguity. Designed category ambiguity remains a visible failure case. The separate Gaussian and categorical Bethe free-energy diagnostics are not compared numerically with policy expected free energy. The quotient benchmark contains 64 transformation-family identifiers and 4096 rows, with 16 families held out from model fitting. The co-primary portfolio includes an interpretable classifier, a temporal probabilistic model, a fixed one-layer tanh recurrent classifier, and surface baselines; the temporal endpoint reaches balanced accuracy 0.775 and macro-F1 0.772 on this frozen bounded benchmark. Held-out identifiers share authored template lineages with the fitting data. Family-resampling intervals and conditional randomization diagnostics therefore describe this finite inventory; the retrospective protocol correction withholds superiority claims. A complementary pinned static-only corpus supplies 5 licensed source projects and 100 source-contract rows, including 40 lexical witnesses, 40 contract-directed near misses, and 20 identity controls. The corpus establishes provenance and coverage; it does not execute arbitrary external binaries or support application-effectiveness claims. Selected normalized machine-state relations are checked by Python, native execution, and a bounded Lean fragment. Exact finite sensing certificates and source-bound reader artifacts make assumptions and failures inspectable. Independent physical replication remains unearned. The contribution is a reproducible substrate for testing assembly-to-inference mechanisms, with explicit limits on semantics, statistical generalization, and external validity.

summary: Modeling-ready feature matrices and machine-readable results of the corrected modeling campaign (v3) reported in the article "Protocol-Induced Optimism and Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Failure in Feature-Based Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction" (Energies, submitted). Seven public lithium-ion aging datasets (CALCE, HUST, MATR, NASA randomized usage, Oxford, NASA PCoE, XJTU), charge and discharge phases, remaining useful life to 80% of the estimated initial capacity (threshold arm at 85%). This version supersedes 1.0.x. The matrices of version 1.0.x contained five capacity-trend descriptors computed over each cell's whole trajectory (temporal leakage) and voltage-capacity curve features for the MATR domain only; results derived from them are not the ones reported in the article. Files: modeling_ready_t80.tar and modeling_ready_t85.tar (feature matrix, target and identifiers per phase at the 80% and 85% thresholds); features_causal.tar (per-dataset feature parquets with history-only trend descriptors and the v3 targets); campanha_v3_results.zip (metrics of all 5,976 fits of the core matrix, the threshold arm, the 20 repeated partitions and the nested source-only selection; permutation importance; learning curves; aggregated tables; integrity gates; logs; per-cell target audit; checksums; frozen environment); supplementary_data_S1-S7.zip (Supplementary Data S1 to S7 of the article as consolidated CSV files, with a column dictionary in the README). SHA256 of every parquet in RELEASE_CHECKSUMS.json and of the three archives in MATRICES_sha256.txt; the companion code record (campanha_v3 1.1.0) verifies them and regenerates the tables. The raw datasets are not redistributed; see the article for sources and licenses. Predictions and model binaries were not saved.

summary: Source code of the article "Protocol-Induced Optimism and Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Failure in Feature-Based Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction" (Energies, submitted). Version 1.1.0 keeps the feature-extraction pipeline of version 1.0.x and adds campanha_v3-1.1.0.zip, the package that produced every result reported in the article. campanha_v3 is an auditable re-run of the modeling campaign: the v1.0.x modeling sources exactly as they ran (pristine/, SHA256), one script per correction with its unified diff (patches/), the patched sources (patched/), new modules for target re-join with history-only trend descriptors, causality and coverage gates, preflight, nested source-only selection, aggregation and release verification (new/), synthetic-data tests with a CI workflow (tests/), the ordered pipeline with gates (scripts/), and docs/ with the change log (file and line references), the SHA256 of the archived feature matrices and result tables (RELEASE_CHECKSUMS.json) and the frozen HPC environment (pip_freeze.txt; Python 3.13, scikit-learn 1.9.0). Defects removed relative to 1.0.x: whole-trajectory capacity-trend descriptors used as features (temporal leakage), deny-list feature selection, per-cell curve validity flags in the matrix, unaudited right-censoring, hard-coded end-of-life threshold and permanence, duplicate feature configurations, untruncated negative predictions, shared seed for partition and estimators, fixed ElasticNet, and a source-only selection that used target-trained models. Details in docs/CHANGELOG.md. The feature matrices and the results are in the companion data record. "bash scripts/verify_release.sh" recomputes the checksums, counts the fits (2,520 core, 360 threshold arm, 1,920 repeated partitions, 1,176 nested selection) and regenerates the manuscript tables from the archived metrics.

summary: Code, independent checks and the record of the Anaxia engine for the paper Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic by Deep Bhattacharjee and Ushashi Bhattacharya. The paper determines, for the heterotic string with the standard embedding on the one-parameter family of quintic threefolds, which vibration modes become which families of charged particles. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. The invariant deformation pairs each family with exactly one partner, so that the mass matrix has determinant psi^70, full rank away from the Fermat point and rank 51 there, where the masses are given in closed form by the Gamma function. The Geometric Selection Conjecture is shown to be equivalent to the existence of one viable vacuum fixed by mirror symmetry, and no smooth quintic and no free quotient of one carries three families. On the three other one-parameter pencils of Fermat type, the sextic in P(1,1,1,1,2), the octic in P(1,1,1,1,4) and the dectic in P(1,1,1,2,5), the 103, 149 and 145 families carry only 96, 122 and 100 distinct characters of symmetry groups of order 108, 128 and 100; every coupling allowed by the symmetry is psi^r times a product of weights; the mass map of the invariant direction has rank 99, 125 and 109 at every member with psi nonzero, so 4, 24 and 36 families stay massless; and no member or free quotient carries three families. The existence of a viable vacuum is open. The archive holds 121 independent checks: a C program for the labels, the couplings allowed by the group and the mass map, a C++ expansion of the Hessian over its 120 permutations, Python checks of the socle, the Hessian, the intersection form of the Fermat quintic and the Gamma values, a Julia check of the Hodge norms, a Macaulay2 computation of the Jacobian ring at two rational values of the modulus with the socle functional on all 3876 monomials of degree fifteen, Python and Macaulay2 checks of the labels, characters, couplings, Jacobian rings and mass maps of the three weighted pencils, and 14 Lean 4 theorems on the counts, the arithmetic of the Hessian and the numbers of the weighted pencils, each axiom-free or depending on propext only. code/run_checks.sh runs them all. code/bllm/ holds the failure, change and retry record of the five targets on the Anaxia engine (release 3.1.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23484160).

summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.

summary: This archive accompanies the article "A Reproducible Webots-Based Benchmarking Framework for UAV Mobility Modeling: Comparative Evaluation of Random Waypoint and Gauss-Markov Trajectories in Urban and Open-Terrain Environments" (Journal of Engineering, University of Baghdad). It contains everything needed to recompute every table and figure of the article from the recorded runs and to re-run any single simulation: - the Webots R2025a worlds (Open Terrain, and Urban with 50 buildings), with the building layout file; - the Python controller, which uses a cascaded PID flight controller with noisy GPS and gyro; - the Random Waypoint and Gauss–Markov reference generators; - the batch runner; - the analysis code (metrics, air-to-ground channel model, paired statistics with Holm correction) and its unit tests; - the 10 Hz logs and metadata of all 450 runs: 120 main runs (2 environments × 2 mobility models × 30 seeds), 210 runs of a memory-coefficient (α) sweep, and 120 ablation runs. A SHA-256 manifest lists every file. See README.md for the folder structure and for how to reproduce the results.
title: UAV mobility benchmark in Webots (Random Waypoint vs Gauss–Markov): code, worlds and logs of 450 simulation runs

summary: This reproducibility release accompanies the revised manuscript, Benchmark Integrity in Three COVID-19 and Mpox Misinformation Datasets: Duplicate Overlap, Cross-Dataset Contamination and Exploratory Label-Quality Signals . The archive provides Python implementations and analytical outputs for evaluating exact and near-duplicate content, evaluation-partition overlap, cross-corpus textual contamination, cross-dataset classification transfer, repeated-seed cross-validation and exploratory out-of-fold label-quality indicators across COVID-19-FNIR, Constraint and an mpox veracity-based analytic subset. The revised release includes five-seed model evaluation, bootstrap uncertainty estimation and a 2,000-replicate group-aware bootstrap analysis that accounts for observations sharing identical normalised texts. The archive also contains saved predictions, machine-readable statistical results, figure files, software requirements and instructions for reproducing the analyses. Original third-party datasets are not redistributed. Data-source information and input-file checksums are provided to support independent verification.

Source data were retrieved through FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) on 30 September and 2 October 2026; users should verify against the World Bank GFDD and IMF FAS files directly.

summary: Julia code, data and result records for the article 'Sparse temporal counterfactual explanations for mixed-integer planning: recourse duality, complexity and stability'. The code computes counterfactual explanations by cost constraint generation (CCG), with dual cuts for editable recourse costs, capacity menus, period budgets and a fixed-witness stability radius, and verifies every explanation independently. The artifact holds the records of all studies: the primary study (320 runs), the external comparison (168 runs), Study 1 (256 attempts), Study 2 (1216 records), Study 3 on recourse levers (40 enumeration cases and 210 runs) and Study 4 on unit commitment (140 enumeration cases and 160 runs). The code is under the MIT license and the public input data keep their own licenses (CC BY 4.0 or Open Government Licence).
title: XOPT v1.0.1: Research Artifact — Code, Data, and Experiments

summary: R package that fits phylogenetic comparative models for continuous traits as Gaussian processes on a tree. Models are built by combining kernels (Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda, kappa and delta, early burst, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, relaxed rates, rate through time, distance-based and user-defined branch-wise kernels); the package writes and fits the corresponding Stan program, with linear-time likelihoods, leave-one-out and leave-clade-out cross-validation, prediction and ancestral-state reconstruction for branch-wise kernels, and tools to check kernel validity and equivalence.
title: phylogp: Phylogenetic Comparative Models as Gaussian Processes

summary: PRISM is a computational framework for predicting peptide cleavage activity across matrix metalloproteinases and generating candidate peptides conditioned on activity profiles, with a focus on MMP13. This archive contains source code, training and evaluation scripts, predictor and generator checkpoints for three training seeds, benchmark training, validation and test data, labelled OOD data, and generator fitting data, preference pairs and conditioning profiles. Installation and usage instructions are provided in README.md. This record archives ExplosionW/PRISM at commit 214b0b03eea7a0697cd0f226ba3d94b77a58b63f. The development repository is https://github.com/ExplosionW/PRISM. The MIT license applies to PRISM’s own code. Reused datasets retain their original licensing terms.
title: PRISM: Peptide Regression and Inverse design for Selective Metalloproteinase substrates

summary: We study Independent Component Analysis (ICA) mixture models. These models consist of mixtures of ICA densities. An ICA density is associated with a random vector whose coordinates become mutually independent after an invertible linear transformation. ICA mixture models are nonparametric extensions of the celebrated family of Gaussian mixtures. We show that in many cases the ICA mixtures are identifiable from the collection of the observed moment tensors, that is, the mixing coefficients, linear transformations, and source moments of order up to $d$ can be identified from the moment tensors of order up to $d$ for generic parameters. We address the problem by studying the corresponding secant varieties and their algebraic properties such as dimensions and Gauss maps. In particular, for $n$-variate distributions, we establish that generically and up to the trivial scaling and permutation symmetries, when $d\geq 5$, the parameters can be recovered uniquely for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ mixture components. For $d=3,4$, we show identifiability up to a finite equivalence class for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ and $0.5 n^{d-2}/d!$ components respectively, where for $d=4$ the mixing coefficients need to be known a priori. The obtained bounds on the component numbers have the maximum possible orders in $n$, and for $d = 3$ and $d\geq 5$, they are also asymptotically sharp.
title: Identifiability from Moments in Independent Component Analysis Mixture Models

summary: Cross-Lingual Jailbreak Evaluation — Final Thesis Data and Outputs This archive accompanies the master's thesis Multilingual Jailbreaks in Language-Specific Large Language Models (Gabriel de Jesus Coelho da Silva; advisor Carlos Becker Westphall; Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, 2026). It contains the study's frozen source-run files and the final thesis analysis release. The source-run files remain unchanged. The study evaluates eight instruction-tuned assistants in four language-matched pairs aligned with Portuguese, Italian, Swedish, and Bulgarian, plus a separate English reference model. StrongREJECT harmful prompts were translated into thirteen attack languages with NLLB-200, submitted to the models, and scored using the official StrongREJECT evaluator after response back-translation where applicable. The analysis combines URIEL+ featural angular distance, BELEBELE-derived IF/CONS/SPEC, and tokenizer diagnostics. The final behavioral results report the graded StrongREJECT score. The choice of this graded outcome and its fractional-logit GEE analysis followed inspection of results and was not pre-specified. Historical binary outputs remain available as provenance, not as the reported thesis results. title: Board-power telemetry logs and per-operation energy statistics for neural-network energy estimation

summary: We present a geometric foundation for gravity based on a microscopic solid-angle postulate. Each mass element is assumed to exert a gravitational influence on a test mass proportional to the solid angle that the test mass subtends as seen from the element's location. For a spherically symmetric source, direct integration yields the inverse-square law without assuming Newtonian gravity---the $1/r^{2}$ behavior emerges purely from geometric dilution. Calibration with Newton's constant gives the Newtonian potential $U(r) = -GMm/r$. Combining this potential with special-relativistic energy conservation in the source rest frame leads to the exact escape velocity \[ v_{\text{esc}}(r)=c\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\bigl(1+GM/(c^{2}r)\bigr)^{2}}}. \] The postulate is then extended to a fully covariant, causally consistent formulation in Minkowski spacetime. Using retarded interactions, we obtain for moving point masses the gravitational analogue of the Liénard--Wiechert potential, confirming that the theory respects Lorentz covariance and finite propagation speed $c$. The resulting scalar theory is formulated entirely in flat spacetime, matches Newtonian gravity in weak fields, and differs from general relativity at order $(GM/c^{2}r)^{2}$ and higher.
tags: solid-angle postulate; scalar gravity; escape velocity; covariant formulation; flat spacetime; inverse-square law; Liénard-Wiechert potential
title: A Solid-Angle Postulate as a Geometric Foundation for Gravity: Escape Velocity and Covariant Formulation in Flat Spacetime

summary: AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.
title: OfficeTown: Generative Organizations for Evolving Agent Intelligence

summary: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. These limitations are especially critical in domains such as insurance, where KPIs, regulatory constraints, and legacy relational systems demand high precision. We introduce a multi-agent, persona-driven NL2SQL framework that combines (1) domain relevance detection, (2) schema-grounded knowledge construction, (3) KPI-aware SQL synthesis, (4) syntax-level self-repair using sqlite execution feedback, and (5) semantic consistency checking via SQL-to-NL reverse engineering. Our system significantly reduces query hallucination and improves semantic fidelity compared to direct LLM prompting. Evaluated on 60 queries (50 from a HuggingFace text-to-SQL dataset and 10 custom domain queries), the system achieves 90% correctness using Mistral across seven coordinated LLM calls showing that this approach can substantially increase the reliability of NL2SQL pipelines in high-stakes environments.
title: NL2SQL with Iterative Self-Refinement

summary: Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) can improve spectrum efficiency and interference control in cognitive radio networks (CRNs) by reconfiguring the propagation environment. This paper presents FMASAC, a federated multi-agent soft actor-critic framework for IRS-assisted CRNs under partial observability, in which distributed secondary users (SUs) jointly select their transmit power and the phase shifts of an assigned subset of IRS elements using only local observations. Primary user (PU) protection is incorporated through an interference-penalized reward, and SUs coordinate by periodically averaging model parameters at a federated server, without exchanging raw observations, channel state information, or replay data. We formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, specify the local learning and aggregation procedure, and characterize its per-round communication cost. Illustrative performance trends contrast FMASAC with centralized SAC, independent SAC, IRS-fixed multi-agent reinforcement learning, and a heuristic CRN strategy. We also outline the simulation-based evaluation and the open challenges, namely constraint handling, agent heterogeneity, and scalability, that are needed to validate the framework.
title: Federated Multiagent Soft Actor Critic for IRS Assisted Cognitive Radio Networks under Partial Observability

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows

summary: Code, independent checks and the record of the Anaxia engine for the paper Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic by Deep Bhattacharjee and Ushashi Bhattacharya. The paper determines, for the heterotic string with the standard embedding on the one-parameter family of quintic threefolds, which vibration modes become which families of charged particles. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. The invariant deformation pairs each family with exactly one partner, so that the mass matrix has determinant psi^70, full rank away from the Fermat point and rank 51 there, where the masses are given in closed form by the Gamma function. The Geometric Selection Conjecture is shown to be equivalent to the existence of one viable vacuum fixed by mirror symmetry, and no smooth quintic and no free quotient of one carries three families. The existence of a viable vacuum is open. The archive holds 64 independent checks: a C program for the labels, the couplings allowed by the group and the mass map, a C++ expansion of the Hessian over its 120 permutations, Python checks of the socle, the Hessian, the intersection form of the Fermat quintic and the Gamma values, a Julia check of the Hodge norms, a Macaulay2 computation of the Jacobian ring at two rational values of the modulus with the socle functional on all 3876 monomials of degree fifteen, and 11 Lean 4 theorems on the counts and the arithmetic of the Hessian, each axiom-free or depending on propext only. code/run_checks.sh runs them all. code/bllm/ holds the failure, change and retry record of the four targets on the Anaxia engine (release 3.0.5, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23469389).
title: Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic: code, checks and engine record

summary: SSTIM Workbench , previously developed as BSC Lab, is the open reference environment for SSTIM , the Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary developed through the W3C Sensory Stimulation Vocabulary Community Group . It has two integrated layers: a precision multi-engine audiovisual stimulation application, and a knowledge layer over the SSTIM ontology. This release freezes SSTIM 0.20.0, published at https://w3id.org/sstim under CC BY 4.0: 18 modules holding 182 OWL classes and 371 properties labelled in English, and 645 SKOS concepts in English, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish, with SHACL validation shapes, four conformance profiles (Kernel, Core, Core Plus, Full), qualified evidence assessments, exposure and ecosystem term modules, and 110 verified external mappings to Wikidata, MeSH, UBERON and SNOMED CT alongside term reuse from BFO, COB, IAO, OBI, PROV-O and W3C ORG. Every mapping is dereferenced at the authority that mints its identifier and carries dated provenance and the reason for its predicate. The version IRI https://w3id.org/sstim/0.20.0 resolves to the frozen artifacts this archive contains. The archive is the whole repository at its release tag: the ontology sources and their frozen snapshot, the Svelte application (Graph Navigator, SPARQL interface, Patch Studio, four selectable audio engines), the validation and release tooling, and the documentation and architecture decision records. Its public reference data include nine published sensory stimulation protocols, from the 40 Hz auditory response of 1981 to a randomized home-use trial of 2022, each encoded from its paper, citing it, and asserting no effect. Licensing is per artifact class, and the three licences above are not alternatives. Each governs a different part of this archive: Apache-2.0 the software, build tooling and JSON contracts; CC BY 4.0 the ontology, vocabulary, public RDF data and documentation; CC0 1.0 the synthetic reference audio. A file carrying its own notice is governed by that notice, and LICENSING.md in the archive is the scope matrix. Scope. Sensory stimulation spans self-directed practice through regulated clinical intervention, and SSTIM describes that whole range: electroconvulsive therapy, interventional neurostimulation and preclinical study designs are published terms. The Workbench itself is general wellness software rather than a medical device, and carries no diagnostic or treatment claim; that is a statement about this implementation, not about the field. Community Group work is not a W3C Recommendation and is not W3C-endorsed technology. Ecosystem fixtures in the release are synthetic; real live-only agent records are kept outside this archive by design. The Workbench's stakeholder directory does list real companies, laboratories, people and projects of the field, each from a public source: it is a listing of relevance, not an agent record, and an entry removed on request is absent from later releases only. Each tagged release is archived here for citation.
title: SSTIM Workbench: Open Sensory Stimulation Platform and SSTIM Ontology

summary: How much classical information can a noisy optical channel carry when both signal energy and preshared entanglement are limited? This work gives an exact capacity frontier for this joint resource problem. It allows one to determine the best asymptotic communication rate, price the benefit of additional entanglement, and distinguish the effect of tolerating errors from that of changing how entanglement is supplied. Exact capacity under two resource constraints The setting is any fixed bosonic Gaussian channel \(\Phi\) with finitely many input and output modes. Signal energy is measured by a positive quadratic Hamiltonian \(H_G=\tfrac12 R^{\mathsf T}GR\), with \(G>0\) and ground energy \(E_0\); \(R\) collects the canonical quadratures. The budgets satisfy \(E\ge E_0\) and \(P\ge0\). For an \(n\)-use code, the mean total signal energy is at most \(nE\), while the same initially shared maximally entangled state has Schmidt rank \(K_n\) satisfying \(\log K_n\le nP\). Thus \(P\) is a strictly supplied entanglement rate. Encoders may be arbitrary joint quantum operations, and decoding may be collective. The classical capacity is \[ C(E,P)=\max_{\substack{U\ge V\;\mathrm{physical}\\ \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(GU)\le E,\;S_G(V)\le P}}\bigl[S_G(\Phi U)+S_G(V)-S_G(\Phi^c V)\bigr]. \] Here \(V\) is a Gaussian seed covariance, \(U\) is the average-input covariance, and \(U-V\) is the displacement-modulation covariance. A covariance is physical when \(V+i\Omega/2\ge0\), where \(\Omega\) is the canonical commutation matrix and the vacuum covariance is \(I/2\). The notation \(S_G\) denotes Gaussian von Neumann entropy, and \(\Phi^c\) is the full complementary channel, including any environment purification. All logarithms are natural, so rates are in nats per channel use. This formula replaces optimization over arbitrary quantum block codes by a finite-dimensional covariance optimization. It supplies both an achievable rate and a converse against non-Gaussian, correlated encodings. At \(P=0\), it also determines the unassisted capacity of general fixed finite-mode Gaussian channels, including channels without a passive decomposition into independent modes. The reduction specifies the exact capacity value; it does not require a closed-form optimizer for every device. Energy and strict entanglement supply respond differently to errors For a fixed allowed average error \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), the exact capacity under the mean-energy constraint is \[ C_\varepsilon(E,P)=C\!\left(E_0+\frac{E-E_0}{1-\varepsilon},\,P\right). \] Allowing failure rescales the mean energy above the ground state, but leaves the strict initial entanglement budget unchanged. The proof uses an exponential strong converse for codes whose inputs obey a hard total-energy cutoff. In a different model, where a readable flag permits random entanglement supply constrained only on average, the work establishes an achievable bound and a strict small-supply advantage for thermal attenuation at positive energy and fixed nonzero error. That comparison identifies the operational importance of the supply rule; it is not a complete capacity characterization of the flagged model. The communication value of entanglement For a thermal attenuator, let \(0<\eta<1\) be the transmissivity, \(b>0\) the output mean photon number for vacuum input, and \(N\) the input mean photon number. Write its capacity as \(C_N(P)\), and define \(g(N)=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N\). The gain from entanglement obeys the sharp bound \[ 0\le C_N(P)-C_N(0)\le\frac{\eta}{1+b}\,P. \] For every fixed \(N>0\), the coefficient \(\eta/(1+b)\) is attained as the initial right derivative at \(P=0\). In the low-photon limit, the stronger resource law is \[ C_N(P)-C_N(0)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}\min\{P,g(N)\}+O(N),\qquad N\downarrow0. \] The remainder is uniform over \(P\ge0\) at fixed \(\eta\) and positive \(b\). Noise therefore determines the conversion efficiency, while \(g(N)\sim N\log(1/N)\) sets the entanglement scale
title: A universal energy–entanglement capacity frontier for Gaussian optical channels

summary: This replication package contains the data, analysis code, and documentation accompanying “Impact Pathways of a Jurisdictional Approach to Slowing Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon” by Jill L. Caviglia-Harris, Thales A. P. West, Daniel W. Harris, Erin O. Sills, and Katrina Mullan.
