summary: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts

summary: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.
title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning

summary: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving

summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained through multi-stage pipelines over heterogeneous data sources, yet developers lack a principled way to pinpoint the specific data responsible for an observed behavior. This lack of observability reduces debugging to reactive patching and makes failures prone to recur under distribution shift or subsequent model updates. To address this limitation, we propose DebugLM, a framework that equips LLMs with built-in data provenance, enabling them to explicitly trace the origins of their behaviors to specific training data sources. Specifically, the model learns to associate its responses with unique provenance tags that indicate the responsible dataset, empowering developers to precisely identify where undesirable behaviors are learned. Building on this capability, DebugLM further supports targeted test-time remediation, enabling developers to selectively trigger targeted refusal for specified data sources without retraining or modifying model parameters. Experiments demonstrate that DebugLM provides accurate behavior tracing in multi-stage training pipelines and effective test-time remediation while preserving the general utility of the model.
title: DebugLM: Learning Traceable Training Data Provenance for LLMs

summary: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt

summary: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.
title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction

summary: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.
title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering

summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

summary: Against Its Own Reverse One comparison of each binary word with its reverse builds the ring’s address, its sphere and its waveform   Driven by Dean A. Kulik October 2026   Status words. A bracket after a statement records how it stands. proved : proved in this paper. STANDS : established earlier in the series or in the literature. RUNS : an exact computation landed where the route put it, with its scope stated; every one is rerun by the scripts of Appendix B. SEALED : the prediction was written and its text hashed (SHA-256) before the computation that tests it was run; the texts and digests are in Appendix A. DEAD END : the computation ran and landed, and the landing belongs to something else, whose owner is named. OPEN : stated and not settled. PULL : an interpretive bridge, not a result. Work run in independent AI-assisted audits is marked independently . Abstract Compare every binary word with its own reverse. Write each mirrored pair of bits as a value beside a difference, the butterfly (u, u ⊕ v) taken across the mirror. The comparison is decided by the outermost pair that differs, and the Hamming weight is carried by the pairs that agree. This paper shows that the ring of all binary words is built from those two readers of one lifted word. The partner map reverses the difference half, or complements the value half when there is no difference. The address of a word is half of what lies below it plus half of the reversal pairs its own value separates, rank(p) = ½(p − π(p) + Δ(p)) + π c (p), where Δ(p) = #{x : x < p ≤ J(x)} has a closed digit form and grows by a borrow chain whose cell is the full adder’s carry with one input complemented; the first 64 bits of π land at 2,427,008,858,123,944,441 from one pass over the 32 bits of each half. The route that grows a word one bit at a time is the lift itself: its residual bits are the mirrored differences, innermost first. On the sphere of radius n and latitude z = wt − n/2, latitude reads only the agreeing pairs, so the poles belong to the palindromes and a word with k disagreeing pairs stays within |z| ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ − k + [n odd]/2; the partner is a reflection, and on palindromes a half-turn about the X-axis. On ring addresses the partner is the complement of the address, so the latitude splits into a Walsh-even body and a Walsh-odd palindrome carrier whose energy share is exactly 2 1−n/2 at even width. Pulled back, each reader is simple in its own coordinates and spread in the other’s: over the bits of a word the comparison needs 2(2 ⌊ n/2 ⌋ − 1) Walsh modes and the latitude n; over ring addresses the comparison is one address bit carrying 99.9% of its energy at n = 20, while the latitude fills 1,036,432 of 1,048,576 modes. The ring is the coordinate system of the comparison. How the paper runs The paper is written from its end. summary: Run records, logs, analyses and binding-event replica trajectories of the streptavidin : fibril ratio sweep simulated by Team Imperial College (iGEM 2026, Imperial College London) with HyFiP-LDF, our open-source coarse-grained HOOMD-blue 7.2.0 Langevin-dynamics model of a protein hydrogel (HET-s(218–289) amyloid fibrils end-labelled with maleimide–PEG–biotin linkers and crosslinked by streptavidin tetramers). The sweep covers six streptavidin : fibril ratios (1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 3) at three random seeds each, 105 ns per run at surrogate conditions (75 nm fibrils, ten times the wet-lab number density, friction scaled by 0.1, 300 nm periodic box), run on one NVIDIA RTX 5090. 13 of 18 runs finished; the configurations and partial logs of the 5 stopped runs are included. Also included are the 52 re-simulations of one binding event (restarted from saved frames with new random seeds at 2 ps resolution) used to study how a biotin finds a streptavidin pocket. For every run: the complete resolved configuration, a run manifest with software versions and every model parameter with its provenance and data-file hashes, the HOOMD energy and temperature log, and the network, thermodynamic and structural analyses. These are the data behind Figures 26–28 and Videos 4–5 of the Simulations page of our wiki. Software: https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/imperial-college/cg-langevin-simulation (Apache-2.0). Atomistic reference data: 10.5281/zenodo.23420371. See README.md inside the archive for the file layout, variables, units and methods.

summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.1 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.1' . The tutorial in German and English, the API guides, release notes and screenshot provenance are included with the source archive. Verification: 984 passing tests, 92.8% coverage, Ruff lint/format checks, warning-free Markdownlint, package metadata checks and fresh-environment installation tests under Python 3.11 and 3.13. Viewer checks include real optimization subprocesses and terminal restoration. These are code and packaging checks, not live-provider benchmarks. Versioning, license and citation Version 0.3.1 . summary: NOTE: 1. The R package to compute NPP from brGDGTs is available in https://github.com/MarcoVidalCordasco/envirolipids  2.  R_Code_and_Analysis_Guide.pdf facilitates navigation through the analytical workflow and helps identifying the code associated with each result presented in the study.  ## 📌 Overview This repository contains an R workflow for analysing branched GDGT (brGDGT) compounds and modelling **Net Primary Productivity (NPP)** using statistical and machine learning approaches. It also includes the full ecological modelling workflow to recosntruct herbivore biomass and carrying capacity of secondary consumers. There are two scripts: * Script_1 * Script_2 The Script_1 performs: * Exploratory data analysis * Statistical modelling (linear, quadratic, GAM) * Random Forest modelling with three validation strategies * Independent dataset validation * NPP reconstruction from Padul-15-05 core * Comparison with climate-derived NPP (Miami model) * Summed Probability Distribution (SPD) analysis for archaeological data * Correlation analysis * Summary statistics and plots The Script_2 performs: * Herbivore density estimations from primary productivity * Population structure modelling using survival curves * Biomass partitioning across body size classes * Secondary consumers carrying capacity calculations * Summary statistics and plots --- ## 📂 Data Requirements The Script_1 expects an Excel file: ``` Dataset_1.xlsx This contains: * A global dataset of present-day measured brGDGTs and associated climatic, edaphic and environmental variables * Areas with in-field NPP measurements * Climate conditions reconstructed in Padul * Archaeological sites, levels and dates for the summed probability distributions ``` The Script_2 expects two additional Excel files: ``` Dataset_2.xlsx This contains: * Herbivore traits (species, body mass, life history traits, etc.), * The wild mammal species list recovered in the region during the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene (including sites and references) * NPP values (actual and potential) obtained from Script_1 * Primary and secondary consumer biomass summaries ``` ``` Prey_preferences.xlsx This contains: * Predator diet composition and annual biomass requirements ``` ## 📦 R Packages A package to apply the random-forest NPP predictions from brGDGTs is under construction --- ## ⚠️ Notes * Ensure working directory is set correctly: ```r setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path)) ``` * All files available in this repository should be saved into the same folder/directory --- ## 📬 Contact # mav54#cam.ac.uk

summary: Example data to reproduce the BAGFOOT2 protocol and vignette: mouse liver ATAC-seq, Fed vs Fasted (3 replicates per condition, mm10). BAGFOOT2 predicts which transcription factors change their activity between two conditions from ATAC-seq data, by combining Tn5 bias-corrected footprint depth and flanking accessibility over archetype motif clusters, with a robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD) test. Files bam_merged.tar.gz: one merged, sorted and indexed BAM file per condition (fed, fasted) bam_replicates.tar.gz: one BAM file per replicate (fed_1-3, fasted_1-3), used for HOMER (large file) tag_directories.tar.gz: HOMER tag directories of the replicates (TD_fed_1 ... TD_fasted_3) macs2.tar.gz: MACS2 peak calls (narrowPeak) per condition bg_files_fed_fasted.tar.gz: BAGFOOT2 (v2.0.0) output for Fed vs Fasted (bagplot, D2 and FDR barplots, result table) The motif database files (mm10, hg38) are NOT in this record. They are downloaded automatically by BAGFOOT2 on first use, from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20782782 How to reproduce Install BAGFOOT2: conda create -n bagfoot2 -c goldsteinlab-tech -c conda-forge -c bioconda bagfoot2 Extract the archives into one project folder: fed_fasted/bam_merged/ (merged BAM files, replicate BAM files and tag directories) fed_fasted/macs2/ (peak files) Run: bagfoot2 -b fed_fasted/bam_merged/ -p fed_fasted/macs2/ -o bg_files_fed_fasted/ -c fed -t fasted -g mm10 --bam_suffix ".sorted.bam" --cores 4 Add --homer TRUE --homer_bin /path/to/homer/bin --reps_control 1,2,3 --reps_treatment 1,2,3 to include HOMER motif enrichment. Code: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 Documentation: https://goldsteinlab-tech.github.io/BAGFOOT2/ RELATED WORKS Is supplement to: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 (Software) References: 10.5281/zenodo.20782782 (Dataset, motif database)

summary: This repository contains the replication materials accompanying the research note Financial Pessimism and the Timing of Saving (Alexander Hansak, University of Graz, 2026). The archive includes the original Python analysis, an independent R implementation of the principal estimators and survey-design standard errors, supplementary empirical analyses, Julia preprocessing scripts, questionnaire documentation, and aggregate estimation results. The canonical Python replay and independent R implementation reproduce 21 reported coefficient and standard-error comparisons on identical model-ready samples. Additional analyses examine saving amounts, subsequent income and employment outcomes, and age heterogeneity. All nine supplementary verification stages passed. The additional empirical specifications have not been independently cross-implemented. The analysis uses the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and Understanding Society (UKHLS), distributed through UK Data Service study 6614 (DOI: 10.5255/UKDA-SN-6614-22). Licensed respondent-level data are not redistributed. Researchers wishing to reproduce the analysis must obtain authorized access to the original survey data. The archive provides source code, execution instructions, numerical verification reports, aggregate outputs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The empirical findings describe conditional associations rather than identified causal effects. Version: 1.1.0 (20 October 2026).

summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. summary: Where Yes and No Become Maybe The nested partner ring read as a folded square: a rolling stack, four providers, a straight-line gradient and a square-root address Driven by Dean A. Kulik  October 2026 Abstract The nested partner ring is Dean Kulik’s construction. Reverse a binary word, unless it is a palindrome, then complement it. Place the smaller member of every pair in ascending order on one half of a circle, set each partner directly opposite its word, and swap the two words that meet at the centre seam. The ring is never held. It is addressed. This paper holds the finished state first and reads everything back from it. Cut each word into its front half and its back half and plot it at the point whose coordinates are the front half and the reversed back half. Representatives fill the triangle above the diagonal of the unit square, partners fill its mirror image below, and palindromes sit on the diagonal, which is itself folded at its midpoint. The square is folded twice, and that double fold is the whole ring. Ten routes run back from the fold, and every one is an algorithm. The spreadsheet’s rolling columns are a two-provider stack, so the counter-clockwise column is the clockwise column three rounds later and the 8-bit cross pairs are the half turn. The ring is half built and half reflected, with a twist confined to its palindromic words. Every ring is the 2-bit ring used as a frame alphabet around the ring two lengths below: four providers, one of which is continuation, so continuation depth falls as 4^(-t) and averages 1/3. The representative density is the straight line 1-t, so a word of value t sits at angle t-t^2/2 plus a tent that is the fold of the diagonal. The seam is the apex where the density reaches zero. The complement branch compiles toward value 1/3 at angle 5/18. Rank and unrank need one quadratic, one integer square root and one bit-reversal count. The radial reader reads the digits of 1-√(1-2u) in the front half of every word. Merging each word with its partner leaves grey exactly where the two disagree: all of it at two bits, half of it in the limit, and all of it again on the diagonal and the anti-diagonal. Twenty-eight lines were sealed before their checks ran. Twenty-seven run as sealed. The twenty-eighth runs at every width except the degenerate width 1, where it lands elsewhere and is routed to its owner. Two claims from the previous session are withdrawn and routed. The open boundary is named in the ledger, Section 14. 1. The held state A word x of width L is an integer written most significant bit first. Write J for reversal and C for complement. The partner is P(x)={■(J(x),&J(x)≠x,@C(x),&J(x)=x.)┤ P is an involution with no fixed point: a palindrome is never its own complement and a non-palindrome is never its own reversal. This is the C1 axiom in its smallest form, since no word may hold its place without a partner to move to. The 2^L words fall into 2^(L-1) pairs. The representative of a pair is its smaller member. Representatives run in ascending order on positions 0 to M-1, with N=2^L and M=N/2. The partner of the representative at position i sits at N-1-i, and positions M-1 and M are swapped. The tape T_L is the ring read as L⋅2^L slices. The spreadsheet’s “sheet” reading, the circle read backwards with 0 and 1 swapped, is S_L=C(J(T_L )). At two bits the circle is T_2=00 10 01 11 and the sheet is S_2=00011011.   Figure 1. Rings 1 to 10, with radial thickness equal to word length and angle measured clockwise from the top. Left: light (1) and gaps (0). Right: every word merged with its facing partner, slice by slice, which leaves grey wherever the pair disagrees. The finished state is held before any route is walked. For even L=2n, split x=f∥g into a front half f and a back half g of n bits each, and place x at (φ,γ)=(f/2^n , J(g)/2^n ). The representatives are the cells strictly above the diagonal

summary: Abstract This integrative research synthesis develops a candidate relational architecture across quantum foundations, physical history, persistent organization, relational time, and the recovery problem for spacetime. Its method is unification by decomposition : constraint, weighting, singular factualization, and retention are treated as distinct operations with distinct evidential burdens. Key Analyses & Framework Quantum Foundations & Entanglement: The double slit separates coherent alternatives, receiver-defined effects, Born weighting, and the $n = 1$ record. The Sorkin hierarchy and reconstruction literature delimit what is already formally known and leave open the physical motivation for second-order weighting. Entanglement is analyzed through a missing-loss audit: spatial routing, operational differentiation, and dynamical decoupling do not by themselves demonstrate ontological severance of a nonfactorizable joint state. Ontology & Event-Factualization: Primitive factualization is treated as a technical event-ontology posit, with fundamental agency as a stronger interpretive hypothesis (alongside objective stochasticity, Bohmian completion, Everettian branching, and collapse dynamics as comparison classes). A present-state coherence veto prevents absolute factualization while coherence-bearing degrees of freedom remain causally accessible to future interactions in which their phase relation can again matter. Retained factual consequences provide the bridge to physical history, memory, differential persistence, and increasingly organized agency. Downstream Physics & Empirical Testing: Transition and stabilization are treated as relational roles of one field-energy reality rather than new substances. The synthesis incorporates a fully exposed prospective transition-stabilization kill test in a driven liquid-to-vapor system and preserves planetary, gravitational, and spacetime extensions as explicitly conditional research branches. Methodological Stance: No universal master equation is claimed. The program is a structured ontology, audit, and research architecture whose modules must earn mathematical or empirical closure independently. Philosophical Extensions (Dual-Aspect Hypothesis): A further dual-aspect factualist hypothesis, with a panexperiential extension, distinguishes the publicly accessible objective face of factual processes from a minimally subjective first-person-like aspect associated with irreducible factual resolution. This is presented as a stronger ontological interpretation, not as an experimentally established consequence. It does not identify an elementary subjective aspect with a subject, mind, or consciousness. Complex biological agency is treated as potentially nested and hierarchically integrated, while the combination of elementary subjective loci into a unified subject is left as an explicit unresolved problem.
title: Unification by Decomposition — A Relational Physical Architecture from Quantum Possibility to Factualization, Retained History, Stabilization, and Spacetime

summary: Abstract: A geometric construction of inverse-square gravity is presented in which solid angle accounts only for spatial dilution, while universal coupling to mass-energy supplies the physical strength of the interaction. This separation avoids treating a body-dependent geometric parameter as a substitute for gravitational mass. For a static spherical source, the construction recovers the exterior Newtonian potential per unit test mass, Φ(r) = -GM/r. Combining this static scalar potential with the special-relativistic energy of the escaping particle gives:   v_esc(r) = c * sqrt( 1 - 1 / (1 + GM / (r * c^2))^2 ) The result is subluminal for all finite r and reduces to the Newtonian escape velocity in the weak-field limit. The model is not presented as a replacement for general relativity, nor as a complete Lorentz-covariant field theory. Rather, it is a flat-spacetime scalar-potential construction that clarifies what follows from solid-angle dilution, universal mass coupling, and special-relativistic energy conservation before additional assumptions, such as wave propagation or optical-gravity extensions, are introduced.   Note on Versioning & Relationship to Prior Work: This paper presents a standalone, refined mathematical derivation focusing specifically on the static scalar formulation and relativistic escape condition. It serves as an independent baseline related to the foundational concepts outlined in the author's broader work ( A Solid-Angle Postulate as a Geometric Foundation for Gravity , DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19333670).

summary: Decompiling Addressable Binary Rings Forced Involutions, the Möbius Difference Bridge, and Radial Witness Topologies   Paradigms of Pure Addressability and Reverse Decompilation Mathematical physics and theoretical computer science conventionally operate in a forward, accumulative direction: axiomatic primitives are posited, state transitions are executed sequentially, and terminal scalar outputs are treated as the primary ontology. When a forward model encounters an underdetermined transition, an irreversible merge, or apparent randomness in symbol generation, traditional analysis attributes that incompleteness to the underlying domain. The reverse-the-gap decompilation principle establishes the exact inverse paradigm. Within a graded transformation substrate, every finite word of every length, every coordinatewise displacement, and every lawful state transition is fully determined at step zero. Nothing is accumulated or newly constructed during execution; structure is rendered exclusively by specifying an address and reading the residual returned by the query. Under this discipline, a gap is never a missing piece of the substrate; it is the exact signature of a reader's finite cut, projection fiber, or declared equivalence relation. summary: RECONFIGURABLE ROBOTIC SWARMS AND CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONAL REGENERATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library | Flagship 02 Prospective Research Atlas — English Review Edition, October 2026 Can a distributed population of heterogeneous modular robots reconstruct an operationally qualified capability after damage, without treating a newly assembled shape as evidence of restored function? Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit develops an interdisciplinary research program on modular morphology, distributed self-assembly, task-dependent graph structure, mechanical qualification, connector fatigue, recoverable actions, and independent post-reconfiguration verification. Its central proposition is deliberately testable: a swarm may change its topology after losing modules, but it earns the stronger name of functional regeneration only when its restored configuration satisfies the original, independently assessed service requirements and does not conceal emerging hazards or latent joint failures. The monograph distinguishes three often conflated networks: mechanical connections that transmit forces, communication links that transmit information, and power connections that transport energy. It then investigates how graph connectivity, geometric rigidity, elastic stiffness, buckling, frictional contact, thermal dissipation, material fatigue, sensing uncertainty, local negotiation, and safe rollback constrain what an apparently repaired swarm can actually do. A prospective twenty-module testbed provides recurring engineering anchors: bridge, gripping, and sensing-tower tasks, blinded removal of modules, unseen configurations, independent qualification, and strong comparisons with redundant fixed structures and specialist replacement procedures. The research architecture includes thirty mathematically diverse derivation plates, eighty-two chapter-level questions and their five individually paginated study units, two hundred falsifiable Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. The companion spreadsheet links physical models, chapter topics, prospective study cards, provenance, source DOI records, and page references to support future research and AI-assisted scientific handoff. Published robotics literature supplies a source-grounded context for modular reconfigurable mechanisms and fault-aware planning, including external DOI records for reviews and an existing fault-tolerant modular system. The manuscript separates those precedents from its own unexecuted research designs. Its two STARLI mother volumes are listed as conceptual ancestry, not as independent experimental validation. Biological regeneration functions as an analogy for staged assessment of restoration, not as evidence of biomedical efficacy, autonomous human-tissue repair, or indefinite machine life. This is a prospective research-atlas REVIEW EDITION. The mathematical relations, study proposals, design seeds, and acceptance thresholds are not experimentally validated findings. External mathematical review, whole-text DOI auditing, and a stronger editorial review for chapter-level semantic repetition remain necessary before scholarly publication. Negative findings, conventional method superiority, irreversible module retirement, and scientific abstention are legitimate outcomes within this research program. summary: 🌟 Summary Ultralytics 8.4.183 expands hardware deployment and improves reliability across training, prediction, data handling, and evaluation. 🚀 📊 Key Changes Axelera Metis support for every YOLO26 task: With Voyager SDK 1.9.0, detection, instance and semantic segmentation, depth estimation, pose, OBB, and classification models can all export, predict, and validate through yolo . The NMS-free detection path is used by default. SDK 1.8 exports remain compatible; the updated setup requires metis-dkms 1.7.0 or newer and supports PyTorch versions below 2.15. Higher Axelera throughput: In the documented COCO128 benchmark, SDK 1.9 reached 109 images per second at batch 32 , compared with 40 images per second on SDK 1.8. Larger prediction batches can improve throughput; batch size 1 remains useful when per-image latency matters. Intel acceleration for LiteRT models: LiteRT exports can now run on Intel CPUs and NPUs, including support for YOLO26 task types such as detection, segmentation, depth, pose, OBB, and classification. More reliable training and depth calibration: Fixes address warmup and gradient accumulation edge cases, MPS memory growth during training, and depth calibration replacing an already-good calibration with a worse one. Interrupted runs can also resume under the same Ultralytics Platform model, and W&B resuming works on Windows. More accurate and robust data workflows: Fixes improve ImageNet-subset classifier validation, accept UTF-8 labels with a byte-order mark, preserve non-ASCII grounding annotations, convert COCO RLE masks for segmentation, and align 16-bit NumPy images with image-file prediction behavior. Prediction, export, and visualization fixes: Negative FastSAM points now reliably exclude masks regardless of prompt order. Other fixes cover very thin images, rectangular INT8 calibration, grayscale LiteRT models, semantic overlay colors, depth-map saving, and several additional edge cases. Platform and documentation updates: Platform documentation now includes Gemma 4 and Nemotron as hosted annotation models and explains new visibility controls and workflows. Benchmark instructions were also clarified for NMS-free evaluation. 🎯 Purpose & Impact Deploy YOLO26 on more hardware and tasks: Axelera users can use one integrated workflow across all seven YOLO26 tasks, while Intel LiteRT users gain CPU and NPU inference options. Get better throughput when processing batches: Axelera SDK 1.9 can substantially increase prediction throughput for larger batches, though actual results depend on hardware and workload. Trust training, validation, and predictions more: The fixes reduce avoidable failures and make reported results better reflect the supplied data and model—for example, correcting classifier label alignment changes ImageNette validation accuracy from 9.45% to 70.37% in the reported test. Keep existing workflows working: Many changes are targeted bug fixes or compatibility improvements; notably, Axelera models exported with SDK 1.8 do not need to be re-exported for SDK 1.9. summary: Quantum illumination uses a retained idler to improve detection of a weak optical return in thermal noise. For a source designer, the practical resource question is how much ideal quantum storage is needed for a specified improvement. This work gives the exact asymptotic answer when the signal-photon budget and the total retained-register dimension are constrained independently. Exact finite-memory frontier Consider a thermal attenuator with transmissivity \(0<\eta<1\) and vacuum-output background occupation \(b>0\), tested against the replacer that returns the same thermal state. For \(n\) parallel uses, every admissible probe obeys a mean total signal-photon ceiling \(nN\) and a strict bound \(\dim R\le\lfloor e^{nP}\rfloor\) on the entire retained register, including retained source records. The memory rate is \(P/\ln2\) ideal qubits per use. With vanishing miss probability, the optimal false-alarm exponent is \[\Xi(N,P)=\eta\ln(1+1/b)N+G\!\left(\min\{P,g(N)\}\right).\] Here all logarithms are natural, \(g(x)=(x+1)\ln(x+1)-x\ln x\), with \(g(0)=0\), and \[G(p)=g(b)+p-F\!\left(g^{-1}(p)\right).\] The function \(F(x)\) is the entropy of the full complementary output for a thermal input of mean occupation \(x\); the complement includes the purification of the thermal environment. The first term in \(\Xi\) is the optimum without retained memory, and \(G\) is the additional detection benefit. The converse covers arbitrary normal mixed probes, correlations across channel uses and collective measurements. Matching sources satisfy the actual finite-register and energy bounds: they allocate photons between signal–idler correlations and a known displacement, and approach the frontier through finite-support preparations. How much storage is useful? The exact saturation rate and initial marginal value are \[P_{\mathrm{sat}}(N)=g(N),\qquad G'(0^+)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}.\] Because \(G\) is strictly increasing and strictly concave, at a positive signal budget \(N>0\) the minimum rate retaining a fixed fraction \(0<r<1\) of the full additive memory benefit is \[P_r(N)=G^{-1}\!\left(rG(g(N))\right)<r\,g(N).\] At low brightness, \(P_r(N)\sim r g(N)\). At high brightness, this fixed-fraction storage cost remains bounded while the exact-saturation cost diverges. The relative detection benefit simultaneously tends to zero: saving a large fraction of the saturation storage does not imply a large improvement over the total no-memory exponent. Connection to optical communication For the same thermal channel, let \(C(N,P)\) denote the classical capacity under the corresponding photon budget and a strict initial maximally entangled Schmidt-rank supply. The two separately defined tasks satisfy \[\Xi(N,P)-\Xi(N,0)=C(N,P)-C(N,0).\] This identity equates optimized incremental values, not the physical resources or protocols. The manuscript explicitly attributes the shared Gaussian-reference contraction and entropy-support tools to the capacity analysis. Its detection-specific contribution is the original-register mixed-probe converse, strict finite-register attainment and operational testing limit. Scope. The result concerns parallel, phase-known thermal attenuation, ideal retained storage and the vanishing-miss Stein criterion. It is an asymptotic resource benchmark rather than a finite-sample receiver or a noisy-memory optimum. The integrated article includes the complete proofs and two figure groups showing both storage cost and the value obtained from it.
title: The memory cost of quantum illumination

summary: Precomputed results for DOST (Distance-preserving Optimization for Spatial Transcriptomics), a method for identifying spatial domains in spatial transcriptomics data. This record accompanies the DOST code (see Related works) and the DOST paper. results.zip contains the outputs of the scripts in the reproducibility/ directory of the code repository, for DOST and for the baseline methods BANKSY, BASS, DR.SC, GraphST, STAGATE, SpaGCN, stCluster and ADEPT. These are the files read by the figure scripts in reproducibility/figures/ . To use the files, unzip results.zip , set dir.output in the figure scripts to the unzipped folder, and run the scripts as described in reproducibility/figures/README.md in the code repository. The datasets are not included. They are publicly available from the BenchmarkST Zenodo records (DLPFC12, BC, mMAMP and mHypothalamus) and from 10x Genomics (Xenium Human Breast); see reproducibility/DOST/README.md in the code repository.
title: Precomputed results for DOST reproducibility

summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory

summary: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts

summary: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention

summary: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis

summary: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.
title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution

summary: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing

summary: Latent memory is gaining ground as a lightweight history supplement for GUI agents. It supplies history to a frozen vision-language model via prefix vectors trained with step-wise cross-entropy (CE). While resulting gains are naturally attributed to encoded history, our controlled experiments show they primarily stem from action revision. The prefix learns to alter the model's default actions. However, this revision is unscoped because step-wise CE pushes outputs toward reference actions at every step without explicitly preserving correct decisions. Consequently, it repairs errors but also breaks 8-13% of initially correct answers. Overall accuracy metrics hide these losses. We therefore propose ScopeMem, a latent-memory method for scoped revision. Its encoder conditions prefix generation on the model's initial answer and is trained to correct errors while preserving correct decisions. On the controlled ablation set, ScopeMem reduces the share of broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than any evaluated CE-trained prefix. On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, ScopeMem outperforms all evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines, enabling a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B to match or surpass GUI-specialized agents and Qwen3-VL-32B.
title: ScopeMem: Latent Memory That Learns Where to Revise Frozen GUI Agents

summary: We study an inverse problem for the variable coefficient Moore Gibson Thompson (MGT) equation in a bounded domain, where the objective is to recover an unknown initial acceleration from boundary measurements of the acoustic field. We establish both injectivity and stability of the associated measurement operator. Injectivity is established through a unique continuation property by applying a theorem of Tataru for analytically principally normal operators. The argument relies on a factorization of the third order operator into wave type components, combined with Carleman estimates and propagation techniques in the spirit of Tataru. Stability is derived through a microlocal analysis of the forward operator, based on the construction of geometric optics approximate solutions and the identification of an elliptic pseudodifferential operator arising from microlocal back propagation of the data. These results connect the MGT inverse problem with the classical theory of hyperbolic inverse problems, such as photoacoustic tomography, while highlighting new features induced by the third order dynamics and damping.
title: An Inverse Problem for the Moore Gibson Thompson Equation: Injectivity and Stability

summary: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.
title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation

summary: We derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) and identify the general moment closure shared by kinetic methods based on the discrete-velocity Boltzmann equation. This closure provides a route to correct lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate reconstruction of the higher-order moments, thereby substantially broadening the scope of existing closure strategies that seek increasingly accurate representations of these moments. These advances establish a unified moment framework bridging LBM and moment methods. The framework enables efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes, overcoming the prohibitive complexity of existing moment methods at high Knudsen numbers. It further provides a common basis for integrating and extending key features of diverse kinetic methods.
title: Bridging the Lattice Boltzmann Method and Moment Methods

summary: We study how many output samples match the worst-case state reconstruction error obtainable from a continuous history under bounded measurement noise. For observable scalar-output linear time-varying systems with $n$ states, $n$ samples suffice for exact reconstruction, whereas at most $n^2$ attain the continuous-history minimax error in the $\ell_\infty$ norm. An explicit construction proves sharpness even for real-analytic systems. For time-invariant systems, strict total positivity yields one $n$-sample schedule optimal for every state coordinate; endpoint-observed tridiagonal cooperative chains satisfy this conclusion in physical coordinates. Interior sensing behaves differently: an explicit three-state family requires four samples despite positivity and distinct real eigenvalues. The strict three-state gap persists under small stabilizing damping. A nilpotent four-state example and an interval proof for a six-state mechanical system give gaps. The results identify how temporal sampling and the prescribed state-error geometry determine the measurements required for minimax reconstruction. Time-domain experiments illustrate the resulting estimation bounds.
title: Beyond Observability: Sharp Sample Bounds for Minimax State Reconstruction

summary: Extensive studies of hidden spin polarization have established a broad class of hidden phenomena in quantum materials. Here, we introduce the hidden piezo-Hall effect, in which strain induces finite anomalous Hall conductivities (AHCs) in individual sectors while the global AHC remains zero. At zero strain, neither the full system nor its sectors exhibit an anomalous Hall effect (AHE). Under uniaxial strain, however, opposite sector AHCs emerge while their sum remains canceled. We establish this effect for a $d$-wave hidden altermagnet using a tight-binding model and first-principles calculations for the experimentally synthesized material $\mathrm{RbV_2Te_2O}$. Rotating the strain direction from the $x$ to the $y$ axis reverses the signs of the sector AHCs without generating a net Hall response. The same symmetry mechanism may also give rise to hidden piezomagneto-optical, piezo-thermal Hall, piezo-Nernst, and piezo-Ettingshausen effects. Our work extends hidden physics to strain-controlled transport and identifies $\mathrm{RbV_2Te_2O}$ as a promising candidate for experimental verification.
title: Hidden piezo-Hall effect
