summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

summary: Against Its Own Reverse One comparison of each binary word with its reverse builds the ring’s address, its sphere and its waveform   Driven by Dean A. Kulik October 2026   Status words. A bracket after a statement records how it stands. proved : proved in this paper. STANDS : established earlier in the series or in the literature. RUNS : an exact computation landed where the route put it, with its scope stated; every one is rerun by the scripts of Appendix B. SEALED : the prediction was written and its text hashed (SHA-256) before the computation that tests it was run; the texts and digests are in Appendix A. DEAD END : the computation ran and landed, and the landing belongs to something else, whose owner is named. OPEN : stated and not settled. PULL : an interpretive bridge, not a result. Work run in independent AI-assisted audits is marked independently . Abstract Compare every binary word with its own reverse. Write each mirrored pair of bits as a value beside a difference, the butterfly (u, u ⊕ v) taken across the mirror. The comparison is decided by the outermost pair that differs, and the Hamming weight is carried by the pairs that agree. This paper shows that the ring of all binary words is built from those two readers of one lifted word. The partner map reverses the difference half, or complements the value half when there is no difference. The address of a word is half of what lies below it plus half of the reversal pairs its own value separates, rank(p) = ½(p − π(p) + Δ(p)) + π c (p), where Δ(p) = #{x : x < p ≤ J(x)} has a closed digit form and grows by a borrow chain whose cell is the full adder’s carry with one input complemented; the first 64 bits of π land at 2,427,008,858,123,944,441 from one pass over the 32 bits of each half. The route that grows a word one bit at a time is the lift itself: its residual bits are the mirrored differences, innermost first. On the sphere of radius n and latitude z = wt − n/2, latitude reads only the agreeing pairs, so the poles belong to the palindromes and a word with k disagreeing pairs stays within |z| ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ − k + [n odd]/2; the partner is a reflection, and on palindromes a half-turn about the X-axis. On ring addresses the partner is the complement of the address, so the latitude splits into a Walsh-even body and a Walsh-odd palindrome carrier whose energy share is exactly 2 1−n/2 at even width. Pulled back, each reader is simple in its own coordinates and spread in the other’s: over the bits of a word the comparison needs 2(2 ⌊ n/2 ⌋ − 1) Walsh modes and the latitude n; over ring addresses the comparison is one address bit carrying 99.9% of its energy at n = 20, while the latitude fills 1,036,432 of 1,048,576 modes. The ring is the coordinate system of the comparison. How the paper runs The paper is written from its end. Section 1 states the finished object: a formula that places any word of any width in the ring of all words, and the same formula read as a change of coordinates. Sections 2 to 9 follow that object back along the path that produced it. Each section opens on the hole the previous result left, names what must fill it by its shape and its neighbours, and shows the fill falling out of what was already built; no section found its result by trying candidates against a readout. Section 10 pulls back and reads the whole. Every value was derived before it was computed; the predictions hashed before their runs are in Appendix A, and every statement is rerun by the scripts of Appendix B. 1. summary: Curated Wearable Physiological Signals for Paediatric ADHD Research, with Task-Aligned Data and EDA Baselines This resource organises existing Empatica EmbracePlus recordings from the BALLADEER paediatric ADHD study into source-traceable native task views, with optional full native context, descriptive quality control (QC) and processed electrodermal activity (EDA). Cohort, acquisition and games are inherited; the added contribution is an inspectable association between observations, original source indices, admitted recording windows, missingness and technical provenance, together with a bounded reuse example. Coverage and signals The inventory comprises 107 participants and five tasks : CogniFit (01), Attention Robots (02), and screen-based Attention Slackline levels 1, 6 and 11 (03–05). EDA overlaps admitted EEG recording spans for 436 participant/task combinations across 104 people , with 1,129,180 finite selected EDA samples . Of 535 possible EDA cells, 77 lack an EEG span and 22 have EEG but no EDA overlap. Availability and temporal overlap do not establish full-task coverage, physiological suitability or final analytical eligibility. The golden layer contains 37,974,199 native rows across supported streams. The complete native projection contains 228,120,776 rows, including 6,779,644 EDA rows with 20 untimed entries, and extends outside task windows. These representations overlap; do not sum them as independent observations or treat time-series samples/task rows as independent participants. Golden native stream Rows Quantity/unit Accelerometer 18,069,607 Three-axis int32 ADC counts; native calibration context retained BVP 18,067,914 Optical pulse waveform, writer-declared nW; not blood pressure EDA 1,129,180 Signed float32 µS Temperature 282,293 float32 °C Steps 56,461 Vendor int32 counts Systolic peaks 368,743 Vendor event times, original indices and UTC nanosecond source time Wearable tags 1 Native event time, original index and UTC microsecond source time Gyroscope 0 Supported schema, empty stream The single tag is not full-cohort coverage. Availability retains missing combinations explicitly. Participant metadata has exactly participant_id , age , gender and group . Identifiers remain strings; recorded gender is not renamed biological sex. Group 1/2 denotes experimental/ADHD recruitment and comparison under the approved interpretation, not assessment-derived diagnosis or uniformly healthy controls. Downloads and reassembly Logical archive Complete size Upload files golden_dataset.zip 606.25 MB 7 native_projection.zip 2955.75 MB 30 quality_control.zip 2.73 MB 1 processed_eda.zip 35.75 MB 1 baseline_reproduction.zip 18.89 MB 1 Each upload file is at most 100,000,000 bytes . Golden and native archives are byte-split into numbered parts; parts are not independently extractable ZIP files . Download all seven golden_dataset.zip.part001 – .part007 files for golden data, or all 30 native_projection.zip.part001 – .part030 files for the native supplement. The other three archives are ordinary single ZIPs. This size is a delivery choice, not a platform limit. Keep archive_registry.json and reassemble.py beside the desired complete part set. Run python3 reassemble.py verify --archive golden_dataset.zip , create a new output directory, then run python3 reassemble.py reassemble golden_dataset.zip --output-dir reassembled . The standard-library helper checks ordered part and complete-ZIP hashes, refuses overwrites and never extracts or runs analysis. Extract the verified ZIP with an ordinary tool into a new empty directory. Substitute the native archive name for that route. For a single ZIP, verify it by name and extract directly. README.md gives exact commands and reconstruction-space guidance. Golden data: primary native wearable task views/events, metadata, schemas, selection membership, QC and scientific provenance; independently usable after its parts are reassembled. Native projection: complete pr

summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.1 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.1' . The tutorial in German and English, the API guides, release notes and screenshot provenance are included with the source archive. Verification: 984 passing tests, 92.8% coverage, Ruff lint/format checks, warning-free Markdownlint, package metadata checks and fresh-environment installation tests under Python 3.11 and 3.13. Viewer checks include real optimization subprocesses and terminal restoration. These are code and packaging checks, not live-provider benchmarks. Versioning, license and citation Version 0.3.1 . MIT license. The source archive includes machine-readable CITATION.cff metadata. Version DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23494842 . The unchanged concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22011370 identifies the software across versions. Source code and issues ; Python package .
title: annotations4all

summary: NOTE: 1. The R package to compute NPP from brGDGTs is available in https://github.com/MarcoVidalCordasco/envirolipids  2.  R_Code_and_Analysis_Guide.pdf facilitates navigation through the analytical workflow and helps identifying the code associated with each result presented in the study.  ## 📌 Overview This repository contains an R workflow for analysing branched GDGT (brGDGT) compounds and modelling **Net Primary Productivity (NPP)** using statistical and machine learning approaches. It also includes the full ecological modelling workflow to recosntruct herbivore biomass and carrying capacity of secondary consumers. There are two scripts: * Script_1 * Script_2 The Script_1 performs: * Exploratory data analysis * Statistical modelling (linear, quadratic, GAM) * Random Forest modelling with three validation strategies * Independent dataset validation * NPP reconstruction from Padul-15-05 core * Comparison with climate-derived NPP (Miami model) * Summed Probability Distribution (SPD) analysis for archaeological data * Correlation analysis * Summary statistics and plots The Script_2 performs: * Herbivore density estimations from primary productivity * Population structure modelling using survival curves * Biomass partitioning across body size classes * Secondary consumers carrying capacity calculations * Summary statistics and plots --- ## 📂 Data Requirements The Script_1 expects an Excel file: ``` Dataset_1.xlsx This contains: * A global dataset of present-day measured brGDGTs and associated climatic, edaphic and environmental variables * Areas with in-field NPP measurements * Climate conditions reconstructed in Padul * Archaeological sites, levels and dates for the summed probability distributions ``` The Script_2 expects two additional Excel files: ``` Dataset_2.xlsx This contains: * Herbivore traits (species, body mass, life history traits, etc.), * The wild mammal species list recovered in the region during the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene (including sites and references) * NPP values (actual and potential) obtained from Script_1 * Primary and secondary consumer biomass summaries ``` ``` Prey_preferences.xlsx This contains: * Predator diet composition and annual biomass requirements ``` ## 📦 R Packages A package to apply the random-forest NPP predictions from brGDGTs is under construction --- ## ⚠️ Notes * Ensure working directory is set correctly: ```r setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path)) ``` * All files available in this repository should be saved into the same folder/directory --- ## 📬 Contact # mav54#cam.ac.uk

summary: Example data to reproduce the BAGFOOT2 protocol and vignette: mouse liver ATAC-seq, Fed vs Fasted (3 replicates per condition, mm10). BAGFOOT2 predicts which transcription factors change their activity between two conditions from ATAC-seq data, by combining Tn5 bias-corrected footprint depth and flanking accessibility over archetype motif clusters, with a robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD) test. Files bam_merged.tar.gz: one merged, sorted and indexed BAM file per condition (fed, fasted) bam_replicates.tar.gz: one BAM file per replicate (fed_1-3, fasted_1-3), used for HOMER (large file) tag_directories.tar.gz: HOMER tag directories of the replicates (TD_fed_1 ... TD_fasted_3) macs2.tar.gz: MACS2 peak calls (narrowPeak) per condition bg_files_fed_fasted.tar.gz: BAGFOOT2 (v2.0.0) output for Fed vs Fasted (bagplot, D2 and FDR barplots, result table) The motif database files (mm10, hg38) are NOT in this record. They are downloaded automatically by BAGFOOT2 on first use, from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20782782 How to reproduce Install BAGFOOT2: conda create -n bagfoot2 -c goldsteinlab-tech -c conda-forge -c bioconda bagfoot2 Extract the archives into one project folder: fed_fasted/bam_merged/ (merged BAM files, replicate BAM files and tag directories) fed_fasted/macs2/ (peak files) Run: bagfoot2 -b fed_fasted/bam_merged/ -p fed_fasted/macs2/ -o bg_files_fed_fasted/ -c fed -t fasted -g mm10 --bam_suffix ".sorted.bam" --cores 4 Add --homer TRUE --homer_bin /path/to/homer/bin --reps_control 1,2,3 --reps_treatment 1,2,3 to include HOMER motif enrichment. Code: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 Documentation: https://goldsteinlab-tech.github.io/BAGFOOT2/ RELATED WORKS Is supplement to: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 (Software) References: 10.5281/zenodo.20782782 (Dataset, motif database)

summary: This repository contains the replication materials accompanying the research note Financial Pessimism and the Timing of Saving (Alexander Hansak, University of Graz, 2026). The archive includes the original Python analysis, an independent R implementation of the principal estimators and survey-design standard errors, supplementary empirical analyses, Julia preprocessing scripts, questionnaire documentation, and aggregate estimation results. The canonical Python replay and independent R implementation reproduce 21 reported coefficient and standard-error comparisons on identical model-ready samples. Additional analyses examine saving amounts, subsequent income and employment outcomes, and age heterogeneity. All nine supplementary verification stages passed. The additional empirical specifications have not been independently cross-implemented. The analysis uses the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and Understanding Society (UKHLS), distributed through UK Data Service study 6614 (DOI: 10.5255/UKDA-SN-6614-22). Licensed respondent-level data are not redistributed. Researchers wishing to reproduce the analysis must obtain authorized access to the original survey data. The archive provides source code, execution instructions, numerical verification reports, aggregate outputs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The empirical findings describe conditional associations rather than identified causal effects. Version: 1.1.0 (20 October 2026).
title: Financial Pessimism and the Timing of Saving: Replication Materials

summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. Other explicitly paced endpoints share endpoint-scoped state below the results directory. Request-level policy belo
title: annotations-orchestration

summary: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

summary: Commit messages provide records of code changes and help developers understand and maintain software. To reduce the manual effort involved in writing them, commit message generation (CMG) approaches automatically generate commit messages that describe code changes in natural language. Existing CMG approaches generally treat CMG as a standalone task and optimize generated messages primarily for similarity to developer-written references. However, this objective may not properly reflect the practical usefulness of generated commit messages. This limitation matters in current AI-assisted software engineering workflows, where commit messages are used as shared information to serve different software engineering activities. To fill this gap, we propose TraceMsg, which uses issue-commit traceability, a representative software engineering activity, to guide commit message generation. TraceMsg is a collaborative multi-agent framework that coordinates message generation, traceability reasoning, and feedback-guided refinement, allowing generated messages to serve traceability while using reasoning feedback to guide issue-conditioned refinement. We evaluate TraceMsg on six open-source projects. The experimental results show that TraceMsg achieves an average Hit@1 of 0.893 and an MRR of 0.911, improving Hit@1 and MRR by 13.16% and 38.75%, respectively, over the best baseline for each metric.
title: Beyond Similarity-Based Generation: Guiding Commit Message Generation with Issue-Commit Traceability

summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.

summary: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery

summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.

summary: GO3 New Release Notes This release introduces major enhancements to GAF 2.2 annotation parsing, native annotation filtering in Rust, transparent .gz support, bidirectional gene–term queries, expanded ontology graph traversal, pairwise GO term similarity/distance matrices, semantic redundancy reduction & clustering, and built-in Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis (ORA). ────── What's New 1. Native GAF Annotation Filtering (load_gaf_terms) Filter annotations directly during Rust-level GAF parsing with zero Python overhead: • evidence_codes: Keep only annotations matching specific evidence codes (e.g., ["EXP", "IDA", "IPI", "IMP", "IGI", "IEP"]), or use only_experimental=True as a shortcut. • exclude_evidence_codes: Exclude specific evidence codes (e.g., ["IEA", "ND"]). • ignore_not=True: Automatically discard negative annotations (NOT qualifiers such as NOT|located_in). • aspects: Restrict loaded annotations to specific GO aspects (["P"], ["F"], ["C"] or "BP", "MF", "CC"). • taxons: Filter by NCBI taxon IDs (["taxon:9606"] or ["9606"]). • assigned_by: Keep only annotations curated by specific databases (e.g., ["UniProt", "MGI"]). 2. Full 17-Column GAF 2.2 Inspection (parse_gaf & GAFAnnotation) • Added go3.parse_gaf(path, ...) returning GAFAnnotation objects with all 17 GAF 2.2 columns (db, db_object_id, db_object_symbol, qualifier, go_id, db_reference, evidence_code, with_from, aspect, db_object_name, db_object_synonym, db_object_type, taxon, date, assigned_by, annotation_extension, gene_product_form_id). • Supports the exact same native filtering arguments as load_gaf_terms, plus to_dict() for seamless DataFrame conversion (pd.DataFrame([a.to_dict() for a in records])). 3. Transparent .gz Compressed File Support • load_obo, load_gaf_terms, and parse_gaf now transparently read .obo.gz and .gaf.gz files on the fly without requiring prior decompression on disk. 4. Bidirectional Gene–Term Lookup API Inspect the loaded GAF index directly from Python: • go3.list_genes(). List all loaded gene symbols. • go3.get_terms_for_gene(gene, ontology=None). Retrieve GO term IDs annotated to a gene (optionally filtered by ontology aspect). • go3.get_genes_for_term(go_id). Retrieve all genes directly annotated to a GO term. 5. Expanded Ontology Graph Traversal (GOTerm) • Added term.descendants (all transitive child terms) alongside term.ancestors. • Added term.relations (Dict[str, List[str]]) exposing typed ontology relationships (part_of, regulates, negatively_regulates, positively_regulates, etc.). • Added go3.list_terms(ontology=None) to list all non-obsolete GO term IDs, optionally filtered by ontology ("BP", "MF", "CC"). 6. Pairwise Term Similarity & Distance Matrices • go3.term_similarity_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Parallelized pairwise similarity matrix (N × N) for a list of GO terms. • go3.term_distance_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Normalized semantic distance matrix (1 - sim, with self-similarity normalized for unbounded metrics like "ic" / "resnik"), ready for scipy, scikit-learn, or umap. 7. Semantic Redundancy Reduction & GO Term Clustering • go3.reduce_redundant_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin", scores=None, prefer="ic"). REVIGO-style greedy semantic deduplication of GO term lists based on custom scores (e.g., -log₁₀(FDR)), Information Content ("ic"), or ontology depth ("depth"). • go3.cluster_go_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin"). Connected-components clustering of semantically related GO terms. 8. Native GO Enrichment Analysis (ORA) • go3.go_enrichment(...) & EnrichmentResult. High-performance Over-Representation Analysis computed in Rust with ontology ancestor propagation (true-path ru

summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.

summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. The repository — https://github.com/Capta1n-n9m0/cafrl-negative — holds the per-video model scores, the decision rules frozen before the runs they adjudicate, every run's configuration and validation curve, the evaluation and statistical harness, the face-crop and re-encode pipeline, the self-audit record with its defect ledger, and two claims maps that give the artifact and method for each reported value row by row. Its tagged tree (v2.0.2) is included here as cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz . This version holds: cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz — the repository at tag v2.0.2 (new). <run>.best.pt — 26 frozen model checkpoints (2.7 GB in all), one file per run: the best.pt (best mean validation AUC) of each run added in revision 1, with checkpoints-r1-manifest.json giving each one's run, architecture, arm, training protocol, augmentation policy, seed, selected epoch, selection metric and SHA-256 (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v2.0.0; no best_valloss.pt ). The v2.0.0 release notes call this payload checkpoints-r1.tar ; the deposit holds the same 26 checkpoints as separate files. checkpoints.tar — 37 frozen model checkpoints (6.0 GB), every best*.pt of the 27 v1.0.0 runs, with checkpoints-manifest.json (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0). crop-coordinates.tar.zst — 48,294 per-video face-crop records: the frames selected, the bounding boxes, the five-point landmarks and the alignment settings. Given the source corpora, obtained under your own data-use agreement, these regenerate the exact crops the models were trained and evaluated on (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0; this version adds no crop coordinates). SHA256SUMS (every file above, the carried ones included) and README-DEPOSIT.md . The v2.0.1 source tarball stays in the v2.0.1 record and is not part of this version. No dataset media is redistributed here or in the repository. FaceForensics++, DeepFakeDetection and Celeb-DF v2 are released by their authors under signed agreements that do not per

summary: Six independent 100 ns molecular dynamics trajectories of human acetylcholinesterase (PDB 4EY7) in complex with two ligands: donepezil, whose dual-site binding mode is established crystallographically in that structure, and N-(1-benzylpiperidin-4-yl)-2-phenyl-1H-benzimidazole-5-carboxamide (DAH-004). Three trajectories per ligand were generated from the same equilibrated structure under identical parameters, differing only in the initial velocity distribution. The deposit contains the production trajectories (water and ions removed, 200 ps sampling), the GROMACS run input files, twelve minimum-distance time series to Trp86 and Trp286 computed with gmx pairdist, the per-window contact occupancy table, and the scripts that generate the figures of the associated manuscript. Software: GROMACS 2026.0, AMBER99SB-ILDN, GAFF2 with AM1-BCC charges, TIP3P water. This version adds the excursion-kinetics analysis: Figure 4 and the script that generates it from the twelve minimum-distance time series.
title: Replica dependence of catalytic-site contact in acetylcholinesterase-ligand simulations: benchmark data

summary: Sorolopha specialis Zhu & Yu sp. nov. Figs 5, 7, 8, 10, 11 Type material. Holotype : China • ♂; Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Pingxiang, Shaoping forest farm; 22 ° 4 ' N, 106 ° 55 ' E; alt. 280 m; 1 Apr. 2013; X. F. Yang leg.; genitalia slide no. YWX 18110. Paratypes : China • 2 ♂♂, 1 ♀; same collection data as for holotype; 2 Apr. 2013 • 1 ♂; Hainan Prov., Yinggeling, Hongkan; 19 ° 48 ' N, 109 ° 30 ' E; alt. 510 m; 17 May. 2015; P. X. Cong, W. Guan, and S. Hu leg. • 1 ♂; Hainan Prov., Wuzhishan Reserve; 18 ° 54 ' N, 109 ° 40 ' E; alt. 740 m; 13 Apr. 2009; Q. Jin and B. B. Hu leg. Diagnosis. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. is very similar to S. ferruginosa and S. nanlingica in forewing pattern, but can be distinguished by the presence of blackish androconial scales on the lower surface of the hindwing in males. In male genitalia morphology, S. specialis sp. nov. resembles several congeners, including S. ferruginosa , S. nanlingica , S. baribaris , and S. viridis Sakagami, 2023. It differs from S. ferruginosa by the valva having a straight neck and a cucullus whose distal part is ~ 2 / 3 the length of the ventral prominence; in S. ferruginosa , the valva has a gently curved neck and a cucullus with distal part ~ 1 / 2 the length of the ventral prominence. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. differs from S. nanlingica and S. baribaris in the male genitalia by the valva with a relatively long neck and a semi-rounded ventral prominence; in contrast, these two species have a valva with a short neck and a ventral prominence of the cucullus that gradually widens outward. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. differs from S. viridis in that the distal part of the cucullus is uniform in width and ~ 2 × as wide as the neck of the valva; whereas in S. viridis , the distal part of the cucullus gradually narrows outward and is approximately equal in width to the neck of the valva. Description. Adult (Fig. 5). Forewing length 6.0– 7.5 mm. Head (Fig. 7): Frons creamy white. Vertex roughly scaled, pale brown suffused with green. Antenna extending to middle of forewing, brown. Labial palpus porrect, creamy white, suffused with pale grey and green laterally; median segment expanded, terminal segment relatively short, stout. Thorax : Collar brown suffused with green basally and pale brown apically. Tegula green basally and brown distally. Dorsum smooth, green suffused with brown, posterior crest indistinct. Hind leg pale brown, tibia and basal subsegment of tarsus with dense, blackish scales in males. Forewing subrectangular; costa nearly straight except for a slightly curved apex, termen slightly oblique; upperside grayish brown; basal seven pairs of costal strigulae green, distal two pairs white; inner margin of wing and area between fold and dorsum green, with tiny, dark brown spots along dorsum; markings indistinguishable, indicated by a few fragmented, ferruginous spots edged with indistinct, blackish lines on central area of wing; apical 1 / 3 of wing (from R 3 to tornus) with white ground color, bearing a narrow, crescent-shaped subapical mark extending from middle of R 4 to distal 2 / 5 of CuA 1 and from 1 / 3 length of M 1 to CuA 1 on termen, dark brown suffused with ferruginous, with inner side surrounded by brown, curving lines, and scattered, pale brown scales between crescent mark and apex; cilia pale brown, with a brown baseline; underside pale brown, except for grayish-white costal strigulae and a white area overlapped by hindwing. Hindwing upperside brown except for white area overlapped by forewing; cilia pale brown, with a brown baseline; underside pale brown, with an elongate-ovoid patch of dense, blackish androconial scales on lower angle of cell (Fig. 8). Abdomen : Terga 3–7 with tufts of long bristles on posterolateral margins in males. Male genitalia (Fig. 10): Tegumen narrow, subtriangular; uncus small and obtuse; socius slender, pendant, r

Labial palpus porrect, creamy white, suffused with pale grey and green laterally; median segment expanded, terminal segment relatively short, stout. summary: Data and R code that reproduce the results of "Divergence Between Absolute Emissions Benchmarks and Output-Adjusted Assessments: Evidence from Korea" (manuscript version 7.7.1, submitted to Energy Economics).   A single command, Rscript reproduce.R, runs 14 analysis scripts (about 15 seconds on a 32-core computer) and lists the 146 numbers reported in the paper in the order in which they appear, each next to the value the package computes or provides. Of the 146 numbers, 121 are recomputed from the distributed data; the other 25 rest on site-level records, coding records of business reports, a page-by-page reading of overseas reports and licensed revenue data, which cannot be distributed, and are provided as computed.   The package requires only R with the jsonlite and ggplot2 packages (versions fixed in renv.lock). The random draws of the original computation are included as files; an included Python script (draws/make_draws.py, numpy) regenerates them byte for byte.   The package of 101 files contains truncated salted hash codes, log changes and ratios for the Korean firm pairs, the overseas pair files, the producer price indices and the boundary audit of the 80 firms in the multi-industry frame. It contains no firm names, business identifiers or levels of emissions, energy, output or revenue for Korean firms. See README.md for the folder layout, the fixed inputs and the results that are provided as computed.   Licences: code under MIT; data produced by the author under CC BY 4.0. Producer price indices and source data remain under their publishers' terms. The README inside the archive is labelled manuscript version 7.7; its data and code are identical to those of version 7.7.1.

summary: This dataset was produced by iGEM Team Al-Nahrain-IRAQ 2026 (AL-Nahrain University, Iraq) as a part of SYNOVA  project , which aim to  predict, optimize and  detect yeast activity . iGEM wiki : https://2026.igem.wiki/al-nahrain-iraq CONTENTS    Metadata.zip ethanol_yield.csv : Experimental metadata for 8 experiments: strain, genetic modification, target gene, growth medium, temperature, carbon source, time, pH and ethanol yield, manually extracted from published studies, with DOI and BioProject for each experiment. R64.csv : S. cerevisiae S288C reference gene annotation (assembly R64-1-1), exported from Ensembl BioMart (accessed August 2026). Columns: RefSeq DNA ID, Gene stable ID, gene description, chromosome, gene start/end (bp), strand (1 = forward, -1 = reverse), gene name, GC content (%), gene type and SGD ID. Empty cells indicate no identifier available in Ensembl. The Gene stable ID (e.g. YPL071C) links this table to the count and SNP files Gene_Expression_ counts.zip : 7 gene-level RNA-seq count files, used as input for differential expression analysis. RNA_ SNPs.zip : 7 SNP files called from the RNA-seq data, with SNP positions mapped to genes using the R64 annotation. DESeq2_Experimental_ model.zip : differential expression analyses for 2 models/comparisons using DESeq2. One model will be selected as the reference workflow for the project's AI component to analyse count data in the same way.   METHODS   RNA-seq / gene expression (Galaxy): FastQC (quality control) → Trimmomatic (adapter and quality trimming) → HISAT2 (alignment to S288C R64) → featureCounts (gene-level counts). DESeq2 differential expression analysis was run in Google Colab, using code written with AI assistance.  SNP analysis (Galaxy): FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → MarkDuplicates → AddOrReplaceReadGroups → bcftools mpileup → bcftools call → bcftools filter → bcftools +setGT → bcftools query. SNP annotation: chromosome/position of each SNP → R64 gene annotation → corresponding gene.  CONTRIBUTIONS  H. R. Abdulateef performed all RNA-seq, SNP and DESeq2 analyses and curated the dataset. H. R .Abdulateef ,T. W. AL-FATAl  , T. N. Taher ,and A. N. Aliyamin collected the data from the literature.
title: AL-Nahrain-IRAQ: RNA-seq gene counts, SNPs and DESeq2 models of ethanol-producing Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains (SYNOVA)

summary: Premessa   Leonardo’s Score non è una ricerca isolata. È un pannello del trittico Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar, insieme a Leonardo’s Rulers e a Leonardo’s CAD: tre indagini nate separate, una sola grammatica metrico-modulare dello spazio. Quella utilizzata da Leonardo da Vinci per costruire i suoi spazi prospettici. Il corpus, depositato su Zenodo, contesta l’idea di una prospettiva albertiana a scacchiera applicata in modo uniforme. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione fino al Cenacolo, Leonardo lascia nel quadro i moduli con cui ha misurato: bugne e mattonelle (geometria inserita), la maglia 4:3 (geometria svelata), i ritmi degli arazzi e dei cassettoni (geometria intonata).   Metodo La ricerca adotta un approccio di retroingegneria: parte da ciò che è visibile e misurabile nelle opere per ricostruire i principi metrici e modulari che ne organizzano lo spazio.   Ricerca: 10.5281/zenodo.20334160     Funzione dell’app L’app è uno strumento di supporto alla ricerca accademica: non la sostituisce, ma la integra, rendendone più accessibili e immediatamente comprensibili i risultati più significativi. È tuttora in fase di sviluppo e viene progressivamente aggiornata con l’avanzamento degli studi.   App: https://comet-zinc-crane-monarch.grok.me     Preface   Leonardo’s Score is not an isolated inquiry. It is one panel of the triptych Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar, with Leonardo’s Rulers and Leonardo’s CAD: three inquiries born apart, one metric-modular grammar of space. The grammar Leonardo da Vinci used to construct his perspectival spaces. The corpus, deposited on Zenodo, challenges the idea of an Albertian checkerboard perspective applied uniformly. From the Annunciation through the Adoration to the Last Supper, Leonardo leaves in the picture the modules he measured with: ashlars and tiles (inserted geometry), the 4:3 mesh (revealed geometry), the rhythms of the tapestries and coffers (tuned geometry). The method is reverse engineering, starting from what can be seen and measured. This app was developed to highlight the most significant findings of the research.         Method The research adopts a reverse-engineering approach: it begins with what is visible and measurable in the works to reconstruct the metric and modular principles that organize their space.   Research: 10.5281/zenodo.20334160   Purpose of the App The app is designed to support academic research: it does not replace it but complements it by making its most significant findings more accessible and easier to understand. It is still under development and is progressively updated as the research advances.   App: https://comet-zinc-crane-monarch.grok.me       Giancarlo De Leo 20 ottobre 2026

summary: Companion code for the preprint "Benchmarking Real-Time DETR Detectors for Multibeam Forward-Looking Sonar: DEIMv2, Detector-Specific Test-Time Fusion, and Domain Shift Analysis on UATD" (Preprints 2026, 2026090449, doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3). Contains the DEIMv2 engine with UATD configs, the TTA/WBF fusion tooling (default --wbf-rule view-dedup; query-level retained as reproduction control), the paired image-level bootstrap CI scripts, the paper's three central results tables as CSV, and unit tests pinning the WBF view-dedup rule and the bootstrap identity property. The UATD dataset itself is NOT redistributed; fetch it from the official figshare channel (article 21331143) via the included download scripts. License: benchmark code MIT; the DEIMv2 engine remains under the DEIMv2 non-commercial license (LICENSE-DEIMv2.md). v3 (2026-09-29): reviewer-comment C13 fix — analysis/bootstrap_ci.py now averages AR@100 over valid recall entries only (excluding the -1 sentinel for classes absent from a bootstrap resample), matching the COCOeval convention already used for mAP. Adds analysis/bootstrap_arfix_recompute.py (analytic recompute of all 14 archived AR@100 bootstrap intervals from the per-replicate CSVs), results/boot_out/*_arfixed.json (defective-vs-fixed intervals; max change 0.001 on any bound, no reported number changes), and tests/test_bootstrap_missing_class.py pinning the fixed behavior. v4 (2026-10-17): adds the DEIMv2-S seed-43/44 fusion summary ( results/ablation_wbf_dedup_seed4344_summary.json ) with its generation script ( tools/ablation_wbf_dedup_seed4344.py ) and the run log ( results/S_seed4344_fusion_20261014.md ), as referenced in the paper's Table II note; README updated (preprint v3 DOI, 90/10 seed-42 split reproduction command, seed-43/44 result registration, and a note cross-checking the vendored WBF against the reference PyPI package ensemble-boxes 1.0.6); manifests regenerated (252 files). v5 (2026-10-18): adds the score-only control ablation for the view-deduplication analysis (paper Sec. III-B): generation script ( tools/ablation_scoreonly_test1.py ) and results ( results/ablation_scoreonly_test1.json , Test_1: query-level vs score-only vs view-dedup, isolating score normalization from member removal); README updated (tool and result registration); manifests regenerated (254 files). The preprint reference remains doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3. v6 (2026-10-19): adds the multi-seed fusion evidence released with the companion paper (arXiv-style short report): per-seed fusion results for RT-DETRv2-R18 ( results/B1_*.json , seeds 42-44, both fusion rules, both test splits), paired per-seed difference table ( results/table3_paired_seed_results.csv ), tau-sensitivity scan and vendored-WBF reference arm ( results/results_tau_sensitivity.json , results/results_wbf_reference.json ; scripts tools/exp_tau_sensitivity.py , tools/exp_wbf_reference.py ; vendored reference implementation in ref_impl/ ); README updated (reproduction and metric-semantics notes); manifests regenerated (275 files). The preprint reference remains doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3. v7 (2026-10-20): adds the sixteen per-view prediction dumps ( results/*_views_test*.json ; 1,440,000 records each: 800 images x top-300 x 6 TTA views) for DEIMv2-S seeds 42-44, RT-DETRv2-R18 seeds 42-44, D-FINE-HGNetV2-S seed 42, and DEIM-HGNetV2-S seed 42, together with per-unit cluster-size statistics ( results/tu_cluster_stats/ ), a provenance record ( results/per_view_dump_provenance.json ), and tools/tu_cluster_stats.py ; ablation_wbf_dedup.py and ablation_wbf_dedup_seed4344.py now read dumps from ../results/ . These dumps back the per-seed fusion results ( results/table3_paired_seed_results.csv ) and the cluster statistics of the companion paper. DEIMv2-M has no per-view dump by design.

summary: CRA-SME is an open-source Python toolkit for research on evidence-based software release decisions under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises. Its release-decision engine evaluates a bundle of build-bound evidence and returns PASS, REVIEW_REQUIRED or FAIL with machine-readable reasons. Missing, stale or tampered evidence never passes, and the tool never asserts legal conformity. Research modules replay historical releases using only the knowledge available on each release date, seed evidence faults, check inventory completeness and support blinded manual validation. Main components Release-decision engine (crasme-gate command and Python API). It has 65 reason codes and is fail-safe on missing, failed, invalid, stale or tampered evidence. Each decision is bound to the build by digest and validated against a JSON Schema. PASS means only “eligible for human conformity review”, and risk scores are never inputs to the gate. Evidence and inventory modules. These cover scan-status records, provenance manifests and traceability units. They include CycloneDX SBOM and lockfile parsers (npm, pnpm, yarn, Go, Cargo, pip, rebar3) and ecosystem-aware version ordering. They evaluate OSV affected ranges and filter the CISA KEV catalogue as of a given date, and apply inventory-completeness rules. Research instruments. These are a time-correct release replay with fail-safe data fetching, a seeded-fault suite of 69 evidence faults, and a validation kit with blinded rater sheets, Cohen’s κ and Wilson intervals. Supporting material. This includes a 46-row CRA obligation catalogue (legally unverified by design), a risk and evidence workbook, SHA-pinned GitHub Actions workflows, protocols for nine experiments (E1–E9), eight executed Jupyter notebooks and 285 tests. New in version 1.3.0 Results of the pre-registered E9 retrospective release replay (pre-registration: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438234 ; registered run 39047161461). The replay covered 144 releases of 20 open-source IoT and network products (2024Q4–2026Q3). – No assessable release shipped a vulnerability that was already KEV-listed (0/119), whereas 58% shipped a version-matched high or critical vulnerability. – The fail-safe engine passed no release with an empty or invalid inventory, but it passed 19 of 20 releases whose inventories were present yet declared incomplete. Exploratory re-analyses: time to first observed absence with Kaplan–Meier bounds, and product-cluster confidence intervals. The post-hoc E9-G completeness-aware gating experiment. It passed none of 24 known-incomplete releases and reduced false passes on seeded faults from 80/130 to 12/130. Resilient OSV retrieval and fail-safe handling of unfetched records (deviations D1–D3, documented in experiments/e9_release_replay/REGISTRATION.md), the validation kit and reproducible figure scripts. Data status. The real data are the E1 pilot outputs and the E9 release sample, inventories and results. The E9 data cache and raw outputs are archived separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23441593 . All other example data are synthetic and labelled as such: the demo release bundle, the mutation suite and the synthetic replay cache. E9 findings are version matches, not confirmed exposures. The registered manual validation is in progress. Limits. These are research instruments only: not legal advice and not a conformity assessment. The open-source projects are used as proxies; no claim is made that they fall under the CRA. Licensing. The code is licensed under Apache-2.0. Documentation, templates, the obligation catalogue, workbooks and notebook text are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSES/ and NOTICE). AI assistance. Parts of the code, documentation and protocols were developed with the assistance of an AI system (Claude, Anthropic). The authors reviewed all outputs and are responsible for

summary: This dataset accompanies the Perspective “Coupling, Not Mirroring: Complementarity and Credibility in Microphysiological System–Digital Twin Integration” (Bertani et al., NAM Journal, submitted 2026). It contains the evidence behind the article’s map of published integrations between microphysiological systems (MPS) and computational models. Forty-two studies were read in full text. Each was classified by the direction of information flow between experiment and model, using six regimes: R0 data extraction, R1 calibration only, R2 calibration and external projection, R3 model-guided design, R4 offline reciprocal cycle and R5 continuous closed loop. The rubric was fixed before the corpus was read. Every classification is supported by locators to the source article (section, page, figure). The script build/build.py regenerates Figure 2, Supplementary Table S1 and every count reported in the article from the records: 8 / 7 / 17 / 5 / 5 / 0 studies across the six regimes; 25 studies evaluate a model output against evidence not used to build the model; 6 project beyond the calibration conditions without evaluating that projection; 11 do neither. Contents: records/: one extraction record per study (Markdown with YAML frontmatter). Each record gives the classification, its provenance, a paraphrased summary and open questions. One further record covers an adjacent experimental system discussed in the article. skills/: the classification rubric (version 1.1), the nine documented readings that settle boundary cases, and the ratification protocol. build/: Python scripts (standard library only) that check consistency across records and build the outputs. out/: the evidence table, Table S1 rows, counts and Figure 2. search/: the Scopus query strings and a recall check against 25 reference studies. provenance/: DOI, Crossref metadata and licence for every classified article. No full text, PDF, figure or bulk extract of the classified articles is included. Verbatim quotations are kept only for articles that Crossref lists under a Creative Commons licence. For the 13 articles without an open licence they have been replaced by placeholders, and the locators are kept. The Scopus exports are not included. The extraction records were drafted by Claude models (Anthropic), one isolated run per article, under the rubric. They were then checked for consistency, and ratified or decided by the authors where flagged; the record shows who made each decision. Some documentation files are in Italian. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for data and documentation, MIT for the code in build/. Quoted passages remain under the licence of their source article.

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. Would it benefit from language editing? No The languages is clear and no major errors could be found hinderig the understanding of the resarch. However some minor issues could be corrected, such as, constant capitalisation of the first letter in column names. Would you
title: Structured PREreview of "Female Signatories and Peace Durability: Replicating Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018)"

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
