summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

summary: We develop a rigorous finite-dimensional mathematical framework connecting the renormalization group, gradient flows, Lyapunov stability, and noncooperative game theory. The central object is a renormalization-group flow written in gradient form, dg_i/dt = β_i(g) = - ∑_j G_ij(g) ∂Γ/∂g_j(g),          (1) where g = (g_1, …, g_n) belongs to an open domain M ⊂ ℝⁿ, Γ is a C² function, and G(g) is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. We associate to this flow a common-payoff game whose payoff is U(g) = - Γ(g).                   (2) We prove, with complete arguments, that ordinary Nash equilibria always imply renormalization-group fixed points, but the converse is false. We then identify the exact condition under which a fixed point becomes a genuine stable equilibrium of the game: a nondegenerate renormalization-group fixed point is asymptotically stable if and only if the Hessian of Γ is positive definite, if and only if it is a strict local minimum of Γ, if and only if it is a strict strong Nash equilibrium of U = -Γ. The distinction between ordinary Nash equilibrium and strong Nash equilibrium is essential. Ordinary Nash equilibria allow only unilateral deviations, while strong Nash equilibria exclude all small joint deviations. We provide explicit counterexamples showing that fixed points need not be Nash equilibria, that ordinary Nash equilibria need not be stable, and that invertibility of G alone does not imply finiteness of equilibria. We also prove global existence results under compactness and finiteness results under Morse nondegeneracy. The paper is self-contained at the level of multivariable calculus, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations, and basic Lyapunov stability theory. The framework is intentionally conditional: it does not claim that the gradient-flow representation has been proven in four-dimensional QCD or in any specific quantum field theory. Those issues are placed in a final section of open problems.

summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

summary: Popper’s (1983, 2002) philosophy of science has enjoyed something of a renaissance in the wake of the replication crisis, offering a philosophical basis for the ensuing science reform movement. However, adherence to Popper’s approach may also be at least partly responsible for the sense of “crisis” that has developed following multiple unexpected replication failures. In this article, I contrast Popper’s approach with that of Lakatos (1978) as well as with a related but problematic approach called naïve methodological falsificationism (NMF; Lakatos, 1978). The Popperian approach is powerful because it is based on logical refutations, but its theories are noncausal and, therefore, potentially lacking in scientific value. In contrast, the Lakatosian approach considers causal theories, but it concedes that these theories are not logically refutable. Finally, NMF represents a hybrid approach that subjects Lakatosian causal theories to Popperian logical refutations. However, its tactic of temporarily accepting a ceteris paribus clause during theory testing may be viewed as scientifically inappropriate, epistemically inconsistent, and “completely redundant” (Lakatos, 1978, p. 40). I conclude that the replication “crisis” makes the most sense in the context of the Popperian and NMF approaches because it is only in these two approaches that the failure to replicate a previously corroborated theory represents a logical refutation of that theory. In contrast, such replication failures are less problematic in the Lakatosian approach because they do not logically refute theories. Indeed, in the Lakatosian approach, replication failures can be temporarily ignored or used to motivate theory development.
title: The replication crisis is less of a "crisis" in Lakatos' philosophy of science than it is in Popper's.

summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.
title: Synthesis and Verification of Transformer Programs

summary: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 allows a child aged sixteen or seventeen who is alleged to have committed a heinous offence to be tried as an adult after a "preliminary assessment" by the Juvenile Justice Board. This paper argues that the transfer mechanism is less a principled answer to serious adolescent offending than a legislative compromise whose costs fall on the procedural guarantees the Act otherwise extends to children. It reads section 15 against the Supreme Court's decisions in Shilpa Mittal and Barun Chandra Thakur, the age-determination case law, and the developmental research on adolescent culpability, and it engages the retributive and victim-centred case for transfer on its own terms. Accountability and rehabilitation, the paper contends, are not two poles to be traded off at a single age threshold. Both depend on institutional capacity that the system has never been resourced to supply: functioning Boards, trained probation staff, individual care plans that are actually followed, and aftercare that reaches young people beyond eighteen. Reform should narrow and proceduralise transfer, introduce statutory diversion, decouple offence classification from the general penal code, and treat implementation failure as a rights violation rather than an administrative shortfall.

summary: Lecture 1 formulated the recommendation problem in abstract terms: a set of users U , a set of items I , and a preference function r(u,i) that must be estimated for the pairs that have not been observed. Every algorithm studied in this course, however, operates on concrete data rather than on abstractions. The quality of a recommender system is therefore bounded by the quality, the structure, and the representation of the data from which it learns. In practice, improving the data frequently brings larger gains than changing the algorithm. A sophisticated model trained on noisy, biased, or poorly prepared data produces poor recommendations, a principle often summarized as garbage in, garbage out . This lecture therefore addresses three questions: è Which data does a recommender system collect, and what do these data really mean? è How can these data be organized and represented so that algorithms can process them? è How must the data be prepared and partitioned before a model is built and assessed? After studying this lecture, the reader should be able to: · Identify the sources and categories of data used in a recommender system; · Characterize explicit and implicit feedback, including their strengths and weaknesses; · Construct a user–item matrix and interpret its sparsity; · Represent users and items as vectors built from interactions and descriptive features; · Apply the main preprocessing operations to ratings and implicit signals; · Split a dataset correctly and avoid information leakage. The path followed by the data throughout this lecture is: Data sources → Feedback signals → User–item matrix → Vector representations → Preprocessing → Data splitting

Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding

summary: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees. To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. At Ethereum's update rate, which leaves a monolithic chain stable, the multi-chain system exhibits extreme load oscillation between full and near-empty blocks, with over half of all blocks at full capacity. Mainstream Cosmos chains already exceed their safe bounds under their default configurations, and the resulting load oscillation raises their block failure rate by an order of magnitude. Guided by this mechanism, we design a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction and stabilizes dynamics in multi-chain environments.
title: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems

summary: Diffusion-based multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) decode by iterative denoising with bidirectional attention, which precludes the standard autoregressive key--value cache. Practical deployments therefore rely on approximate caching that reuses intermediate states across denoising steps. Tracing the context-token information flow reveals three disruptions. Within a step, caching disperses the attention that anchors a position on nearby context tokens. Across steps, similarity-based refresh is not staleness-aware, so some positions are decoded against stale key--value states. Across layers, the deep-layer entropy of the context fails to converge where repetition arises. We accordingly propose CoTA++, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that counteracts each disruption where it originates: Context-Token Attention Re-anchoring re-forms the attention routing against the current context, Decode-Aware Refresh reserves part of the cache's refresh budget for the positions about to be committed, and Context-Token Entropy-Guided Voting discounts the confidence of a position by the deep-layer entropy of its context, which reorders the unmasking. summary: How much classical information can a noisy optical channel carry when both signal energy and preshared entanglement are limited? This work gives an exact capacity frontier for this joint resource problem. It allows one to determine the best asymptotic communication rate, price the benefit of additional entanglement, and distinguish the effect of tolerating errors from that of changing how entanglement is supplied. Exact capacity under two resource constraints The setting is any fixed bosonic Gaussian channel \(\Phi\) with finitely many input and output modes. Signal energy is measured by a positive quadratic Hamiltonian \(H_G=\tfrac12 R^{\mathsf T}GR\), with \(G>0\) and ground energy \(E_0\); \(R\) collects the canonical quadratures. The budgets satisfy \(E\ge E_0\) and \(P\ge0\). For an \(n\)-use code, the mean total signal energy is at most \(nE\), while the same initially shared maximally entangled state has Schmidt rank \(K_n\) satisfying \(\log K_n\le nP\). Thus \(P\) is a strictly supplied entanglement rate. Encoders may be arbitrary joint quantum operations, and decoding may be collective. The classical capacity is \[ C(E,P)=\max_{\substack{U\ge V\;\mathrm{physical}\\ \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(GU)\le E,\;S_G(V)\le P}}\bigl[S_G(\Phi U)+S_G(V)-S_G(\Phi^c V)\bigr]. \] Here \(V\) is a Gaussian seed covariance, \(U\) is the average-input covariance, and \(U-V\) is the displacement-modulation covariance. A covariance is physical when \(V+i\Omega/2\ge0\), where \(\Omega\) is the canonical commutation matrix and the vacuum covariance is \(I/2\). The notation \(S_G\) denotes Gaussian von Neumann entropy, and \(\Phi^c\) is the full complementary channel, including any environment purification. All logarithms are natural, so rates are in nats per channel use. This formula replaces optimization over arbitrary quantum block codes by a finite-dimensional covariance optimization. It supplies both an achievable rate and a converse against non-Gaussian, correlated encodings. At \(P=0\), it also determines the unassisted capacity of general fixed finite-mode Gaussian channels, including channels without a passive decomposition into independent modes. The reduction specifies the exact capacity value; it does not require a closed-form optimizer for every device. Energy and strict entanglement supply respond differently to errors For a fixed allowed average error \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), the exact capacity under the mean-energy constraint is \[ C_\varepsilon(E,P)=C\!\left(E_0+\frac{E-E_0}{1-\varepsilon},\,P\right). \] Allowing failure rescales the mean energy above the ground state, but leaves the strict initial entanglement budget unchanged. The proof uses an exponential strong converse for codes whose inputs obey a hard total-energy cutoff. In a different model, where a readable flag permits random entanglement supply constrained only on average, the work establishes an achievable bound and a strict small-supply advantage for thermal attenuation at positive energy and fixed nonzero error. That comparison identifies the operational importance of the supply rule; it is not a complete capacity characterization of the flagged model. The communication value of entanglement For a thermal attenuator, let \(0<\eta<1\) be the transmissivity, \(b>0\) the output mean photon number for vacuum input, and \(N\) the input mean photon number. Write its capacity as \(C_N(P)\), and define \(g(N)=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N\). The gain from entanglement obeys the sharp bound \[ 0\le C_N(P)-C_N(0)\le\frac{\eta}{1+b}\,P. \] For every fixed \(N>0\), the coefficient \(\eta/(1+b)\) is attained as the initial right derivative at \(P=0\). In the low-photon limit, the stronger resource law is \[ C_N(P)-C_N(0)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}\min\{P,g(N)\}+O(N),\qquad N\downarrow0. \] The remainder is uniform over \(P\ge0\) at fixed \(\eta\) and positive \(b\). Noise therefore determines the conversion efficiency, while \(g(N)\sim N\log(1/N)\) sets the entanglement scale
title: A universal energy–entanglement capacity frontier for Gaussian optical channels

summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.

summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. The hourly water levels and daily rainfall were obtained from the Royal Irrigation Department (RID), Thailand, and are not included because redistribution permission has not been confirmed; with those data, the retrospective analyses can be re-run from the scripts provided. The record supports a manuscript and does not constitute validation of an autonomous flood-warning system.   Supports the manuscript submitted to *Natural Hazards*: *Selecting hourly water-level forecasting models for flood warning in small-to-medium basins of Thailand: benchmarks, leakage control and operational verification*. Every retrospective result is based on the open-source Python ANN (P.87 with 5 hidden units), with leakage checks and a 76-day operational record. - New analysis code: `python_main_evaluation.py`, `model_comparison.py` (all methods on the hours common to every method; Table 2, Fig. 3), `gbm_benchmark.py` (XGBoost), `infold_selection.py` (in-fold LASSO; base, causal-wavelet and rainfall pools; Table 3), `rain_daily_parse.py` (daily-rainfall parser; rainfall not included), `export_travel_time_data.py` and `export_travel_time_py.py` (Fig. 5 values), `rain_delta_rmse.py` (per-year rainfall effect), `gbm_tuned.py` and `gbm_tuned_eval.py` (nested-tuned XGBoost), `swrm_additions.py` (90% prediction intervals, P.87 one-unit check, P.85 bias and stage relation), `code/ann/python/ann_rerun.py` (5 hidden units for P.87; whole-year early stopping). - GRU: `lstm_benchmark.py` updated (`--cell gru`) and `hpc/slurm/gru_erawan.sbatch` added. - New results: `python_main_evaluation.json`, `model_comparison.json` and per-year CSVs, `gbm_runs.json`, `gru_benchmark.json`, `infold_selected_*.json`, `rain_delta_rmse_per_year.csv`, `gbm_tuned_runs.json`, `gbm_tuned_eval.json`, `swrm_additions.json`, `operational_evaluation_20261017.json` (window to 17 October 2026), per-year metrics of the ANN reruns. - `figures/`: the eight figures of the Natural Hazards manuscript (Fig1–Fig8); earlier figures remain in versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. - Removed: the MATLAB reference scripts with their registry builder and MATLAB-vs-Python comparison files (published separately by T. Chaipimonplin; `registry.json` is kept), and all figure-drawing scripts (the record ships the final figures only). - Environment: scikit-learn 1.7.1, xgboost 3.4.1, scipy 1.16.1 added.

summary: GO3 New Release Notes This release introduces major enhancements to GAF 2.2 annotation parsing, native annotation filtering in Rust, transparent .gz support, bidirectional gene–term queries, expanded ontology graph traversal, pairwise GO term similarity/distance matrices, semantic redundancy reduction & clustering, and built-in Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis (ORA). ────── What's New 1. Native GAF Annotation Filtering (load_gaf_terms) Filter annotations directly during Rust-level GAF parsing with zero Python overhead: • evidence_codes: Keep only annotations matching specific evidence codes (e.g., ["EXP", "IDA", "IPI", "IMP", "IGI", "IEP"]), or use only_experimental=True as a shortcut. • exclude_evidence_codes: Exclude specific evidence codes (e.g., ["IEA", "ND"]). • ignore_not=True: Automatically discard negative annotations (NOT qualifiers such as NOT|located_in). • aspects: Restrict loaded annotations to specific GO aspects (["P"], ["F"], ["C"] or "BP", "MF", "CC"). • taxons: Filter by NCBI taxon IDs (["taxon:9606"] or ["9606"]). • assigned_by: Keep only annotations curated by specific databases (e.g., ["UniProt", "MGI"]). 2. Full 17-Column GAF 2.2 Inspection (parse_gaf & GAFAnnotation) • Added go3.parse_gaf(path, ...) returning GAFAnnotation objects with all 17 GAF 2.2 columns (db, db_object_id, db_object_symbol, qualifier, go_id, db_reference, evidence_code, with_from, aspect, db_object_name, db_object_synonym, db_object_type, taxon, date, assigned_by, annotation_extension, gene_product_form_id). • Supports the exact same native filtering arguments as load_gaf_terms, plus to_dict() for seamless DataFrame conversion (pd.DataFrame([a.to_dict() for a in records])). 3. Transparent .gz Compressed File Support • load_obo, load_gaf_terms, and parse_gaf now transparently read .obo.gz and .gaf.gz files on the fly without requiring prior decompression on disk. 4. Bidirectional Gene–Term Lookup API Inspect the loaded GAF index directly from Python: • go3.list_genes(). List all loaded gene symbols. • go3.get_terms_for_gene(gene, ontology=None). Retrieve GO term IDs annotated to a gene (optionally filtered by ontology aspect). • go3.get_genes_for_term(go_id). Retrieve all genes directly annotated to a GO term. 5. Expanded Ontology Graph Traversal (GOTerm) • Added term.descendants (all transitive child terms) alongside term.ancestors. • Added term.relations (Dict[str, List[str]]) exposing typed ontology relationships (part_of, regulates, negatively_regulates, positively_regulates, etc.). • Added go3.list_terms(ontology=None) to list all non-obsolete GO term IDs, optionally filtered by ontology ("BP", "MF", "CC"). 6. Pairwise Term Similarity & Distance Matrices • go3.term_similarity_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Parallelized pairwise similarity matrix (N × N) for a list of GO terms. • go3.term_distance_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Normalized semantic distance matrix (1 - sim, with self-similarity normalized for unbounded metrics like "ic" / "resnik"), ready for scipy, scikit-learn, or umap. 7. Semantic Redundancy Reduction & GO Term Clustering • go3.reduce_redundant_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin", scores=None, prefer="ic"). REVIGO-style greedy semantic deduplication of GO term lists based on custom scores (e.g., -log₁₀(FDR)), Information Content ("ic"), or ontology depth ("depth"). • go3.cluster_go_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin"). Connected-components clustering of semantically related GO terms. 8. Native GO Enrichment Analysis (ORA) • go3.go_enrichment(...) & EnrichmentResult. High-performance Over-Representation Analysis computed in Rust with ontology ancestor propagation (true-path ru

summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.
title: engiNIR: A universal engineering tool for near-infrared spectra and hyperspectral imaging

summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. The repository — https://github.com/Capta1n-n9m0/cafrl-negative — holds the per-video model scores, the decision rules frozen before the runs they adjudicate, every run's configuration and validation curve, the evaluation and statistical harness, the face-crop and re-encode pipeline, the self-audit record with its defect ledger, and two claims maps that give the artifact and method for each reported value row by row. Its tagged tree (v2.0.2) is included here as cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz . This version holds: cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz — the repository at tag v2.0.2 (new). <run>.best.pt — 26 frozen model checkpoints (2.7 GB in all), one file per run: the best.pt (best mean validation AUC) of each run added in revision 1, with checkpoints-r1-manifest.json giving each one's run, architecture, arm, training protocol, augmentation policy, seed, selected epoch, selection metric and SHA-256 (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v2.0.0; no best_valloss.pt ). The v2.0.0 release notes call this payload checkpoints-r1.tar ; the deposit holds the same 26 checkpoints as separate files. checkpoints.tar — 37 frozen model checkpoints (6.0 GB), every best*.pt of the 27 v1.0.0 runs, with checkpoints-manifest.json (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0). crop-coordinates.tar.zst — 48,294 per-video face-crop records: the frames selected, the bounding boxes, the five-point landmarks and the alignment settings. summary: This dataset was produced by iGEM Team Al-Nahrain-IRAQ 2026 (AL-Nahrain University, Iraq) as a part of SYNOVA  project , which aim to  predict, optimize and  detect yeast activity . iGEM wiki : https://2026.igem.wiki/al-nahrain-iraq CONTENTS    Metadata.zip ethanol_yield.csv : Experimental metadata for 8 experiments: strain, genetic modification, target gene, growth medium, temperature, carbon source, time, pH and ethanol yield, manually extracted from published studies, with DOI and BioProject for each experiment. R64.csv : S. cerevisiae S288C reference gene annotation (assembly R64-1-1), exported from Ensembl BioMart (accessed August 2026). Columns: RefSeq DNA ID, Gene stable ID, gene description, chromosome, gene start/end (bp), strand (1 = forward, -1 = reverse), gene name, GC content (%), gene type and SGD ID. Empty cells indicate no identifier available in Ensembl. The Gene stable ID (e.g. YPL071C) links this table to the count and SNP files Gene_Expression_ counts.zip : 7 gene-level RNA-seq count files, used as input for differential expression analysis. RNA_ SNPs.zip : 7 SNP files called from the RNA-seq data, with SNP positions mapped to genes using the R64 annotation. DESeq2_Experimental_ model.zip : differential expression analyses for 2 models/comparisons using DESeq2. One model will be selected as the reference workflow for the project's AI component to analyse count data in the same way.   METHODS   RNA-seq / gene expression (Galaxy): FastQC (quality control) → Trimmomatic (adapter and quality trimming) → HISAT2 (alignment to S288C R64) → featureCounts (gene-level counts). DESeq2 differential expression analysis was run in Google Colab, using code written with AI assistance.  SNP analysis (Galaxy): FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → MarkDuplicates → AddOrReplaceReadGroups → bcftools mpileup → bcftools call → bcftools filter → bcftools +setGT → bcftools query. SNP annotation: chromosome/position of each SNP → R64 gene annotation → corresponding gene.  CONTRIBUTIONS  H. R. Abdulateef performed all RNA-seq, SNP and DESeq2 analyses and curated the dataset. H. R .Abdulateef ,T. W. AL-FATAl  , T. N. Taher ,and A. N. Aliyamin collected the data from the literature.
title: AL-Nahrain-IRAQ: RNA-seq gene counts, SNPs and DESeq2 models of ethanol-producing Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains (SYNOVA)

summary: Companion code for the preprint "Benchmarking Real-Time DETR Detectors for Multibeam Forward-Looking Sonar: DEIMv2, Detector-Specific Test-Time Fusion, and Domain Shift Analysis on UATD" (Preprints 2026, 2026090449, doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3). Contains the DEIMv2 engine with UATD configs, the TTA/WBF fusion tooling (default --wbf-rule view-dedup; query-level retained as reproduction control), the paired image-level bootstrap CI scripts, the paper's three central results tables as CSV, and unit tests pinning the WBF view-dedup rule and the bootstrap identity property. summary: CRA-SME is an open-source Python toolkit for research on evidence-based software release decisions under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises. Its release-decision engine evaluates a bundle of build-bound evidence and returns PASS, REVIEW_REQUIRED or FAIL with machine-readable reasons. Missing, stale or tampered evidence never passes, and the tool never asserts legal conformity. Research modules replay historical releases using only the knowledge available on each release date, seed evidence faults, check inventory completeness and support blinded manual validation. Main components Release-decision engine (crasme-gate command and Python API). It has 65 reason codes and is fail-safe on missing, failed, invalid, stale or tampered evidence. Each decision is bound to the build by digest and validated against a JSON Schema. PASS means only “eligible for human conformity review”, and risk scores are never inputs to the gate. Evidence and inventory modules. These cover scan-status records, provenance manifests and traceability units. They include CycloneDX SBOM and lockfile parsers (npm, pnpm, yarn, Go, Cargo, pip, rebar3) and ecosystem-aware version ordering. They evaluate OSV affected ranges and filter the CISA KEV catalogue as of a given date, and apply inventory-completeness rules. Research instruments. These are a time-correct release replay with fail-safe data fetching, a seeded-fault suite of 69 evidence faults, and a validation kit with blinded rater sheets, Cohen’s κ and Wilson intervals. Supporting material. This includes a 46-row CRA obligation catalogue (legally unverified by design), a risk and evidence workbook, SHA-pinned GitHub Actions workflows, protocols for nine experiments (E1–E9), eight executed Jupyter notebooks and 285 tests. New in version 1.3.0 Results of the pre-registered E9 retrospective release replay (pre-registration: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438234 ; registered run 39047161461). The replay covered 144 releases of 20 open-source IoT and network products (2024Q4–2026Q3). – No assessable release shipped a vulnerability that was already KEV-listed (0/119), whereas 58% shipped a version-matched high or critical vulnerability. – The fail-safe engine passed no release with an empty or invalid inventory, but it passed 19 of 20 releases whose inventories were present yet declared incomplete. Exploratory re-analyses: time to first observed absence with Kaplan–Meier bounds, and product-cluster confidence intervals. The post-hoc E9-G completeness-aware gating experiment. It passed none of 24 known-incomplete releases and reduced false passes on seeded faults from 80/130 to 12/130. Resilient OSV retrieval and fail-safe handling of unfetched records (deviations D1–D3, documented in experiments/e9_release_replay/REGISTRATION.md), the validation kit and reproducible figure scripts. Data status. The real data are the E1 pilot outputs and the E9 release sample, inventories and results. The E9 data cache and raw outputs are archived separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23441593 . All other example data are synthetic and labelled as such: the demo release bundle, the mutation suite and the synthetic replay cache. E9 findings are version matches, not confirmed exposures. The registered manual validation is in progress. Limits. These are research instruments only: not legal advice and not a conformity assessment. The open-source projects are used as proxies; no claim is made that they fall under the CRA. Licensing. The code is licensed under Apache-2.0. Documentation, templates, the obligation catalogue, workbooks and notebook text are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSES/ and NOTICE). AI assistance. Parts of the code, documentation and protocols were developed with the assistance of an AI system (Claude, Anthropic). The authors reviewed all outputs and are responsible for

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: The island of St. Vincent and the other Windward Islands in the southeastern Caribbean were chosen as a field site for the study of weak mountain wakes. By the authorsメ definition, a モweak wakeヤ forms when the potential vorticity generated by a mountain is not strong enough to advect itself into eddies; rather, it is simply advocated downstream by the ambient flow. GOES-8 and Landsat sunlit images unambiguously revealed that the mountainous Windward Islands have remarkably long straight wakes. The length of St. Vincentメs wake exceeds 300 km although its width is only 20 km. Near the islands, the wake structures reflect the details of the island topography. These wakes do not exhibit any obvious diurnal effect. Boat surveys in the lee of St. Vincent confirmed the existence of features seen in the images: the sharp wake boundary, the small valley-induced jet embedded in the near wake, and the absence of any reverse flow. Aircraft surveys gave evidence of descent over the island and showed that the wake air is relatively warm and dry. The length of the wake (L) agrees with the formula L = H/2CD (where H is the wake depth and CD is the surface drag coefficient), implying that the reacceleration of the wake air is caused by the ambient streamwise pressure gradient rather than by lateral entrainment of momentum or geostrophic adjustment. Two numerical models were used to simulate St. Vincentメs wake, a single-layer hydrostatic model and a 3D nonhydrostatic model. Both models indicated that air descent, acceleration, wave breaking, and weak potential vorticity generation occur over the island, causing a long straight wake. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: The Wake of St. Vincent - FGDC XML metadata artifact

The length of St. Vincentメs wake exceeds 300 km although its width is only 20 km. Near the islands, the wake structures reflect the details of the island topography. These wakes do not exhibit any obvious diurnal effect. Boat surveys in the lee of St. Vincent confirmed the existence of features seen in the images: the sharp wake boundary, the small valley-induced jet embedded in the near wake, and the absence of any reverse flow. Aircraft surveys gave evidence of descent over the island and showed that the wake air is relatively warm and dry. The length of the wake (L) agrees with the formula L = H/2CD (where H is the wake depth and CD is the surface drag coefficient), implying that the reacceleration of the wake air is caused by the ambient streamwise pressure gradient rather than by lateral entrainment of momentum or geostrophic adjustment. Two numerical models were used to simulate St. Vincentメs wake, a single-layer hydrostatic model and a 3D nonhydrostatic model. Both models indicated that air descent, acceleration, wave breaking, and weak potential vorticity generation occur over the island, causing a long straight wake. summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. summary: The studies and the guidelines built on them answer for groups. The decision is for one patient, and the gap between the two is bridged by the clinician’s intuition, which practice does not train and almost nobody measures. This note describes a short session that does both: a lecture, a demonstration, then real cases with immediate, sourced feedback and a private report. The examples are obstetric and from early breast cancer; the problem and the method are the same in every field of medicine, because every clinical decision is made for one patient from evidence about groups.
title: Deciding for one patient: training clinical intuition

summary: The NOAA/NASA Pathfinder Program SSM/I Level 3 EASE-Grid Brightness Temperatures will consist of three series produced on CD-ROM, one series each for the EASE-Grid Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere and Cylindrical (global) projections. Grids represent spatially interpolated data. The interpolation technique maximizes the radiometric integrity of original brightness temperature values, maintain high spatial and temporal precision, and involve no averaging of original swath data. Coverage is global and spans the Pathfinder SSM/I Benchmark period, from 1 August 1987 through 30 November 1988. Resolution is 25 km for all channels and 12.5 km for the 85 GHz channels. There are 18 brightness temperature files per day for a given projection (nine each for ascending and descending passes), and two (ascending and descending) corresponding time files. Data are contained in flat binary files, either one image per file consisting of two-dimensional 2-byte integer arrays of brightness temperatures in tenths of Kelvins, or in the case of time files, two-dimensional 1-byte integer arrays consisting of GMT in tenths of hours. Data are available as processing is completed, with completion of the data set projected for the end of 1995. Data are available via ftp, on CD-ROM and through the Internet. Contact NSIDC User Services for information. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Ease-Grid Brightness Temperatures - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: Sea Surface Temperature, Wave Height and Period Measurement Details: 16 offshore, coastal and inshore moored buoys with on-board data loggers and telemetry via GOES; onboard calculation of significant wave height and peak period. Various starting dates, beginning as early as 1988. Publication: "Technical details on data processing, calibration etc are available in ""Meteorological and Oceanographic Measurements from Canadian Weather Buoys - a Review of Sensors, Data Reduction, Transmission, Quality Control and Archival Methods"", 1996. Prepared by Axys Environmental Consulting Ltd. for Environment Canada. Copy in IOS Library Technical Records." IOSPBS Data Distribution: Historical have been assembled from various sources (MEDS and PWC) and are available at IOS. [Share_data disk: \METBUOY]. Real-time data are received at IOS and eventually replaced by data from AES that has been through their QC/QA procedures. PSARC_Utility: Data are archived at their original sampling interval (hourly). There have been subjected to AES quality control, but there are gaps in the data due to sensor or system failures. We have not assembled daily or monthly summaries of these data. Real time data (unverified by AES) are available at IOS. Improvements: "Data are archived at their original sampling interval (hourly). There have been subjected to AES quality control, but there are gaps in the data due to sensor or system failures. We have not assembled daily or monthly summaries of these data. Real time data (unverified by AES) are available at IOS. Some additional work is required to merge data formats (particularly ""time"" coding). Processes could be developed to automatically generate daily and monthly summary files, which are likely to be more relevant for stock assessment use. In addition, we could attempt to reconstruct the time series BACK in time by extracting data at these locations from the COADS or REYNOLDS datasets." Base Internet/URL -- ( http:/www.ios.bc.ca ) ( http://www.jodc.go.jp/service.htm ) [ A TCODE project ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: Abstract : Background: The production of high-quality planting material during the nursery stage is essential for establishing productive, competitive, and sustainable oil palm plantations. Genetic material and container type may influence seedling development. Objective: To evaluate the growth of seedlings of two oil palm varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.), produced using two container types. Methods: The experiment was conducted in Macuspana, Tabasco, Mexico. Seedling growth was evaluated in two varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana, using tube containers and plastic bags. A randomized complete block design was established with four treatments and four replications, with 100 seedlings per replication (400 seedlings per treatment; 1,600 seedlings in total). Plant height, number of leaves, and stipe diameter were measured every 15 days over 180 days. The same agronomic management was applied to all treatments. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Tukey’s multiple comparison test. Results: Significant differences among treatments were detected for the evaluated growth variables. For plant height, T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) showed the greatest value at 180 days, reaching 68.37 ± 0.61 cm. For number of leaves, T1 (Deli × Compacta in tube containers; DxCt) and T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) recorded 12.95 ± 0.11 and 12.38 ± 0.10 leaves, respectively, at 180 days. For stipe diameter, T1 and T2 showed the highest values at 180 days, with 2.21 ± 0.03 and 2.19 ± 0.03 cm, respectively, whereas T4 recorded 1.95 ± 0.02 cm. Conclusions: Under the conditions evaluated, seedlings produced in tube containers showed greater plant height and number of leaves at the end of the nursery period. Stipe diameter was higher in the Deli × Compacta material than in the Compacta × Ghana material at 180 days. These results support the potential use of tube containers for nursery production.

summary: Graduate students increasingly need publication literacy that combines scientific writing, research integrity, journal selection, and the ability to navigate peer review. This study profiled the understanding of reputable scientific article writing among students in a Master's Program in Sports Coaching Education and identified areas that require targeted academic support. The study used a descriptive quantitative design with total sampling. Forty-three active master's students completed a closed Likert-scale questionnaire after a scientific writing workshop. The instrument covered six domains: scientific article structure, the IMRaD system, publication ethics and plagiarism, reputable-journal selection, citation and referencing, and peer review and revision. Scores were converted into percentages using the procedure defined in the study protocol. The overall understanding score was 75.58%, which the progress report classified as "Good Understanding" because it remained below the 76% threshold for the highest category. Four comparatively weaker items were writing IMRaD sections according to scientific conventions (68.6%), identifying appropriate information for each IMRaD section (69.8%), responding appropriately to reviewer comments (70.1%), and distinguishing scientific articles from popular or opinion articles (71.8%). The findings indicate that students possess a relatively strong conceptual foundation but still need support in applied genre knowledge and publication-process skills. Writing clinics should therefore prioritize guided IMRaD practice, article deconstruction, simulated reviewer-response exercises, and structured journal-selection activities. Because the survey was administered after the workshop and no baseline measure was available, the results describe current understanding and do not establish workshop effectiveness.

summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
title: ENDOSCOPIC EVALUATION OF THE ANTIREFLUX VALVE AFTER FUNDOPLICATION: SYNTHESIS OF THE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSAL OF A FUNCTIONAL ENDOSCOPIC SCORE
