summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "An Exploratory Evaluation of Targeted Label Poisoning in a Client-Local Feature Federated Ensemble for Chest X-Ray Classification." It contains code and saved experimental results for an exploratory study of Pneumonia-to-Normal label poisoning in four-class chest X-ray classification. The study uses 20,795 images from three public sources, with 20,557 perceptual groups kept intact across experimental partitions. The package covers 212 completed training jobs, including main and component comparisons, classifier-head sensitivity, image-model references, candidate probability banks, and earlier-poisoning experiments. The main comparisons and image-model references use ten deterministic seeds. The classifier-head and GRU-structure study uses three seeds. Included materials comprise dataset manifests and image checksums, perceptual-group metadata, split assignments, seeds and configurations, held-out predictions, candidate probabilities, numerical summaries, result figures, analysis and verification scripts, and scientific execution-source snapshots. Additional fixed-model analyses examine validation availability, validation-label contamination, and artifact retention. The README and reproducibility guide explain verification, reanalysis, environment requirements, and dataset reconstruction. Dataset images and model checkpoints are not included. Obtain the source images separately under their applicable access and use terms: COVID-19 Radiography Database: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/covid19-radiography-database COVID19, Pneumonia, Normal Chest X-ray Images: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sachinkumar413/covid-pneumonia-normal-chest-xray-images Tuberculosis Chest X-ray Dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/tuberculosis-tb-chest-xray-dataset The included metadata identify the exact study images for reconstruction from the original source bytes. The attack direction was selected exploratorily, perceptual grouping does not establish patient independence, and source-held-out generalization was not evaluated. summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.
title: Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions

summary: Audio source separation models must preserve fine spectral structure while keeping the cost of the separator tractable. Band-split architectures reduce this cost by manually partitioning the spectrum into predefined frequency bands and encoding each band as a token, but the same boundaries are used for every mixture. Because informative spectral structure varies with source content, fixed boundaries can merge discriminative components or spend tokens where little resolution is needed. We introduce Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), an end-to-end framework that adapts boundary locations and band widths to each mixture under a fixed band-token budget. DBS predicts content-conditioned boundary scores within frequency blocks, selects a prescribed number of boundaries using hard Top-$K$, and applies content-dependent pooling to obtain compact band tokens. After separation, it smooths and expands these tokens to the original STFT grid, refines them along frequency, and decodes complex masks with a frequency-shared head. DBS improved separation over the corresponding static models on DnR v2, MUSDB18-HQ, and EchoSet, with DBS-BSRNN achieving relative gain of 29.0% in average SI-SDR on DnR v2. These results and boundary analyses on DnR v2 show that content-adaptive frequency partitioning benefits multiple separator backbones under a fixed band-token budget. Code and audio demos are available at https://cslikai.cn/Dynamic-Band-Splitting
title: Learning Where to Split: Dynamic Band Splitting for Audio Source Separation

summary: Speech anonymization is evaluated with automatic speaker verification attackers whose performance depends on the attribute distribution of both their training and evaluation data, which may bias privacy estimates for some speaker groups. To alleviate this issue, we introduce VoxAnon, a dataset built from VoxCeleb1 and 2 with training and evaluation splits balanced across gender, age, accent, and pitch. We extract and cross-check attributes using two complementary methods, balance trial lists per subgroup, and draw test/enrollment utterances from distinct video sources in order to limit linguistic and session bias. Comparing VoxAnon with unbalanced training and test data across four attackers and three anonymizers, we show that attribute imbalance changes which subgroups appear hardest to re-identify, in directions that depend on the attribute. In the balanced setting, residual disparities persist, mostly tied to accent and pitch, and depend on the anonymizer/attacker pair. Code and trial lists are publicly available.
title: VoxAnon: A balanced dataset for a fair evaluation of speech anonymization

summary: Although room impulse responses (RIRs) encode source-distance cues, conventional monaural source separation focuses on recovering audio content without estimating source-specific RIRs, losing the associated spatial information. To address this limitation, we propose Distance-Aware Monaural Source Separation using Multi-RIR Estimation (DAMSEP), the first end-to-end framework that is jointly trained for source separation and multi-source RIR estimation from a single-microphone mixture. DAMSEP integrates a separation backbone with shared dereverberation and RIR estimation modules to jointly recover clean sources and source-specific complex convolutive transfer functions under source estimation and reverberant reconstruction objectives, enabling relative near/far ordering through the direct-to-reverberant ratios of the corresponding RIRs. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce HETMIXR, which spans heterogeneous source content and diverse simulated room conditions with source-specific RIRs and geometric distance annotations. Experiments on HETMIXR demonstrate superior performance in source separation, RIR estimation, and distance ordering. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of source supervision and reverberant reconstruction, while additional evaluations show generalization to single-speaker inputs and mixtures generated using measured RIRs from an unseen room. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Wenanzhi/DAMSEP.
title: DAMSEP: Distance-Aware Monaural Source Separation using Multi-RIR Estimation

summary: Audio deepfakes generated by neural text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems threaten speaker verification and public discourse at scale. The core challenge is cross-dataset generalization: detectors trained on one synthesis pipeline collapse on unseen forgeries. We argue that this failure is primarily because of structural synthetic speech artifacts which are multi-timescale trajectory anomalies. Though every existing detector aggregates a fixed-window frame statistics, this misaligns the architecture with the signal. We propose FlowFake, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) architecture whose hidden state evolves via a learned ODE, with per-neuron adaptive time constants simultaneously resolving spectral (10ms) and prosodic (2s) cues. At only 34K parameters FlowFake achieves formal BIBO stability and O(dt^4) integration error. On a four-dataset cross domain benchmark (ASVspoof2019-LA, FakeOrReal, InTheWild, MLAAD), FlowFake reaches 75.29% on ASVspoof2019 trained only on FakeOrReal and 79.97% trained only on MLAAD. It outperforms RawGAT-ST and Whisper-DF on every evaluated pair and matching SSL Wav2vec2 (300x larger) at 0.01% of its parameter count. The source code is available on : https://github.com/GhostRider2023/FlowFake

summary: We develop a rigorous finite-dimensional mathematical framework connecting the renormalization group, gradient flows, Lyapunov stability, and noncooperative game theory. The central object is a renormalization-group flow written in gradient form, dg_i/dt = β_i(g) = - ∑_j G_ij(g) ∂Γ/∂g_j(g),          (1) where g = (g_1, …, g_n) belongs to an open domain M ⊂ ℝⁿ, Γ is a C² function, and G(g) is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. We associate to this flow a common-payoff game whose payoff is U(g) = - Γ(g).                   (2) We prove, with complete arguments, that ordinary Nash equilibria always imply renormalization-group fixed points, but the converse is false. We then identify the exact condition under which a fixed point becomes a genuine stable equilibrium of the game: a nondegenerate renormalization-group fixed point is asymptotically stable if and only if the Hessian of Γ is positive definite, if and only if it is a strict local minimum of Γ, if and only if it is a strict strong Nash equilibrium of U = -Γ. The distinction between ordinary Nash equilibrium and strong Nash equilibrium is essential. Ordinary Nash equilibria allow only unilateral deviations, while strong Nash equilibria exclude all small joint deviations. We provide explicit counterexamples showing that fixed points need not be Nash equilibria, that ordinary Nash equilibria need not be stable, and that invertibility of G alone does not imply finiteness of equilibria. We also prove global existence results under compactness and finiteness results under Morse nondegeneracy. The paper is self-contained at the level of multivariable calculus, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations, and basic Lyapunov stability theory. The framework is intentionally conditional: it does not claim that the gradient-flow representation has been proven in four-dimensional QCD or in any specific quantum field theory. Those issues are placed in a final section of open problems.
title: Gradient-Flow Renormalization Group as a Common-Potential Game: A Rigorous Equivalence Between Asymptotically Stable Fixed Points and Strict Strong Nash Equilibria

summary: Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, and code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. Representative quantitative findings illustrate substantial existing burdens, but attribution studies, ecological associations, exposure models, displacement records, and conditional forecasts measure different quantities and cannot be combined into a universal five-year trajectory (Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026; Clement et al., 2021). Compound hazards and service interdependencies can increase losses beyond the directly affected sector, while repeated shocks can reduce the capacity to recover or adapt (Zscheischler et al., 2018; IPCC, 2023). A reporting framework is proposed that records the outcome, population, baseline, geography, time horizon, emissions and development assumptions, adaptation, and uncertainty for each indicator. The central contribution is an integrated interpretation and measurement architecture, not a new forecast of global mortality, migration, or societal collapse. Effective assessment should preserve evidence of serious and interacting harms without converting uncertain thresholds or heterogeneous studies into unsupported calendar-specific predictions.

summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. summary: The rapid expansion of the gig economy, facilitated by digital talent platforms, has fundamentally reconfigured the nature of work, employment relationships, and organizational structures. This paradigm shift from stable, long-term employment to a fluid workforce of contractors, freelancers, and project-based talent presents profound challenges to conventional leadership theories and practices. Traditional models, predicated on hierarchical authority, stable organizational boundaries, and enduring psychological contracts, are proving increasingly inadequate for orchestrating a workforce characterized by autonomy, transience, and distributed networks. This paper conducts a critical review of existing leadership literature—including transformational, adaptive, and emerging platform leadership theories—assessing their applicability and limitations in the gig context. Synthesizing insights from organizational behavior, strategic management, and technology studies, we propose a novel integrated framework: the Fluid Leadership Ecosystem (FLE) Model. The FLE model conceptualizes leadership not as a function of individual authority but as the cultivation of a dynamic ecosystem across three core dimensions: Relational Architecture, Algorithmic Stewardship, and Capability Cultivation. We argue that effective leadership in this new era requires designing trust-enabling infrastructures, ensuring human-centric governance of management algorithms, and fostering portable skill development for a transient workforce. This paper introduces novel theoretical perspectives, including temporal leadership dynamics, polycontextual leadership challenges, and the concept of reverse leadership flows from workers to platforms. By presenting a comprehensive model supported by data visualizations and identifying avenues for empirical validation, this research offers a forward-looking agenda for both scholars and practitioners navigating the complexities of leadership in the 21st-century workforce.
title: The Gig Economy and Talent Platforms: New Models of Leadership for Managing a Fluid Workforce

summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. summary: Who supplies, controls and sustains the services needed to inspect and continue AI-assisted research? This article approaches that question through institutional economics and an evolutionary analogy grounded in market competition. It compares targeted evidence with maintained support against fuller research histories with curated access and support. Three activities organize the comparison: scrutiny of a specified claim, reprocessing retained material under a new question, and continuation of unfinished inquiry. A worked access-review example identifies the rights, expertise, labour and resources required, including conditions under which targeted provision is preferable. Market competition supplies the foundational analogy for evolutionary pressure. Repeated decisions about submissions, paid services, funding and volunteer labour can change which research capabilities remain available and which practices spread. Because competing venues can share infrastructure, institutions and their supporting facilities may follow different paths. The article distinguishes internal revision, transmission and differential support, and separates institutional persistence from scientific validity. JOSS and Rainfall Rescue illustrate particular activities and relationships without establishing the comparative benefits of fuller AI histories. The analysis also addresses selective recording, behaviour under scrutiny, unequal burdens and self-selection. Its contribution connects institutional design to the continuing work and support needed to make research records usable.

( Under Review ) ABSTRACT Alluvial meanders dynamically adjust their planform and channel geometry, yet classical meander theory assumes a spatially uniform, constant channel width and continuous bank retreat, failing to capture episodic bank collapse and non-uniform width adjustments in transitional meandering rivers. Situated along the geomorphic continuum between single-thread and wandering streams, transitional meanders exhibit pronounced spatial width variations that break cross-sectional symmetry. Here, we develop a physically closed, reduced-complexity morphodynamic framework coupling a three-parameter asymptotic expansion of the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged flow equations, continuous basal toe scour with transient pore-water suction, threshold-governed cantilever limit equilibrium, and a mass-conserving sediment partition driving inner point-bar progradation. The formulation demonstrates that the spatial phase relationship between channel width oscillations and centerline curvature steers the spatial displacement of outer-bank shear stress hotspots: channel constriction upstream of the bend apex amplifies cutbank shear stress, whereas channel expansion decelerates flow and promotes point-bar accretion. Discrete slump-block deposits provide self-adaptive hydraulic shielding that stabilizes the toe and regulates decadal channel relaxation. Hindcasting the 40-year morphodynamic evolution of the transitional Powder River, Montana, across 34 monumented cross sections reproduces post-flood channel widening and subsequent multi-decadal recovery narrowing across 228 discrete collapse events, while in the limit of uniform width the model recovers classical constant-width meander theory with first-order convergence along the meandering Juruá River. summary: Popper’s (1983, 2002) philosophy of science has enjoyed something of a renaissance in the wake of the replication crisis, offering a philosophical basis for the ensuing science reform movement. However, adherence to Popper’s approach may also be at least partly responsible for the sense of “crisis” that has developed following multiple unexpected replication failures. In this article, I contrast Popper’s approach with that of Lakatos (1978) as well as with a related but problematic approach called naïve methodological falsificationism (NMF; Lakatos, 1978). The Popperian approach is powerful because it is based on logical refutations, but its theories are noncausal and, therefore, potentially lacking in scientific value. In contrast, the Lakatosian approach considers causal theories, but it concedes that these theories are not logically refutable. Finally, NMF represents a hybrid approach that subjects Lakatosian causal theories to Popperian logical refutations. However, its tactic of temporarily accepting a ceteris paribus clause during theory testing may be viewed as scientifically inappropriate, epistemically inconsistent, and “completely redundant” (Lakatos, 1978, p. 40). I conclude that the replication “crisis” makes the most sense in the context of the Popperian and NMF approaches because it is only in these two approaches that the failure to replicate a previously corroborated theory represents a logical refutation of that theory. In contrast, such replication failures are less problematic in the Lakatosian approach because they do not logically refute theories. Indeed, in the Lakatosian approach, replication failures can be temporarily ignored or used to motivate theory development.
title: The replication crisis is less of a "crisis" in Lakatos' philosophy of science than it is in Popper's.

summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.
title: Synthesis and Verification of Transformer Programs

summary: The following dataset contains images and band count estimates of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. It is intended to assist with the replication of the results for the study: Automated reading of vertebral images for aging shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) using Bayesian deep learning. Samples were obtained from two primary sources: recreational game fishing competitions primarily from the North Island between 1994 and 2003, and through the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) Fisheries Observer Programme between 2002 and 2003, primarily from the South Island (Bishop et al., 2006). Shortfin mako vertebrae images (n=146, belonging to 131 unique sharks) were obtained from previous ageing studies using band counts (Bishop et al., 2006; Francis, 2016). These section pairs were filtered by image quality with lower quality images being excluded, resulting in a reduced dataset of 133 section pairs. Each section pair was isolated, resulting in a complete dataset of 266 half bow-tie section images. We compared the following three deep learning methods: DeepEnsembling, a mixture of Laplace approximations, and multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian to predict the band counts by human readers using a dataset of 146 images of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. Multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian offered marginally superior predictive power and uncertainty calibration, and its predictions typically matched estimates provided by human readers. We conclude that the application of deep learning for automated vertebrae reading demonstrated strong initial promise.

summary: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 allows a child aged sixteen or seventeen who is alleged to have committed a heinous offence to be tried as an adult after a "preliminary assessment" by the Juvenile Justice Board. This paper argues that the transfer mechanism is less a principled answer to serious adolescent offending than a legislative compromise whose costs fall on the procedural guarantees the Act otherwise extends to children. It reads section 15 against the Supreme Court's decisions in Shilpa Mittal and Barun Chandra Thakur, the age-determination case law, and the developmental research on adolescent culpability, and it engages the retributive and victim-centred case for transfer on its own terms. Accountability and rehabilitation, the paper contends, are not two poles to be traded off at a single age threshold. Both depend on institutional capacity that the system has never been resourced to supply: functioning Boards, trained probation staff, individual care plans that are actually followed, and aftercare that reaches young people beyond eighteen. summary: Lecture 1 formulated the recommendation problem in abstract terms: a set of users U , a set of items I , and a preference function r(u,i) that must be estimated for the pairs that have not been observed. Every algorithm studied in this course, however, operates on concrete data rather than on abstractions. The quality of a recommender system is therefore bounded by the quality, the structure, and the representation of the data from which it learns. In practice, improving the data frequently brings larger gains than changing the algorithm. A sophisticated model trained on noisy, biased, or poorly prepared data produces poor recommendations, a principle often summarized as garbage in, garbage out . This lecture therefore addresses three questions: è Which data does a recommender system collect, and what do these data really mean? è How can these data be organized and represented so that algorithms can process them? è How must the data be prepared and partitioned before a model is built and assessed? After studying this lecture, the reader should be able to: · Identify the sources and categories of data used in a recommender system; · Characterize explicit and implicit feedback, including their strengths and weaknesses; · Construct a user–item matrix and interpret its sparsity; · Represent users and items as vectors built from interactions and descriptive features; · Apply the main preprocessing operations to ratings and implicit signals; · Split a dataset correctly and avoid information leakage. The path followed by the data throughout this lecture is: Data sources → Feedback signals → User–item matrix → Vector representations → Preprocessing → Data splitting
title: Lecture Notes on Recommender Systems

summary: We develop a counterfactual semantics based on reopening partial information states. Evaluation first removes enough stated content to leave the antecedent’s attributes unresolved, retaining what the chosen scope protects, then asserts the antecedent and considers the surviving consistent refinements. Would and might quantify over the admissible alternatives; a weighted extension supplies graded evaluations. The principal result concerns finite models with fully supported residues. When a conjunctive antecedent reopens each constituent attribute, adding a supported conjunct can remove the grounds of another conclusion. A four-attribute countermodel therefore violates Cautious Monotony, excluding any smooth preferential representation that preserves the evaluable verdicts. We also establish a sufficient nesting condition for Cut and exhibit its failure without that condition. The conjunctive reopening rule is an explicit interpretive commitment; its suitability for ordinary-language counterfactuals remains an empirical question. The account uses declared dependencies, scope restrictions, and priorities, while the quantitative extension assumes a weight kernel. Comparisons with belief revision, premise semantics, update semantics, and causal intervention identify the consequences of reopening an attribute rather than merely making its proposed value consistent with retained information.
title: Counterfactual Evaluation by Reopening Information States

summary: Space Semiconductor Fabrication and Starship Nanofoundries at the Limit English Description and Research Position This research monograph asks which semiconductor unit processes could achieve a defensible mission advantage in microgravity, vacuum, radiation, remote-operation, and closed-resource environments. It does not assume that a complete advanced fab can operate in space. Instead, it compares crystal growth, deposition, etching, lithography, metrology, bonding, packaging, repair, and recycling against ground manufacture plus transport, launched spares, on-orbit packaging, and local repair. Every claimed advantage must survive matched controls, full functional qualification, and explicit mass, energy, heat, crew, contamination, maintenance, waste, and return ledgers. The volume contains 82 chapters with five research sections per chapter, 30 linked formula derivations, 200 detailed Research Gates, DOI-anchored references, and a formula-chapter-experiment-Gate crosswalk. Its central contribution is a mission-scale evidence architecture that connects process physics to contained workcells, independent metrology, safe autonomy, repair, return, circular resources, cross-platform reproduction, and successor reconstruction. Safety and irreversible environmental harm operate as hard vetoes rather than compensable score components. The literature base includes peer-reviewed DOI sources on microgravity semiconductor growth, in-space manufacturing, additive nanomanufacturing, atomic-layer processing, radiation effects, lunar resource extraction, digital twins, autonomous laboratories, and reproducible science. Recent orbital results are treated as early evidence for specific mechanisms, not as confirmation of a complete space foundry. summary: Emergency-stop circuits built by engineering technology students are routinely treated as safe once they pass a functional test at commissioning, yet the relay contact welding that dominates their failure modes is invisible to such tests and accumulates silently across the workshop's operating life. The framework represents a student-built circuit as a series safety function whose integrity is degraded by contact welding, and derives the conditions under which a welded contact converts a demanded stop into an undetected loss of safety function. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The evaluation indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect at 80% power falls as the number of clusters rises. The framework proposes that workshop safety assurance should shift from commissioning-time functional testing to integrity monitoring that is sensitive to contact welding, and the design analysis implies that cluster-level evaluations of such interventions require cluster counts well above those typical of single-institution studies.

summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for compositional regression functions, but inference for intermediate layers faces questions. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We then introduce an augmented $ρ$-fractional posterior that reweights layer decompositions by a non-saturating identity-deviation penalty. The augmentation changes posterior odds between symmetry-related decompositions by an exponential penalty ratio. Under proper choices of the penalty and a prior mass condition, it preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction, while shrinking the redundant layers towards the identity mapping. Thus, the likelihood does not identify a unique ``true'' set of layers; the augmentation favors identity-biased parsimonious decompositions within an equivalence class of layers; uniqueness of a selected representative is not established.

summary: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. summary: Which biological findings enter a reported explanation depends on how the model population was constructed, a choice predictive validation alone does not reveal. We fitted 10,000 L2-regularised logistic regression models to TCGA pan-cancer tumour-versus-normal data: 100 regularisation strengths on 100 train-test splits, with patients fixed within each split. Strongly and weakly regularised models differ in mean accuracy by only 0.21 percentage points, yet prioritise different genes systematically with regularisation strength. Averaging explanations across a hyperparameter grid produces a top-50 panel sharing 41 genes with a single fitted model, but which model depends on the grid centre (Spearman correlation 0.92, 350 simulated practitioners). For 43 of 50 practitioners, the panel combines genes from strongly and weakly regularised models more fully than any fitted model: the explanation belongs to no model whose accuracy was established. A conventional grid recovers only a quarter of genes favoured exclusively by the strongest regularisation. HMGCS2 ranks among the top 50 in 73 of 100 strongly regularised fits and no weakly regularised fits, yet appears in none of 50 simulated reports. Reconstructing a published biomarker workflow on 20 cohort resamples reveals a different failure: the closest refit contains only 23 of the averaged panel's 50 genes, and no panel gene appears in all 20 refits. We define model-relative provenance as how much of a panel any single fitted model contains, distinct from workflow provenance recording how an analysis was run. We provide measurements to make the model population, the choice that selects from it, and that provenance reportable.

summary: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases

summary: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.

summary: Laser cladding enables bi-material components with tailored surface properties, but cyclic loading makes fatigue resistance of the whole component critical. This study examined the bending fatigue life (R = 0.1) of unalloyed steels S235J2 and S355J2 and high-strength steels S460NL and S690QL clad with aluminium bronze Metco 51NS, a combination typical of tube-bending mandrels. Fatigue strength at 10⁷ cycles was 4.0, 3.4, 3.8 and 4.5 kN, respectively, so high-strength steels performed only slightly better or similarly. Cracks always initiated on the surface of the cladding and crossed the defect-free interface. The base material is therefore not decisive for fatigue life, which is governed by the surface layer, provided cladding parameters are optimal. summary: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. Our system significantly reduces query hallucination and improves semantic fidelity compared to direct LLM prompting. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. summary: How much classical information can a noisy optical channel carry when both signal energy and preshared entanglement are limited? This work gives an exact capacity frontier for this joint resource problem. It allows one to determine the best asymptotic communication rate, price the benefit of additional entanglement, and distinguish the effect of tolerating errors from that of changing how entanglement is supplied. Exact capacity under two resource constraints The setting is any fixed bosonic Gaussian channel \(\Phi\) with finitely many input and output modes. Signal energy is measured by a positive quadratic Hamiltonian \(H_G=\tfrac12 R^{\mathsf T}GR\), with \(G>0\) and ground energy \(E_0\); \(R\) collects the canonical quadratures. The budgets satisfy \(E\ge E_0\) and \(P\ge0\). For an \(n\)-use code, the mean total signal energy is at most \(nE\), while the same initially shared maximally entangled state has Schmidt rank \(K_n\) satisfying \(\log K_n\le nP\). Thus \(P\) is a strictly supplied entanglement rate. Encoders may be arbitrary joint quantum operations, and decoding may be collective. The classical capacity is \[ C(E,P)=\max_{\substack{U\ge V\;\mathrm{physical}\\ \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(GU)\le E,\;S_G(V)\le P}}\bigl[S_G(\Phi U)+S_G(V)-S_G(\Phi^c V)\bigr]. \] Here \(V\) is a Gaussian seed covariance, \(U\) is the average-input covariance, and \(U-V\) is the displacement-modulation covariance. A covariance is physical when \(V+i\Omega/2\ge0\), where \(\Omega\) is the canonical commutation matrix and the vacuum covariance is \(I/2\). The notation \(S_G\) denotes Gaussian von Neumann entropy, and \(\Phi^c\) is the full complementary channel, including any environment purification. All logarithms are natural, so rates are in nats per channel use. This formula replaces optimization over arbitrary quantum block codes by a finite-dimensional covariance optimization. It supplies both an achievable rate and a converse against non-Gaussian, correlated encodings. At \(P=0\), it also determines the unassisted capacity of general fixed finite-mode Gaussian channels, including channels without a passive decomposition into independent modes. The reduction specifies the exact capacity value; it does not require a closed-form optimizer for every device. Energy and strict entanglement supply respond differently to errors For a fixed allowed average error \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), the exact capacity under the mean-energy constraint is \[ C_\varepsilon(E,P)=C\!\left(E_0+\frac{E-E_0}{1-\varepsilon},\,P\right). \] Allowing failure rescales the mean energy above the ground state, but leaves the strict initial entanglement budget unchanged. The proof uses an exponential strong converse for codes whose inputs obey a hard total-energy cutoff. In a different model, where a readable flag permits random entanglement supply constrained only on average, the work establishes an achievable bound and a strict small-supply advantage for thermal attenuation at positive energy and fixed nonzero error. That comparison identifies the operational importance of the supply rule; it is not a complete capacity characterization of the flagged model. The communication value of entanglement For a thermal attenuator, let \(0<\eta<1\) be the transmissivity, \(b>0\) the output mean photon number for vacuum input, and \(N\) the input mean photon number. Write its capacity as \(C_N(P)\), and define \(g(N)=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N\). The gain from entanglement obeys the sharp bound \[ 0\le C_N(P)-C_N(0)\le\frac{\eta}{1+b}\,P. \] For every fixed \(N>0\), the coefficient \(\eta/(1+b)\) is attained as the initial right derivative at \(P=0\). In the low-photon limit, the stronger resource law is \[ C_N(P)-C_N(0)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}\min\{P,g(N)\}+O(N),\qquad N\downarrow0. \] The remainder is uniform over \(P\ge0\) at fixed \(\eta\) and positive \(b\). Noise therefore determines the conversion efficiency, while \(g(N)\sim N\log(1/N)\) sets the entanglement scale
title: A universal energy–entanglement capacity frontier for Gaussian optical channels

summary: RECONFIGURABLE ROBOTIC SWARMS AND CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONAL REGENERATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library | Flagship 02 Prospective Research Atlas — English Review Edition, October 2026 Can a distributed population of heterogeneous modular robots reconstruct an operationally qualified capability after damage, without treating a newly assembled shape as evidence of restored function? Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit develops an interdisciplinary research program on modular morphology, distributed self-assembly, task-dependent graph structure, mechanical qualification, connector fatigue, recoverable actions, and independent post-reconfiguration verification. Its central proposition is deliberately testable: a swarm may change its topology after losing modules, but it earns the stronger name of functional regeneration only when its restored configuration satisfies the original, independently assessed service requirements and does not conceal emerging hazards or latent joint failures. The monograph distinguishes three often conflated networks: mechanical connections that transmit forces, communication links that transmit information, and power connections that transport energy. It then investigates how graph connectivity, geometric rigidity, elastic stiffness, buckling, frictional contact, thermal dissipation, material fatigue, sensing uncertainty, local negotiation, and safe rollback constrain what an apparently repaired swarm can actually do. A prospective twenty-module testbed provides recurring engineering anchors: bridge, gripping, and sensing-tower tasks, blinded removal of modules, unseen configurations, independent qualification, and strong comparisons with redundant fixed structures and specialist replacement procedures. The research architecture includes thirty mathematically diverse derivation plates, eighty-two chapter-level questions and their five individually paginated study units, two hundred falsifiable Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. The companion spreadsheet links physical models, chapter topics, prospective study cards, provenance, source DOI records, and page references to support future research and AI-assisted scientific handoff. Published robotics literature supplies a source-grounded context for modular reconfigurable mechanisms and fault-aware planning, including external DOI records for reviews and an existing fault-tolerant modular system. The manuscript separates those precedents from its own unexecuted research designs. Its two STARLI mother volumes are listed as conceptual ancestry, not as independent experimental validation. Biological regeneration functions as an analogy for staged assessment of restoration, not as evidence of biomedical efficacy, autonomous human-tissue repair, or indefinite machine life. This is a prospective research-atlas REVIEW EDITION. The mathematical relations, study proposals, design seeds, and acceptance thresholds are not experimentally validated findings. External mathematical review, whole-text DOI auditing, and a stronger editorial review for chapter-level semantic repetition remain necessary before scholarly publication. Negative findings, conventional method superiority, irreversible module retirement, and scientific abstention are legitimate outcomes within this research program. summary: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts

summary: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. summary: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. summary: Data and R code that reproduce the results of "Divergence Between Absolute Emissions Benchmarks and Output-Adjusted Assessments: Evidence from Korea" (manuscript version 7.7.1, submitted to Energy Economics).   A single command, Rscript reproduce.R, runs 14 analysis scripts (about 15 seconds on a 32-core computer) and lists the 146 numbers reported in the paper in the order in which they appear, each next to the value the package computes or provides. Of the 146 numbers, 121 are recomputed from the distributed data; the other 25 rest on site-level records, coding records of business reports, a page-by-page reading of overseas reports and licensed revenue data, which cannot be distributed, and are provided as computed.   The package requires only R with the jsonlite and ggplot2 packages (versions fixed in renv.lock). The random draws of the original computation are included as files; an included Python script (draws/make_draws.py, numpy) regenerates them byte for byte.   The package of 101 files contains truncated salted hash codes, log changes and ratios for the Korean firm pairs, the overseas pair files, the producer price indices and the boundary audit of the 80 firms in the multi-industry frame. It contains no firm names, business identifiers or levels of emissions, energy, output or revenue for Korean firms. See README.md for the folder layout, the fixed inputs and the results that are provided as computed.   Licences: code under MIT; data produced by the author under CC BY 4.0. Producer price indices and source data remain under their publishers' terms. summary: The island of St. Vincent and the other Windward Islands in the southeastern Caribbean were chosen as a field site for the study of weak mountain wakes. By the authorsメ definition, a モweak wakeヤ forms when the potential vorticity generated by a mountain is not strong enough to advect itself into eddies; rather, it is simply advocated downstream by the ambient flow. GOES-8 and Landsat sunlit images unambiguously revealed that the mountainous Windward Islands have remarkably long straight wakes. The length of St. Vincentメs wake exceeds 300 km although its width is only 20 km. Near the islands, the wake structures reflect the details of the island topography. These wakes do not exhibit any obvious diurnal effect. Boat surveys in the lee of St. Vincent confirmed the existence of features seen in the images: the sharp wake boundary, the small valley-induced jet embedded in the near wake, and the absence of any reverse flow. Aircraft surveys gave evidence of descent over the island and showed that the wake air is relatively warm and dry. The length of the wake (L) agrees with the formula L = H/2CD (where H is the wake depth and CD is the surface drag coefficient), implying that the reacceleration of the wake air is caused by the ambient streamwise pressure gradient rather than by lateral entrainment of momentum or geostrophic adjustment. Two numerical models were used to simulate St. Vincentメs wake, a single-layer hydrostatic model and a 3D nonhydrostatic model. Both models indicated that air descent, acceleration, wave breaking, and weak potential vorticity generation occur over the island, causing a long straight wake. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: The Wake of St. Vincent - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: On 25 April 1992, a magnitude-7.1 Ms earthquake occurred near Cape Mendocino, California, at the southern end of the Cascadia Subduction Zone. Seismological analyses suggest an almost pure dip-slip reverse fault, with subduction of the Gorda Plate beneath the North American Plate. Modeling and observations of crustal deformation due to this fault mechanism produces uplift of the ocean bottom in relatively shallow water just offshore. A tsunami was generated that was measured by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration sea level gauges along the California, southern Oregon, and Hawaii coastlines and in the deep ocean in the Gulf of Alaska. Several records are characterized by two distinct packets of tsunami energy, the first representing propagation along a minimum time path traversing deep offshore water, the second an apparent edge wave mode trapped along the coast. The largest peak-to-trough amplitude of 1.1 m was recorded at Crescent City in the second packet, approximately 3-4 hours after arrival of the first tsunami wave. Observations of this tsunami will be discussed along with some numerical model results to explain the source area and propagation characteristics. [Reference: Gonz£lez, F.I., E.N. Bernard, and K. Satake. The Cape Mendocino tsunami, 25 April 1992. In Tsunami: Progress in Prediction, Disaster Prevention and Warning, Y. Tsuchiya and N. Shuto (eds.), Series of Advances in Natural and Technological Hazards Research, Kluwer Academic Publishers, 151-158 (1995).] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: Seawater concentrations of dimethylsulfide (DMS) and atmospheric concentrations of DMS, sulfur dioxide, methanesulfonate (MSA), and non-sea-salt (nss) sulfate were measured over the eastern Pacific Ocean between 105° and 110°W from 20°N to 60°S during February and March 1989. Although the samples collected in the southern hemisphere appear to be of marine origin, no significant correlation was found between the latitudinal distributions of DMS, SO, MSA, and nss SO. However, an inverse correlation (r = 0.87) was found between atmospheric temperature and the MSA to nss SO molar ratio in submicrometer aerosol particles with a decrease in temperature corresponding to an increase in the molar ratio. Although this trend is consistent with laboratory results indicating the favored production of MSA at lower temperatures, it is contrary to southern hemisphere baseline station data. This suggests either a decrease in the supply of DMS relative to nonmarine sources of nss SO at the baseline stations in winter or additional mechanisms that affect the relative production of MSA and nss SO. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: Acoustic extensometer instruments capable of making precise daily measurements of horizontal distance were deployed across the north rift zone of Axial Volcano in June 1996 and were in place when a submarine eruption began on Axialメs south rift zone in January 1998. The instruments recorded a gradual 9-cm extension over a 405-m baseline leading up to the eruption, and then an abrupt, 4-cm contraction at the time of the eruption. An elastic point-source deformation model shows that deflation of Axialメs summit can explain both the 4-cm distance decrease at the extensometer array and a 3.2-m subsidence measured by another instrument in the caldera, if the pressure source is located at a depth of 3.8 km below the center of the caldera. The 9-cm distance increase may represent pre-eruption spreading across the rift zone. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

The instruments recorded a gradual 9-cm extension over a 405-m baseline leading up to the eruption, and then an abrupt, 4-cm contraction at the time of the eruption. An elastic point-source deformation model shows that deflation of Axialメs summit can explain both the 4-cm distance decrease at the extensometer array and a 3.2-m subsidence measured by another instrument in the caldera, if the pressure source is located at a depth of 3.8 km below the center of the caldera. The 9-cm distance increase may represent pre-eruption spreading across the rift zone. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: The fact that vigorous hydrothermal discharge occurs on ridge segments with a variety of spreading rates and morphological characteristics makes it difficult to discern the large-scale geological controls on the distribution of hydrothermal venting along the mid-ocean ridge. We undertook to simplify this problem by mapping the distribution of hydrothermally produced thermal and light attenuation anomalies along the crest of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, a medium-rate spreading center with segments of markedly differing morphology. Hydrothermal anomalies were detected by towing a high-precision conductivity-temperature-depth- transmissometer (CTDT) package in a sawtooth pattern through the lowermost 1000 m of the water column above each segment. These surveys, conducted between 1985 and 1989, have produced the first quantitative and continuous visualizations of hydrothermal plumes along a multisegment portion of the mid-ocean ridge. Hydrothermal discharge is strongest on those segments, or portions of segments, where the apparent magmatic budget is highest, as indicated by the degree of along-axis inflation and other morphological characteristics. This correspondence implies that magma is episodically delivered in small and spatially discontinuous bodies of melt rather than by the constant resupply of a steady state magma chamber. We propose that the probability of discharge occurring at any point on the mid-ocean ridge is proportional to the spreading rate. This probability, scaled by the observation that significant plumes presently emanate from ~20% of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, is expected to range from ~5% on the slowest-spreading ridge to ~50% on the fastest-spreading ridge. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: Tetrahedral head models of 100 Human Connectome Project (HCP) Young Adult subjects, built for finite-element simulation of transcranial magnetic stimulation, with a series of remeshed versions of one subject for mesh-convergence studies. The files are the data used by the cuNIBS manuscripts and benchmark suite. The subjects are the 100 HCP S1200 subjects selected by Berger et al. (2025). We segmented each subject's T1-weighted and T2-weighted scans, taken from the scans Berger et al. distribute, with SimNIBS 4.6 CHARM at default settings, without manual correction. The one non-default setting is --forceqform, which the HCP scans need because their qform and sform orientations disagree. The meshes have 3.94 to 5.53 million tetrahedra (median 4.79 million) and carry all nine CHARM tissue tags. Contents: subjects/<id>.h5: one head mesh per subject, with its EEG cap positions. The ID is the HCP subject ID. ladder/<id>_s<NNN>.h5: one subject remeshed at eight resolutions from 1.71 to 21.2 million tetrahedra. Every element length is scaled by NNN/100. Format: HDF5 files written by HeadMesh.save in cuNIBS, uncompressed. The tissue tags follow CHARM and are stored with the mesh. The meshes are derived from HCP data and carry no names or other identifying information beyond the HCP subject ID. Use is subject to the HCP Open Access Data Use Terms, in addition to the CC BY 4.0 license. Software: cuNIBS ( https://github.com/vcubiomag/cunibs ). The code release that reproduces the manuscripts' results is v0.5.0 (DOI to be added). Acknowledgement: Data were provided by the Human Connectome Project, WU-Minn Consortium (Principal Investigators: David Van Essen and Kamil Ugurbil; 1U54MH091657), funded by the 16 NIH Institutes and Centers that support the NIH Blueprint for Neuroscience Research, and by the McDonnell Center for Systems Neuroscience at Washington University. Those awards funded the acquisition of the data and not this work.
