summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. summary: Philosophy of science has well-developed criteria for when structure is real: patterns that compress and predict, mechanisms with constitutively relevant components, causally emergent macro-variables, statistical boundaries that screen an interior from an exterior. These criteria are also used to tell us which systems are units, individuals in their own right rather than selections we make. I argue that this promotion fails, and that the accounts of individuality built on it have not shown that anything is a unit. Real structure is often shared by rival cuts of the same substrate, whereas unity requires something that resolves rivalries between cuts. Individuating a unit therefore involves two burdens: realized modal support, which real-structure criteria discharge, and a unit ground, an organization of the realizer that makes this cut the unit. I state adequacy conditions for unit grounds, separate their holding from their evidential discharge, and propose a constitutive intervention test with matched negative controls and a selectivity condition. Applied to real patterns, Markov blankets, information-theoretic individuality, causal emergence, integrated information and individuating mechanisms, the conditions show what each account lacks: some fail to discriminate between rival cuts, some discriminate by maximizing a measure whose maximizing cut still owes a ground, and some supply candidate grounds without a way of resolving rivalries in which both rivals are units. Partial audits of a key–value server, a bacterial cell and a heating loop suggest that the bottleneck is not relevance, for which discharging experiments can be specified, but screening the exterior and discriminating between rival cuts. In object-oriented programming, where Kay modelled the objects of Smalltalk on biological cells, the two burdens visibly come apart: one declared profile, equally well realized, can rest on candidate grounds of very different strength, down to a bare declaration. The upshot is disciplined abundance: units can be many and nested, but nothing becomes a unit through packaging, unions, target-selected subcuts or boundaries alone. A double stratification problem, of levels and of stages, remains open.
title: Real Structure Is Not Yet Unity: Unit Grounds and Disciplined Abundance

summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

summary: Clustered federated learning (CFL) can suffer from cluster collapse. In particular, under unfavorable initialization, early client assignments concentrate heterogeneous groups on one cluster model, which is then trained toward a pooled compromise, while another model receives no updates. Since the current models determine client routing and routing determines subsequent model updates, we formulate clustered federated learning as control of an unknown dynamical system, with cluster models as the evolving state, client routing patterns as the control input, and routing interventions as state dependent controllers. In a two group linear model, we identify an initialization region in which greedy routing makes collapse self reinforcing. We then derive finite horizon error dynamics showing how routing interventions can reverse collapse by repeatedly training the starved model, primarily with updates from its compatible group. Motivated by this condition, each client uses blocked EXP3 to choose between greedy routing and interventions that redirect updates toward unused models. Experiments show that with simpler predictors and faster specialist formation, autonomous controller selection recovers usable specialists from unfavorable starts that trap standard CFL baselines. In transformed FEMNIST, the synchronized-entry configuration with persistent commitment recovers usable specialists in settings where the autonomous controller configuration often does not. Code and scripts for reproducing the experiments and figures are available at https://github.com/prsinha1/FedRecover.
title: The Dynamics of Collapse and Recovery in Clustered Federated Learning

summary: Online search activity is widely used as a digital trace of information seeking during epidemics, but its predictive value is often reduced to correlation, a selected lag, or a single forecast-error score. We examine eight pre-specified Google Trends-COVID-19 pairs in both directions using matched LightGBM forecasts over rolling 400-day windows and horizons of 1-14 days. Log-RMSE gain is combined with forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE), which captures horizon-dependent changes in the signed error distribution. The resulting directional predictive signature comprises response class, RMSE effect, FEDE endpoint and early-slope responses, persistence across rolling regimes, and horizon profile. For screening candidate directions, we also introduce a relative persistence-weighted directional predictive response strength (DPRS) on a within-study 0-100 scale; 100 denotes the strongest observed response in the comparison set, not an absolute coupling maximum. The pairs show concordant, RMSE-only, FEDE-only, and mixed responses. "loss of smell" -> reported cases is accuracy-dominant, with mean log-RMSE gain 0.104 (about 9.9% equivalent RMSE reduction) and DPRS 100, whereas the reverse direction is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.048; DPRS=42). "covid test" -> positive rate is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.039; positive in 72% of windows; DPRS=98) despite negative RMSE gain, while "lockdown" -> stringency is the clearest concordant case (DPRS=78). World-level symptom/case pairs are less persistent. Thus, forecast accuracy and error-distribution dynamics are complementary, predictive effects can be direction- and metric-dependent, and forecast horizon is part of the relationship. Aggregated regime-level patterns should not be extrapolated to individual time points or interpreted as evidence of causality.
title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Predictive Dynamics in Google Search and COVID-19 Time Series: A Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Analysis

summary: In this work, we study a fractional diffusion model in time and space, formulated in an open and bounded domain, involving a Caputo fractional derivative of order $μ\in(0,1)$ with respect to a time scale function $Ψ$, together with a spectral fractional Laplacian operator of order $s\in(0,1)$. The associated direct problem is analyzed, as well as the inverse problem of temporal reconstruction from final data, which is inherently ill-posed. Through a spectral representation, the instability of the problem and the effect of the choice of the function $Ψ$ on the amplification of spectral modes are examined.
title: Backward Homogeneous Heat Equation with $Ψ$-Caputo Time Derivative and Spectral Fractional Laplacian

summary: Reliable microstructural parameter estimation in diffusion MRI (dMRI) critically depends on the acquisition protocol. Yet, common protocol design criteria may not fully reflect estimator bias, parameter constraints, and nonlinear fitting behavior in complex inverse problems. Here, we introduce Protocol Optimization via Loss Assessing Parameter Recovery (POLAR), an end-to-end framework that searches the continuous acquisition space and directly minimizes multiparameter recovery error through noisy signal simulation and the chosen model fitting. We demonstrate POLAR spanning distinct microstructural environments: the Cylinder-Zeppelin model for white matter, Neurite Exchange Imaging (NEXI) for gray matter, and Cellular Exchange Imaging (CEXI) for permeable cells. Across independent held-out parameter sets, POLAR consistently outperformed model-specific reference designs, reducing RMSE by up to $50\%$ for Cylinder-Zeppelin and $74\%$ for CEXI, while reducing NEXI exchange time bias by $70\%$. These gains across distinct biophysical models, acquisition settings, and reference design strategies demonstrate the benefit of optimizing acquisition protocols through the downstream parameter-estimation problem. POLAR provides a flexible, model-specific and estimator-aware framework for designing dMRI protocols tailored to the microstructural parameters and experimental conditions of interest.
title: Diffusion MRI protocol design for reliable parameter recovery: a unified framework across biophysical models

summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) provides an ultrafast probe of quantum materials, yet conventional spectral observables do not generally furnish a common signature of band topology. Here we show that quantum-light-driven HHG opens an additional information channel through the photon statistics of the emitted harmonics. Using the Haldane Chern insulator and the time-reversal-invariant Kane-Mele topological insulator, we calculate helicity-resolved equal-time intensity correlations and identify a common enhancement of high-order harmonic correlations in the topological phases. For the Haldane model, a dichroic correlation constructed from opposite helicity channels reverses sign with the Chern number. These signatures originate from the distinct nonlinear response sampled by quantum fluctuations of the driving field and are absent from the corresponding mean harmonic spectra as a common classifier. Our results establish photon-correlation spectroscopy as a route to interrogate topological matter with quantum light and provide a bridge between strong-field solid-state physics and quantum optics.
title: Attosecond Quantum Optical Spectroscopy of Topological Materials

summary: To defend against backdoor attacks on neural networks, the defender must identify the verifier function that determines whether an input is a trigger, rather than rejecting individual triggers in isolation, since an attacker can generate new triggers satisfying the same verifier faster than they can be blocked. If a backdoor verifier could be installed with the asymmetry of a cryptographic authentication scheme, in which only the attacker can produce trigger inputs while the defender cannot reverse-engineer the verifier from observations, learning-based defense would be impossible in principle. We show that no such asymmetry can arise from poisoning-based installation, in which the only verifier-dependent input to training is a poisoned dataset. The argument is a reduction. A training procedure that installs a verifier from poisoned data, so that the backdoor fires on unseen triggers while benign behavior is preserved, is itself a learner for that verifier. Any verifier that is computationally hard to learn is therefore impossible to install through poisoning, and any verifier that poisoning can install is reconstructible by a white-box defender holding comparably many labeled trigger observations. A complementary argument shows that a secret key supplied to the model at inference is observable to the same defender. The result takes representative trigger observations as given and concerns when the backdoor fires rather than what it does. Experiments on instruction-tuned large language models confirm the dichotomy, with no configuration yielding a backdoor that is both effective for the attacker and irrecoverable for the defender.
title: Poisoning-Based Backdoors Are Not Cryptographic

summary: In the present paper, we proceed with the research initiated in (S. Antontsev \emph{et al.}, Inverse Problems, 2021). We study the inverse problem for the Kelvin--Voigt equations with $p$-Laplacian and with a right-hand side in the integral over-determination condition, which approximates a discontinuous function at $t=0$. We rescale the problem in a neighbourhood $[0,1/n]$ and pass to the limit as $n$ approaches infinity. This leads to the inverse problem on an infinitesimal initial layer, which transforms the initial velocity into a new one.
title: Kurzweil's impulsive inverse problem for the Kelvin--Voigt equations with $p$-Laplacian

summary: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.
title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems

summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents

summary: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.
title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control

summary: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
title: Large Flow Language Models

summary: Python/NGSolve implementation and reference data accompanying the manuscript “A hybridization-derived interior penalty Nitsche method for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion” by Vincent Fontaine (23-page version, 21 October 2026). The package contains the three IPN symmetry variants, strongly imposed Dirichlet variants, benchmark and figure-generation drivers, and stored numerical reference results for heterogeneous anisotropic checkerboard diffusion, the Kellogg singular benchmark, and controlled comparisons of transmissibility and contrast-blind flux-jump weighting. The numerical results are unchanged; no simulations were rerun during preparation. SHA-256 manifests and an integrity-only checker are included. Original software is licensed under BSD-3-Clause; original reference data and package documentation under CC BY 4.0, with separate scope described in LICENSE.txt. Existing third-party notices apply. The manuscript and its source files retain their separate manuscript licensing status.
title: IPN for Heterogeneous and Anisotropic Diffusion: Reproducibility Software and Reference Data

summary: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
title: MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

summary: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines

summary: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.
title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report

summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

summary: This is a study commissioned by the Panel for the Future of Science and Technology, European Parliament: Generative Artificial Intelligence could strengthen open science by improving accessibility, findability, and usability. Still, under less favourable conditions, it could also weaken scientific exchange by obscuring provenance, deepening dependency on opaque infrastructures, and reinforcing inequalities and increasing synthetic overload, in which large volumes of AI-generated scientific content overwhelm the capacity of researchers and systems to verify, interpret, and trust information. This study describes how Generative AI is reshaping scientific exchange within the broader framework of open science. It shows that the main policy challenge is not whether Generative AI will be used in scientific exchange, but under what institutional, infrastructural, and normative conditions it can support reliable research, and knowledge valorisation. The European Union should treat scientific exchange as public-interest infrastructure and enact policies to support skills, strengthened provenance, transparency, reproducibility, inclusion, and strategic capacity in an AI-mediated research environment. This report provides specific policy options tackling the risks that can be associated with the use of AI in scientific exchange. This study is prepared for, and addressed to, the Members and staff of the European Parliament as background material to assist them in their parliamentary work. The content of the document is the sole responsibility of its author(s) and any opinions expressed herein should not be taken to represent an official position of the Parliament.
title: Open science and the effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in scientific exchange: Policy options for reliable research

summary: ExM Explorer is a search engine for expansion microscopy (ExM) experiments compiled from the literature. For each study, it records the organisms expanded, the protocol used (fixation, anchoring, gel composition, homogenization, expansion factor), and the antibodies, dyes and stains applied, with their outcome and a link to the source publication. Version 1.0 covers 381 studies, 301 species, 1,483 primary antibodies and 608 dyes and stains. The database was built from 579 full texts identified by searches of PubMed and Europe PMC (including bioRxiv and medRxiv). Each paper was read individually by a large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic), followed by deterministic curation and eight quality controls. This archive contains the portal (a single HTML file that runs offline), the database with its column dictionary, the provenance of every PDF and the curation log, the EukProt v3 species list used to place coverage on the eukaryotic tree, the code that generates and validates the portal, the extraction and curation scripts with their logs, and the quality-control outputs. Full methods and limitations are described in METHODS.md. Code is released under the MIT License and data under CC BY 4.0.

summary: In variational damage models, Lipschitz regularization can be introduced by imposing a pointwise bound on the gradient of the damage field, thereby controlling its spatial regularity without adding a gradient-dependent contribution to the energy. After spatial discretization, this condition gives rise to local inequality constraints and associated Lagrange multipliers, whose number increases with mesh refinement. This work introduces the Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) formulation, in which these local constraints are replaced by a single differentiable global constraint and a single Lagrange multiplier, independently of the discretization size. Despite this reduction of the dual problem, the local constraint structure is retained through the gradient of the aggregation operator, which defines effective local multipliers. Under suitable structural properties, these multipliers concentrate on the locally active constraints as the aggregation approaches the exact maximum, asymptotically recovering the local Karush--Kuhn--Tucker structure of the original problem. A consistent primal--dual Newton solver is developed for the aggregated damage problem. The resulting bordered system admits a scalar Schur complement reduction. For the class of aggregation operators considered here, the consistent Hessian further decomposes into a sparse local contribution and a rank-one correction. Exploiting this structure through the Sherman--Morrison formula reduces the exact Newton correction to sparse subproblems involving only local contributions, together with low-cost global scalar and vector operations. The sparse computational structure of the underlying local problem can therefore be exploited despite the global nature of the aggregated constraint. One- and two-dimensional numerical assessments confirm the predicted aggregation accuracy, the recovery of the pointwise Lipschitz-constrained response, and the applicability of the formulation under mesh refinement. The results also provide a first assessment of the computational performance of the proposed formulation.
title: Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) regularization of damage and fracture: a single-constraint, single-multiplier formulation retaining local computational structure

After spatial discretization, this condition gives rise to local inequality constraints and associated Lagrange multipliers, whose number increases with mesh refinement. This work introduces the Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) formulation, in which these local constraints are replaced by a single differentiable global constraint and a single Lagrange multiplier, independently of the discretization size. Despite this reduction of the dual problem, the local constraint structure is retained through the gradient of the aggregation operator, which defines effective local multipliers. Under suitable structural properties, these multipliers concentrate on the locally active constraints as the aggregation approaches the exact maximum, asymptotically recovering the local Karush--Kuhn--Tucker structure of the original problem. A consistent primal--dual Newton solver is developed for the aggregated damage problem. The resulting bordered system admits a scalar Schur complement reduction. For the class of aggregation operators considered here, the consistent Hessian further decomposes into a sparse local contribution and a rank-one correction. Exploiting this structure through the Sherman--Morrison formula reduces the exact Newton correction to sparse subproblems involving only local contributions, together with low-cost global scalar and vector operations. The sparse computational structure of the underlying local problem can therefore be exploited despite the global nature of the aggregated constraint. One- and two-dimensional numerical assessments confirm the predicted aggregation accuracy, the recovery of the pointwise Lipschitz-constrained response, and the applicability of the formulation under mesh refinement. The results also provide a first assessment of the computational performance of the proposed formulation.

summary: We calculate the separately marked, canonical-cover-compatible deformation groupoid of B=(P(1,1,4); (xyz^2=0), (xy=0)). Its smooth normal space has dimension 16, with an explicit action of a two-dimensional torus and the involution interchanging x and y. The calculation recovers every deformation in this functor, removes the intrinsic automorphism gauge, and proves arbitrary Artinian base change for all positive and negative reflexive powers of the marked sheaves. Power-product maps to one-mark cover-compatible functors are finite; an equivariant finite-map lemma gives exact pullback of character GIT. Under an additional equivalence with the reduced K-compactification stacks, three fixed rays yield the uniform K/VGIT comparison near (7/16,1/16). The required reverse family comparison is left open. Thus the unconditional results concern the cover-compatible functor, and the K-moduli-germ conclusion is a conditional application.
title: Canonical-cover-compatible deformations of a marked weighted projective plane

summary: Abstract (it)   Leonardo's Spatial Grammar è l’app che raccoglie le tre ricerche dedicate rispettivamente all’Annunciazione, all’Adorazione dei Magi e al Cenacolo: Leonardo's Rulers , Leonardo's CAD e Leonardo's Score . Non aggiunge una quarta indagine, ma riunisce i tre studi in una lettura unitaria, già depositata nel corpus accademico omonimo. Il corpus mette in discussione l’idea di un’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci e propone, in alternativa, un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione dei Magi, fino al Cenacolo, emerge una grammatica spaziale in evoluzione: la rigida scacchiera lascia il posto a un sistema di righelli inseriti; la misura, inizialmente monodirezionale, diventa un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo è la retroingegneria CAD, applicata secondo il « banale aristotelico »: partire da ciò che l’opera mostra e che si può misurare. Bugne, mattonelle, arcate, arazzi e cassettoni non sono quinte, ma strumenti lasciati in vista, da cui le proporzioni — la progressione 1:2:3, il modulo 4:3 e i ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1 — si ricavano dalle stesse opere. Gli spazi restituiti sono misurabili, architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane. Le interpretazioni esoteriche e le simbologie non falsificabili restano fuori dal perimetro. L’app come strumento di lettura Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar riunisce le app dedicate alle singole ricerche e ne offre un accesso coordinato. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. summary: Background:  Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Beyond their primary glucose-lowering actions, both drug classes exert profound organ-protective effects. Objective:  This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on the molecular, cellular, and physiological mechanisms driving the cardio- and nephroprotective outcomes of SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs. Methods:  A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases following PRISMA guidelines for studies published between 2018 and 2026. Results:  SGLT2i act primarily via hemodynamic restoration, reducing intraglomerular pressure through tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF), shifting myocardial energetics toward ketone utilization, inhibiting Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger 1 and 3 (NHE1/NHE3), and suppressing renal/cardiac inflammation and fibrosis. GLP-1RAs act predominantly via anti-inflammatory pathways, endothelial protection, reduction of oxidative stress, inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, and attenuation of renal hyperfiltration via systemic anti-atherosclerotic pathways. Conclusion: SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs display distinct yet complementary molecular pathways. Their synergistic mechanism provides a strong rationale for combined therapy to achieve optimal cardiorenal protection in clinical practice.
tags: SGLT2 inhibitors; GLP-1 receptor agonists; Cardioprotection; Nephroprotection; Tubuloglomerular feedback; Myocardial energetics; Endothelial dysfunction.

summary: Background:  Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Their synergistic mechanism provides a strong rationale for combined therapy to achieve optimal cardiorenal protection in clinical practice.

summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.

summary: This dataset provides a national-scale map of mean annual rainfall erosivity (R-factor) across China at a spatial resolution of 90 m, generated using a machine-learning framework combining Random Forest (RF) and Cubist models. The map was developed using environmental predictors representing geographic location, topography, climate, and vegetation conditions. It is provided in GeoTIFF format using the WGS 84 geographic coordinate reference system (EPSG:4326), with pixel values expressed in MJ mm ha-1 h-1 yr-1. The dataset provides a reliable baseline for accurate national and regional soil erosion assessment, spatially explicit soil erosion modelling, targeted soil and water conservation planning, and scalable integration with high-resolution earth system datasets. Due to the website uploading issues, the map was devided into 12 tiles. This dataset is asscoated to the "A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning" by Zeng et al. (Submitted). Manuscript citation: Zeng, R., Xu, J., Chen, T., Lin, D., Zhu, X., Teng, H., Yu, W., Fu, Z., Du, Y., Chang, J., Chen, S.,Shi, Z. A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning. Submitted. When using the data, please cite repositories as well as the original manuscript. For any questions on the data, please contact Dr. Songchao Chen (chensongchao@zju.edu.cn).

summary: Version 1.5 contains the manuscript as submitted to the Journal of Software: Evolution and Process , together with the analyses added in the final pre-submission revision. Under paper/jsep/ it holds the submitted PDF, the LaTeX source, the figure files, the bibliography, the build scripts and claim_ledger.json ; the build regenerates main.tex byte for byte from the archived result files. reports/post_review.json and formal-stock-v1/ add the stock of pinned references over time, the period split of conversions, and the owner-clustered intervals. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.
title: PinTrace: two waves of SHA pinning in GitHub Actions (replication data and results)

summary: Arabica coffee is highly sensitive to warming, yet its suitability is rarely assessed alongside the ecological and legal limits on forest conversion. We mapped land suitability in montane northern Vietnam on a 30 m grid from twelve climatic, topographic and soil criteria, weighted by a literature-based fuzzy analytic hierarchy process and screened by a non-compensatory ecological exclusion overriding high scores elsewhere. Projections cover 2041–2070 under two high-emission pathways (SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) with five global climate models. Climatically suitable land covers 55,182 km²; the exclusion removed 26.6% of the domain. On the ensemble mean it contracts by 19.9–24.4%, and by 16.7–19.8% where at least three of five models agree; the highly suitable class loses 64–69%, and the median elevation of suitable land rises 127–161 m. Intersected with the baseline and a non-agricultural mask, that area yields long-term cultivable land of 44,094 km² (SSP3-7.0) and 41,862 km² (SSP5-8.5). Of that, 6.5% lies in special-use forest, treated as legally unavailable for coffee; 30.4% in protection forest, where statutory ceilings leave of the order of 4,000 km² usable; about 60% is under tree cover, leaving 17,815 km² unforested. Discrimination is good (AUC = 0.846, 95% CI 0.820–0.872), but absence data come from one province and absolute areas respond more to classification thresholds than to the climate signal: these maps screen rather than authorise land. Because the suitable belt rises while the topographic ceiling and forest estate do not, adaptation itself risks driving forest conversion; it should favour shade-grown coffee on farmland, not standing forest.

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: The island of St. Vincent and the other Windward Islands in the southeastern Caribbean were chosen as a field site for the study of weak mountain wakes. By the authorsメ definition, a モweak wakeヤ forms when the potential vorticity generated by a mountain is not strong enough to advect itself into eddies; rather, it is simply advocated downstream by the ambient flow. GOES-8 and Landsat sunlit images unambiguously revealed that the mountainous Windward Islands have remarkably long straight wakes. The length of St. Vincentメs wake exceeds 300 km although its width is only 20 km. Near the islands, the wake structures reflect the details of the island topography. These wakes do not exhibit any obvious diurnal effect. Boat surveys in the lee of St. Vincent confirmed the existence of features seen in the images: the sharp wake boundary, the small valley-induced jet embedded in the near wake, and the absence of any reverse flow. Aircraft surveys gave evidence of descent over the island and showed that the wake air is relatively warm and dry. The length of the wake (L) agrees with the formula L = H/2CD (where H is the wake depth and CD is the surface drag coefficient), implying that the reacceleration of the wake air is caused by the ambient streamwise pressure gradient rather than by lateral entrainment of momentum or geostrophic adjustment. Two numerical models were used to simulate St. Vincentメs wake, a single-layer hydrostatic model and a 3D nonhydrostatic model. Both models indicated that air descent, acceleration, wave breaking, and weak potential vorticity generation occur over the island, causing a long straight wake. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: The Wake of St. Vincent - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Reconstruction of Monthly Mean 700-mb Heights from Surface Data by Reverse Specification - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: The studies and the guidelines built on them answer for groups. The decision is for one patient, and the gap between the two is bridged by the clinician’s intuition, which practice does not train and almost nobody measures. This note describes a short session that does both: a lecture, a demonstration, then real cases with immediate, sourced feedback and a private report. The examples are obstetric and from early breast cancer; the problem and the method are the same in every field of medicine, because every clinical decision is made for one patient from evidence about groups.
title: Deciding for one patient: training clinical intuition

summary: The NOAA/NASA Pathfinder Program SSM/I Level 3 EASE-Grid Brightness Temperatures will consist of three series produced on CD-ROM, one series each for the EASE-Grid Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere and Cylindrical (global) projections. Grids represent spatially interpolated data. The interpolation technique maximizes the radiometric integrity of original brightness temperature values, maintain high spatial and temporal precision, and involve no averaging of original swath data. Coverage is global and spans the Pathfinder SSM/I Benchmark period, from 1 August 1987 through 30 November 1988. Resolution is 25 km for all channels and 12.5 km for the 85 GHz channels. There are 18 brightness temperature files per day for a given projection (nine each for ascending and descending passes), and two (ascending and descending) corresponding time files. Data are contained in flat binary files, either one image per file consisting of two-dimensional 2-byte integer arrays of brightness temperatures in tenths of Kelvins, or in the case of time files, two-dimensional 1-byte integer arrays consisting of GMT in tenths of hours. Data are available as processing is completed, with completion of the data set projected for the end of 1995. Data are available via ftp, on CD-ROM and through the Internet. Contact NSIDC User Services for information. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Ease-Grid Brightness Temperatures - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Sea Surface Temperature, Wave Height and Period Measurement Details: 16 offshore, coastal and inshore moored buoys with on-board data loggers and telemetry via GOES; onboard calculation of significant wave height and peak period. Various starting dates, beginning as early as 1988. Publication: "Technical details on data processing, calibration etc are available in ""Meteorological and Oceanographic Measurements from Canadian Weather Buoys - a Review of Sensors, Data Reduction, Transmission, Quality Control and Archival Methods"", 1996. Prepared by Axys Environmental Consulting Ltd. for Environment Canada. Copy in IOS Library Technical Records." IOSPBS Data Distribution: Historical have been assembled from various sources (MEDS and PWC) and are available at IOS. [Share_data disk: \METBUOY]. Real-time data are received at IOS and eventually replaced by data from AES that has been through their QC/QA procedures. PSARC_Utility: Data are archived at their original sampling interval (hourly). There have been subjected to AES quality control, but there are gaps in the data due to sensor or system failures. We have not assembled daily or monthly summaries of these data. Real time data (unverified by AES) are available at IOS. Improvements: "Data are archived at their original sampling interval (hourly). There have been subjected to AES quality control, but there are gaps in the data due to sensor or system failures. We have not assembled daily or monthly summaries of these data. Real time data (unverified by AES) are available at IOS. Some additional work is required to merge data formats (particularly ""time"" coding). Processes could be developed to automatically generate daily and monthly summary files, which are likely to be more relevant for stock assessment use. In addition, we could attempt to reconstruct the time series BACK in time by extracting data at these locations from the COADS or REYNOLDS datasets." Base Internet/URL -- ( http:/www.ios.bc.ca ) ( http://www.jodc.go.jp/service.htm ) [ A TCODE project ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: On 25 April 1992, a magnitude-7.1 Ms earthquake occurred near Cape Mendocino, California, at the southern end of the Cascadia Subduction Zone. Seismological analyses suggest an almost pure dip-slip reverse fault, with subduction of the Gorda Plate beneath the North American Plate. Modeling and observations of crustal deformation due to this fault mechanism produces uplift of the ocean bottom in relatively shallow water just offshore. A tsunami was generated that was measured by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration sea level gauges along the California, southern Oregon, and Hawaii coastlines and in the deep ocean in the Gulf of Alaska. Several records are characterized by two distinct packets of tsunami energy, the first representing propagation along a minimum time path traversing deep offshore water, the second an apparent edge wave mode trapped along the coast. The largest peak-to-trough amplitude of 1.1 m was recorded at Crescent City in the second packet, approximately 3-4 hours after arrival of the first tsunami wave. Observations of this tsunami will be discussed along with some numerical model results to explain the source area and propagation characteristics. [Reference: Gonz£lez, F.I., E.N. Bernard, and K. Satake. The Cape Mendocino tsunami, 25 April 1992. In Tsunami: Progress in Prediction, Disaster Prevention and Warning, Y. Tsuchiya and N. Shuto (eds.), Series of Advances in Natural and Technological Hazards Research, Kluwer Academic Publishers, 151-158 (1995).] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

summary: Seawater concentrations of dimethylsulfide (DMS) and atmospheric concentrations of DMS, sulfur dioxide, methanesulfonate (MSA), and non-sea-salt (nss) sulfate were measured over the eastern Pacific Ocean between 105° and 110°W from 20°N to 60°S during February and March 1989. Although the samples collected in the southern hemisphere appear to be of marine origin, no significant correlation was found between the latitudinal distributions of DMS, SO, MSA, and nss SO. However, an inverse correlation (r = 0.87) was found between atmospheric temperature and the MSA to nss SO molar ratio in submicrometer aerosol particles with a decrease in temperature corresponding to an increase in the molar ratio. Although this trend is consistent with laboratory results indicating the favored production of MSA at lower temperatures, it is contrary to southern hemisphere baseline station data. This suggests either a decrease in the supply of DMS relative to nonmarine sources of nss SO at the baseline stations in winter or additional mechanisms that affect the relative production of MSA and nss SO. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Variations in the Methanesulfonate to Sulfate Molar Ratio in Submicrometer Marine Aerosol Particles over the South Pacific Ocean - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Acoustic extensometer instruments capable of making precise daily measurements of horizontal distance were deployed across the north rift zone of Axial Volcano in June 1996 and were in place when a submarine eruption began on Axialメs south rift zone in January 1998. The instruments recorded a gradual 9-cm extension over a 405-m baseline leading up to the eruption, and then an abrupt, 4-cm contraction at the time of the eruption. An elastic point-source deformation model shows that deflation of Axialメs summit can explain both the 4-cm distance decrease at the extensometer array and a 3.2-m subsidence measured by another instrument in the caldera, if the pressure source is located at a depth of 3.8 km below the center of the caldera. The 9-cm distance increase may represent pre-eruption spreading across the rift zone. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Evidence for Deformation Associated with the 1998 Eruption of Axial Volcano, Juan de Fuca Ridge, from Acoustic Extensometer Measurements - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: The fact that vigorous hydrothermal discharge occurs on ridge segments with a variety of spreading rates and morphological characteristics makes it difficult to discern the large-scale geological controls on the distribution of hydrothermal venting along the mid-ocean ridge. We undertook to simplify this problem by mapping the distribution of hydrothermally produced thermal and light attenuation anomalies along the crest of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, a medium-rate spreading center with segments of markedly differing morphology. Hydrothermal anomalies were detected by towing a high-precision conductivity-temperature-depth- transmissometer (CTDT) package in a sawtooth pattern through the lowermost 1000 m of the water column above each segment. These surveys, conducted between 1985 and 1989, have produced the first quantitative and continuous visualizations of hydrothermal plumes along a multisegment portion of the mid-ocean ridge. Hydrothermal discharge is strongest on those segments, or portions of segments, where the apparent magmatic budget is highest, as indicated by the degree of along-axis inflation and other morphological characteristics. This correspondence implies that magma is episodically delivered in small and spatially discontinuous bodies of melt rather than by the constant resupply of a steady state magma chamber. We propose that the probability of discharge occurring at any point on the mid-ocean ridge is proportional to the spreading rate. This probability, scaled by the observation that significant plumes presently emanate from ~20% of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, is expected to range from ~5% on the slowest-spreading ridge to ~50% on the fastest-spreading ridge. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Hydrothermal Venting and the Apparent Magmatic Budget of the Juan de Fuca Ridge - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Tetrahedral head models of 100 Human Connectome Project (HCP) Young Adult subjects, built for finite-element simulation of transcranial magnetic stimulation, with a series of remeshed versions of one subject for mesh-convergence studies. The files are the data used by the cuNIBS manuscripts and benchmark suite. The subjects are the 100 HCP S1200 subjects selected by Berger et al. (2025). We segmented each subject's T1-weighted and T2-weighted scans, taken from the scans Berger et al. distribute, with SimNIBS 4.6 CHARM at default settings, without manual correction. The one non-default setting is --forceqform, which the HCP scans need because their qform and sform orientations disagree. The meshes have 3.94 to 5.53 million tetrahedra (median 4.79 million) and carry all nine CHARM tissue tags. Contents: subjects/<id>.h5: one head mesh per subject, with its EEG cap positions. The ID is the HCP subject ID. ladder/<id>_s<NNN>.h5: one subject remeshed at eight resolutions from 1.71 to 21.2 million tetrahedra. Every element length is scaled by NNN/100. Format: HDF5 files written by HeadMesh.save in cuNIBS, uncompressed. The tissue tags follow CHARM and are stored with the mesh. The meshes are derived from HCP data and carry no names or other identifying information beyond the HCP subject ID. Use is subject to the HCP Open Access Data Use Terms, in addition to the CC BY 4.0 license. Software: cuNIBS ( https://github.com/vcubiomag/cunibs ). The code release that reproduces the manuscripts' results is v0.5.0 (DOI to be added). Acknowledgement: Data were provided by the Human Connectome Project, WU-Minn Consortium (Principal Investigators: David Van Essen and Kamil Ugurbil; 1U54MH091657), funded by the 16 NIH Institutes and Centers that support the NIH Blueprint for Neuroscience Research, and by the McDonnell Center for Systems Neuroscience at Washington University. Those awards funded the acquisition of the data and not this work.
title: CHARM head models of 100 Human Connectome Project subjects with a mesh-resolution ladder, as HDF5 files for cuNIBS

summary: Adaptive Biohybrid Interfaces and Self Repairing Prostheses at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 23   30 Physicalized Models   82 Chapters   200 Research Gates Adaptive Biohybrid Interfaces and Self Repairing Prostheses at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on whether prosthetic and implant interfaces can detect wear and tissue change, repair locally, and then independently re-prove mechanical, sensing, and biological function. The book separates surface closure, electrical signal return, and controller compensation from durable recovery. Every intervention may change material composition, residual stress, impedance, sensor calibration, debris production, and tissue exposure; repair therefore creates a new qualification event rather than restoring an assumed past state. Thirty physicalized models connect fracture and delamination, viscoelasticity, continuum damage, reaction-diffusion healing, reservoir depletion, dynamic covalent rebonding, tribocorrosion, wear debris, micromotion, residual stress, Bayesian remaining life, electrochemical impedance, conductive percolation, charge injection, neural-signal drift, recalibration, foreign-body dynamics, fibrosis transport, mechanoinflammation, tissue remodeling, osseointegration, biofilm risk, thermal safety, inverse defect localization, barrier-constrained control, material accountability, accelerated aging, repeated repair, and joint biohybrid requalification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with hidden cracks, delamination, drift, debris, tissue shift, repeated repair, uncertain defect identity, and accelerated aging performed by an independent laboratory. The work is a preclinical research framework rather than a clinical repair procedure or deployment authorization. Unknown defects, unsafe heat or charge, rising immune burden, lost calibration ancestry, changing accelerated-aging mechanisms, and inadequate remaining life are noncompensable vetoes. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Biohybrid Repair Passport, binds the defect, loading history, materials, repair authority and action, retrieved and shed matter, immune state, recalibration, aging evidence, remaining-life interval, and independent verdict into one auditable interface record. summary: Patient Specific Regenerative Microfactories and Swarm Manufacturing at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 22   30 Physicalized Models   82 Chapters   200 Research Gates Patient Specific Regenerative Microfactories and Swarm Manufacturing at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on manufacturing individualized cells, scaffolds, microtissues, and therapeutic components through distributed robotic systems without weakening lot release quality. The book treats every patient as a distinct manufacturing lot. Starting material, cell genealogy, material flow, agent action, calibration, environmental state, contamination evidence, identity, purity, maturation, and blind terminal function remain linked throughout production. Personalization changes the process path but never waives the release contract. Thirty physicalized models connect stochastic lot release, population dynamics, clonal diversity, living-product mass balance, contamination transport, Bayesian sterility, microfluidic residence time, oxygen and thermal transport, scaffold maturation, viscoelasticity, adhesion injury, swarm allocation, fault-bounded consensus, common-cause reliability, calibration drift, sensor fusion, change detection, small-lot inference, potency, multivariate release, logistics, recipe portability, provenance, economics, and robust joint qualification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with donor shift, contamination, agent failure, supply interruption, calibration drift, reagent substitution, incomplete genealogy, and blinded transfer to a second laboratory. The work is a preclinical manufacturing research framework rather than a clinical protocol or release authorization. Contamination, identity failure, unclosed genealogy, invalid calibration, and failed independent function are noncompensable vetoes. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Regenerative Microfactory Capsule, binds patient material, lineage, agent capability, process state, substitutions, deviations, blind potency, release, quarantine, and terminal disposition into one auditable and portable evidence object. summary: Understanding the behavior of black-box data-driven controllers is a key challenge in modern control design. In this work, we propose an eXplainable AI (XAI) methodology based on Inverse Optimal Control (IOC) to obtain local explanations for the behavior of a controller operating around a given region. Specifically, we extract the weights assigned to tracking errors and control effort in the implicit cost function that a black-box controller is optimizing, offering a more transparent and interpretable representation of the controller’s underlying objectives. This approach presents connections with well-established XAI techniques, such as Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) since it is still based on a local approximation of the control policy. However, the explanation provided by our method offers a structured and more control-relevant perspective. Numerical examples demonstrate that the inferred cost function consistently provides a deeper understanding of the controller’s decision-making process.
title: eXplainable AI for data driven control: an inverse optimal control approach
