summary: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.
title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

summary: Version 1.1 extends the interrupted conversion series to 18 months and adds a late-wave summary with commit-level concentration. The measurement files are unchanged from version 1.0. Replication data and published results for a longitudinal study of SHA pinning in GitHub Actions workflows after the March 2025 tj-actions/changed-files compromise. The study follows 455 public repositories that depended on the compromised Action from six months before to eighteen months after the incident and reconstructs every external uses: reference and every change to it from the default-branch Git history. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.
title: PinTrace: GitHub Actions SHA pinning after the tj-actions/changed-files compromise (replication data and results)

summary: Python/NGSolve implementation and reference data accompanying the manuscript “A hybridization-derived interior penalty Nitsche method for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion” by Vincent Fontaine (23-page version, 21 October 2026). The package contains the three IPN symmetry variants, strongly imposed Dirichlet variants, benchmark and figure-generation drivers, and stored numerical reference results for heterogeneous anisotropic checkerboard diffusion, the Kellogg singular benchmark, and controlled comparisons of transmissibility and contrast-blind flux-jump weighting. The numerical results are unchanged; no simulations were rerun during preparation. SHA-256 manifests and an integrity-only checker are included. Original software is licensed under BSD-3-Clause; original reference data and package documentation under CC BY 4.0, with separate scope described in LICENSE.txt. Existing third-party notices apply. The manuscript and its source files retain their separate manuscript licensing status.
title: IPN for Heterogeneous and Anisotropic Diffusion: Reproducibility Software and Reference Data

summary: This record contains the Python model scripts and result files supporting the article “Biogas as a Resilience Fuel for Wastewater Treatment under Chronic Grid Failure: Demand-Based Design, Gas Storage and Economics for Three Lebanese Plants” (Awad and El-Samra,  Energies , 2026),. The model assesses whether biogas from sludge digestion can keep three Lebanese wastewater treatment plants (Al Ghadir, Tripoli and Saida) running through daily grid blackouts of 4, 12 and 20 h. It estimates biogas and CHP power from the influent COD load; builds plant electricity demand bottom-up from pumping heads and aeration oxygen requirements; computes the power adequacy ratio (biogas power / essential load); sizes gas storage for fixed blackout blocks and through an hourly simulation of random outages; counts methane over a full 24-h boundary, including leakage, CHP and flare slip and a sludge-disposal counterfactual; and evaluates NPV, payback and GHG savings for alternative operating configurations, including surplus export and a PV–battery alternative. Nineteen uncertain inputs are propagated jointly through 10,000 Monte Carlo draws, with Spearman rank sensitivity per blackout scenario. Contents: task1–task14 (.py): model scripts, one per analysis step (baseline model, bottom-up demand, Al Ghadir configurations, gas storage, Monte Carlo uncertainty and sensitivity, surplus export, plausibility checks, secondary-plant demand, sludge counterfactual, hourly outage simulation, PV–battery comparison, Tripoli and Saida economics, Table 5 checks, upgrades and avoided sludge disposal) convergence.py: Monte Carlo and hourly-simulation convergence checks (Tables S2 and S3 of the article) make_figures.py: reproduces Figures 3–7 of the article (600 dpi) *_results.xlsx: output of each script README.txt: run order and dependencies
title: Biogas as a Resilience Fuel for Wastewater Treatment under Chronic Grid Failure: Scripts and Results

summary: Safe autonomous navigation of UASs requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid system, or runtime assurance mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides

summary: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.
title: MemDev-Bench: Does Memory Help Code Agents?Benchmarking Memory Systems over Real Repository Histories

summary: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.
title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.
title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

summary: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
title: MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

summary: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models

summary: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.
title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation

summary: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self-attention, reducing token count while retaining block-level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench-Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static-scene revisitation performance on R2M-Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.
title: Recast the Past: Stable Long Video Generation with Full Context Memory

summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

summary: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.
title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

summary: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making. In response, prototype-based models in explainable AI have attracted growing attention for their ability to retrieve visually similar examples as faithful explanations. Although these models achieve competitive classification accuracy, they often exhibit degraded explanation quality across datasets with varying characteristics, limiting their practical applicability. We draw on insights from cognitive neuroscience, particularly the human memory system, which encodes input-relevant information into representations that support recognition. We propose an Engram Memory Network (EMN), a model that emulates the ventral visual stream and inferior temporal cortex in the human brain. Central to this model is a Hopfield-inspired memory module that iteratively retrieves representative prototypes. These memory-refined latents are used for both reconstruction and classification, encouraging the selected prototypes to capture input-relevant information across diverse datasets. To address the lack of standardized evaluation for prototype explanations, we assess three complementary aspects: perceptual similarity (LPIPS and DISTS) for perceived resemblance, subclass alignment, measuring whether prototypes match the input's fine-grained category beyond supervised labels, and information preservation (NMI), measuring how much input information is captured by selected prototypes. Experiments show that EMN improves visual similarity by 17.06%, subclass alignment by 104.57%, and NMI by 42.42% on average across CIFAR-10/100, MNIST, HAM10000, and CUB-200, while achieving the highest average classification accuracy (87.62%) among all methods. These findings underscore the effectiveness of neuroscience-inspired explanation mechanisms in advancing the interpretability and reliability of prototype-based models.
title: Engram Memory Network: Brain-Inspired Prototype Explanations

summary: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines

summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

summary: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly being deployed into radiation-challenging environments in spacecraft, particle accelerators, and, soon, space-based data centers. Instantiated as a learned orchestration of numbers stored in persistent memory, models are susceptible to continual degradation as high-energy particles corrupt data. At inference time, new data passed through the network fundamentally break the off-line assumptions and guarantees of a static model determined during training. To preserve the quality and efficacy of the models, fault tolerance against bit flips is a clear objective. In this work we developed a runtime method for repairing the quantized weights of neural networks (NNs) after bit flips on commodity, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware, without storing extra replicas. Our work extends the well-established Fault-Aware Training (FAT) paradigm by adding an alignment penalty to concentrate undamaged activations and weights into a low-rank subspace, and we then reconstruct flagged corrupted coordinates from the uncorrupted survivors. We call this method {\it Projection Healing} and apply it to six regression benchmarks on quantized NNs. Holding a FAT checkpoint fixed and toggling only the runtime heal gives a further ${\sim}23\%$ reduction in the native-unit excess integral. Across those datasets the method extends the operational scrub interval by a median of $2.04\times$ at a $+5\%$ RMSE degradation and $1.96\times$ at $+50\%$, compared with $1.62\times$ and $1.07\times$ for classical Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). summary: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly being deployed into radiation-challenging environments in spacecraft, particle accelerators, and, soon, space-based data centers. Instantiated as a learned orchestration of numbers stored in persistent memory, models are susceptible to continual degradation as high-energy particles corrupt data. At inference time, new data passed through the network fundamentally break the off-line assumptions and guarantees of a static model determined during training. To preserve the quality and efficacy of the models, fault tolerance against bit flips is a clear objective. We call this method {\it Projection Healing} and apply it to six regression benchmarks on quantized NNs. Holding a FAT checkpoint fixed and toggling only the runtime heal gives a further ${\sim}23\%$ reduction in the native-unit excess integral. Across those datasets the method extends the operational scrub interval by a median of $2.04\times$ at a $+5\%$ RMSE degradation and $1.96\times$ at $+50\%$, compared with $1.62\times$ and $1.07\times$ for classical Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). summary: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
title: AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction with Anchor-Based Residual Memory for Temporal Graph Neural Networks

summary: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.
title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report

summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $τ^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings

summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

summary: This is a study commissioned by the Panel for the Future of Science and Technology, European Parliament: Generative Artificial Intelligence could strengthen open science by improving accessibility, findability, and usability. Still, under less favourable conditions, it could also weaken scientific exchange by obscuring provenance, deepening dependency on opaque infrastructures, and reinforcing inequalities and increasing synthetic overload, in which large volumes of AI-generated scientific content overwhelm the capacity of researchers and systems to verify, interpret, and trust information. This study describes how Generative AI is reshaping scientific exchange within the broader framework of open science. It shows that the main policy challenge is not whether Generative AI will be used in scientific exchange, but under what institutional, infrastructural, and normative conditions it can support reliable research, and knowledge valorisation. The European Union should treat scientific exchange as public-interest infrastructure and enact policies to support skills, strengthened provenance, transparency, reproducibility, inclusion, and strategic capacity in an AI-mediated research environment. This report provides specific policy options tackling the risks that can be associated with the use of AI in scientific exchange. This study is prepared for, and addressed to, the Members and staff of the European Parliament as background material to assist them in their parliamentary work. The content of the document is the sole responsibility of its author(s) and any opinions expressed herein should not be taken to represent an official position of the Parliament.
title: Open science and the effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in scientific exchange: Policy options for reliable research

summary: ExM Explorer is a search engine for expansion microscopy (ExM) experiments compiled from the literature. For each study, it records the organisms expanded, the protocol used (fixation, anchoring, gel composition, homogenization, expansion factor), and the antibodies, dyes and stains applied, with their outcome and a link to the source publication. Version 1.0 covers 381 studies, 301 species, 1,483 primary antibodies and 608 dyes and stains. The database was built from 579 full texts identified by searches of PubMed and Europe PMC (including bioRxiv and medRxiv). Each paper was read individually by a large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic), followed by deterministic curation and eight quality controls. This archive contains the portal (a single HTML file that runs offline), the database with its column dictionary, the provenance of every PDF and the curation log, the EukProt v3 species list used to place coverage on the eukaryotic tree, the code that generates and validates the portal, the extraction and curation scripts with their logs, and the quality-control outputs. Full methods and limitations are described in METHODS.md. Code is released under the MIT License and data under CC BY 4.0.
title: ExM Explorer

summary: This dataset provides supporting numerical artifacts for the manuscript “Reduced-Regularity Consistency for a Direct ABC-Adapted L1-Type Operator: Analysis and Diffusion Benchmarks.” The archive contains the locked Problem-1 FDM/FEM common-resolution results, the Chebyshev spectral results, the Problem-1 temporal-contamination audit and its derived summary, the Problem-2 Q=64 FDM/Spectral graded-mesh validation results, and the FEM Pilot-2 console-verified summary. A README, artifact manifest, and SHA-256 checksum list document the archive contents, integrity checks, evidence status, and item-specific limitations. This is a supporting-data archive, not a complete source-code or computational-environment release. The archived CSV files were retained from the project artifacts and integrity-checked during packaging; the original numerical experiments were not rerun for this deposit. The FEM Pilot-2 file is a console-verified summary rather than a complete raw export. Known provenance limitations are documented in the accompanying README and manifest. The Q=64 results show refinement trends consistent with the stated consistency upper bound for the tested cases. They do not establish sharpness of the estimate or an unconditional fully discrete convergence theorem.
tags: Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative; fractional diffusion; ABC-L1 discretization; numerical analysis; finite difference method; finite element method; Chebyshev spectral collocation; graded temporal meshes; numerical reproducibility.
title: Supporting numerical data for: Reduced-Regularity Consistency for a Direct ABC-Adapted L1-Type Operator: Analysis and Diffusion Benchmarks

summary: In variational damage models, Lipschitz regularization can be introduced by imposing a pointwise bound on the gradient of the damage field, thereby controlling its spatial regularity without adding a gradient-dependent contribution to the energy. After spatial discretization, this condition gives rise to local inequality constraints and associated Lagrange multipliers, whose number increases with mesh refinement. This work introduces the Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) formulation, in which these local constraints are replaced by a single differentiable global constraint and a single Lagrange multiplier, independently of the discretization size. Despite this reduction of the dual problem, the local constraint structure is retained through the gradient of the aggregation operator, which defines effective local multipliers. Under suitable structural properties, these multipliers concentrate on the locally active constraints as the aggregation approaches the exact maximum, asymptotically recovering the local Karush--Kuhn--Tucker structure of the original problem. A consistent primal--dual Newton solver is developed for the aggregated damage problem. The resulting bordered system admits a scalar Schur complement reduction. For the class of aggregation operators considered here, the consistent Hessian further decomposes into a sparse local contribution and a rank-one correction. Exploiting this structure through the Sherman--Morrison formula reduces the exact Newton correction to sparse subproblems involving only local contributions, together with low-cost global scalar and vector operations. The sparse computational structure of the underlying local problem can therefore be exploited despite the global nature of the aggregated constraint. One- and two-dimensional numerical assessments confirm the predicted aggregation accuracy, the recovery of the pointwise Lipschitz-constrained response, and the applicability of the formulation under mesh refinement. The results also provide a first assessment of the computational performance of the proposed formulation.
title: Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) regularization of damage and fracture: a single-constraint, single-multiplier formulation retaining local computational structure

summary: We calculate the separately marked, canonical-cover-compatible deformation groupoid of B=(P(1,1,4); (xyz^2=0), (xy=0)). Its smooth normal space has dimension 16, with an explicit action of a two-dimensional torus and the involution interchanging x and y. The calculation recovers every deformation in this functor, removes the intrinsic automorphism gauge, and proves arbitrary Artinian base change for all positive and negative reflexive powers of the marked sheaves. Power-product maps to one-mark cover-compatible functors are finite; an equivariant finite-map lemma gives exact pullback of character GIT. Under an additional equivalence with the reduced K-compactification stacks, three fixed rays yield the uniform K/VGIT comparison near (7/16,1/16). The required reverse family comparison is left open. Thus the unconditional results concern the cover-compatible functor, and the K-moduli-germ conclusion is a conditional application.
title: Canonical-cover-compatible deformations of a marked weighted projective plane

summary: Abstract (it)   Leonardo's Spatial Grammar è l’app che raccoglie le tre ricerche dedicate rispettivamente all’Annunciazione, all’Adorazione dei Magi e al Cenacolo: Leonardo's Rulers , Leonardo's CAD e Leonardo's Score . Non aggiunge una quarta indagine, ma riunisce i tre studi in una lettura unitaria, già depositata nel corpus accademico omonimo. Il corpus mette in discussione l’idea di un’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci e propone, in alternativa, un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione dei Magi, fino al Cenacolo, emerge una grammatica spaziale in evoluzione: la rigida scacchiera lascia il posto a un sistema di righelli inseriti; la misura, inizialmente monodirezionale, diventa un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo è la retroingegneria CAD, applicata secondo il « banale aristotelico »: partire da ciò che l’opera mostra e che si può misurare. Bugne, mattonelle, arcate, arazzi e cassettoni non sono quinte, ma strumenti lasciati in vista, da cui le proporzioni — la progressione 1:2:3, il modulo 4:3 e i ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1 — si ricavano dalle stesse opere. Gli spazi restituiti sono misurabili, architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane. Le interpretazioni esoteriche e le simbologie non falsificabili restano fuori dal perimetro. L’app come strumento di lettura Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar riunisce le app dedicate alle singole ricerche e ne offre un accesso coordinato. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.
title: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO2

summary: This dataset provides a national-scale map of mean annual rainfall erosivity (R-factor) across China at a spatial resolution of 90 m, generated using a machine-learning framework combining Random Forest (RF) and Cubist models. The map was developed using environmental predictors representing geographic location, topography, climate, and vegetation conditions. It is provided in GeoTIFF format using the WGS 84 geographic coordinate reference system (EPSG:4326), with pixel values expressed in MJ mm ha-1 h-1 yr-1. The dataset provides a reliable baseline for accurate national and regional soil erosion assessment, spatially explicit soil erosion modelling, targeted soil and water conservation planning, and scalable integration with high-resolution earth system datasets. Due to the website uploading issues, the map was devided into 12 tiles. This dataset is asscoated to the "A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning" by Zeng et al. (Submitted). Manuscript citation: Zeng, R., Xu, J., Chen, T., Lin, D., Zhu, X., Teng, H., Yu, W., Fu, Z., Du, Y., Chang, J., Chen, S.,Shi, Z. A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning. Submitted. When using the data, please cite repositories as well as the original manuscript. For any questions on the data, please contact Dr. Songchao Chen (chensongchao@zju.edu.cn).
title: A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning

The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.
title: PinTrace: two waves of SHA pinning in GitHub Actions (replication data and results)

summary: This Zenodo record contains the public participant package for the FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue (HCF) Competition, a blind round-robin benchmark for fatigue-life prediction of 42CrMo4+QT steel under multiaxial high-cycle fatigue loading. Participants are asked to submit fatigue-life predictions for plain and notched hollow cylindrical specimens subjected to combined axial and torsional loading, including in-phase and 90° out-of-phase loading histories, with constant internal pressure. The package includes the competition rules, start-here guide, experimental basis, calibration data, public blind load matrix, specimen geometry information, manufacturing documentation, roughness and residual-stress characterisation, test setup and test-sequence descriptions, and participant submission templates. All files are provided as zipped folders to preserve the folder structure of the competition package.
title: FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue Competition: Participant Package for Blind Fatigue-Life Prediction

summary: Arabica coffee is highly sensitive to warming, yet its suitability is rarely assessed alongside the ecological and legal limits on forest conversion. We mapped land suitability in montane northern Vietnam on a 30 m grid from twelve climatic, topographic and soil criteria, weighted by a literature-based fuzzy analytic hierarchy process and screened by a non-compensatory ecological exclusion overriding high scores elsewhere. Projections cover 2041–2070 under two high-emission pathways (SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) with five global climate models. Climatically suitable land covers 55,182 km²; the exclusion removed 26.6% of the domain. On the ensemble mean it contracts by 19.9–24.4%, and by 16.7–19.8% where at least three of five models agree; the highly suitable class loses 64–69%, and the median elevation of suitable land rises 127–161 m. Intersected with the baseline and a non-agricultural mask, that area yields long-term cultivable land of 44,094 km² (SSP3-7.0) and 41,862 km² (SSP5-8.5). Of that, 6.5% lies in special-use forest, treated as legally unavailable for coffee; 30.4% in protection forest, where statutory ceilings leave of the order of 4,000 km² usable; about 60% is under tree cover, leaving 17,815 km² unforested. Discrimination is good (AUC = 0.846, 95% CI 0.820–0.872), but absence data come from one province and absolute areas respond more to classification thresholds than to the climate signal: these maps screen rather than authorise land. Because the suitable belt rises while the topographic ceiling and forest estate do not, adaptation itself risks driving forest conversion; it should favour shade-grown coffee on farmland, not standing forest.
tags: Coffea arabica; land suitability; fuzzy AHP; CMIP6 SSP scenarios; elevation shift; coffee–forest trade-off
title: Climate change shifts Arabica coffee suitability upslope and constrains long-term cultivable land: implications for coffee cultivation and forest conservation in montane northern Vietnam

summary: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.
title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs

summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.

summary: Despite rapid progress in text-to-motion generation, existing methods are commonly designed for single-shot generation. When users are dissatisfied with specific motion details, they are often forced to regenerate the entire sequence from scratch, which is computationally inefficient and potentially destroys previously established kinematic context. A practical generation system should instead support iterative user feedback and refine only the affected spatio-temporal regions while preserving the remaining motion. Therefore, we introduce a conversational motion generation paradigm that requires the system to coordinate instruction understanding, motion generation, localized editing, and quality assessment. Recent advances in LLM-driven multi-agent systems provide a promising foundation for such role-specialized coordination. To tackle these challenges, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent RefinemenT Framework (SMART) is proposed for conversational motion generation. Within SMART, to preserve semantic consistency, we design a semantic-guided masked motion editing mechanism, which precisely grounds natural language feedback into spatiotemporal motion regions to enable localized refinements without altering unedited regions. To reduce redundant exploration, we propose a memory-based self-evolving strategy that dynamically accumulates motion editing knowledge from interaction history and reuses past successful experience. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SMART effectively supports multi-turn conversational motion generation and enables efficient motion refinement.

summary: This paper addresses decentralized estimation and control of heterogeneous multi-agent systems communicating over directed switching topologies. The objective is to satisfy cooperative tasks that require coordination among agents according to a time-invariant task graph. To address the potential mismatch between the communication and task graphs, each agent is equipped with a k-hop Prescribed Performance State Observer (k-hop PPSO) to estimate the states of agents up to k communication hops away using only information exchanged with its 1-hop neighbors. A novel prescribed performance funnel construction is developed to account for the switching communication topology, and a sufficient lower bound on the dwell-time is derived to guarantee the prescribed performance specifications under topology variations. Further analysis shows that, if the desired control objective is achieved with exact knowledge of the required nonlocal states and the resulting closed-loop system is uniformly set-ISS with respect to the state estimation error, then replacing these states with their estimates guarantees convergence to a neighborhood of the desired set. The size of this neighborhood can be made arbitrarily small by appropriately selecting the observer performance bounds. A simulation study demonstrates task satisfaction under directed switching topologies.
title: Observer-Based Control for Multi-Agent Systems under Communication-Task Graph Mismatch and Directed Switching Topologies

summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.
title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor

summary: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. summary: Agentic system design is increasingly shifting from hand-crafted prompts and workflows toward automated search over agentic programs and interaction structures, with multi-agent systems receiving growing attention. Yet a central question remains unresolved: when does an automatically generated multi-agent structure exhibit a functionally meaningful division of responsibility? We argue that automated multi-agent design should move beyond searching for effective architectures toward identifying which responsibilities are functionally necessary, how they should be allocated, and when they should change. To explore this, we propose Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design (AMOD), which treats organization itself as a first-class design object, explicitly modeling how agent teams are composed, what functional responsibilities the agents assume, how they coordinate, and how collective decisions are made. We formulate AMOD as an execution-driven design loop. For each task, an automated designer instantiates an organization by assigning functional responsibilities and coordination rules to a set of agents. After execution, task outcomes, intermediate artifacts, and interaction traces are examined to identify which responsibilities may be missing, duplicated, or ineffective, and the organization is revised accordingly. We also propose testing discovered responsibilities by removing them, replacing them with generic roles, or changing their assignment under matched resource budgets, with complementary evaluations. AMOD provides a principled foundation for evidence-based and adaptive multi-agent organization design.

summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.

summary: Terra Scientific Pipelines Service Overview Terra Scientific Pipelines Service, or teaspoons, facilitates running a number of defined scientific pipelines on behalf of users that users can't run themselves in Terra. The most common reason for this is that the pipeline accesses proprietary data that users are not allowed to access directly, but that may be used as e.g. a reference panel for imputation. Supported pipelines Current supported pipelines are: [in development] Imputation (TODO add link/info) Architecture WIP architecture doc Linked LucidChart Development This codebase is in initial development. Requirements This service is written in Java 17, and uses Postgres 13. To run locally, you'll also need: jq - install with brew install jq vault - see DSP's setup instructions here Note that for Step 7, "Create a GitHub Personal Access Token", you'll want to choose the "Tokens (classic)" option, not the fine-grained access token option. Java 17 - can be installed manually or through IntelliJ which will do it for you when importing the project Postgres 13 - multiple solutions here as long as you have a postgres instance running on localhost:5432 the local app will connect appropriately Postgres.app https://postgresapp.com/ Brew https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/postgresql@13 Tech stack Java 17 temurin Postgres 13.1 Gradle - build automation tool SonarQube - static code security and coverage Trivy - security scanner for docker images Jib - docker image builder for Java Local development To run locally: Make sure you have the requirements installed from above. We recommend IntelliJ as an IDE. Clone the repo (if you see broken inputs build the project to get the generated sources) Run the commands in scripts/postgres-init.sql in your local postgres instance. You will need to be authenticated to access Vault. Run scripts/write-config.sh Run ./gradlew bootRun to spin up the server. Navigate to http://localhost:8080/# If this is your first time deploying to any environment, be sure to use the admin endpoint /api/admin/v1/updatePipelineWorkspaceId/{pipelineName}/{workspaceId} to set your pipeline's workspace id. Workspace id can be found through the terra ui workspace dashboard or through the Rawls GET workspace endpoint. Local development with debugging If using Intellij (only IDE we use on the team), you can run the server with a debugger. Follow the steps above but instead of running ./gradlew bootRun to spin up the server, you can run (debug) the App.java class through intellij and set breakpoints in the code. Be sure to set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=config/tsps-sa.json in the Run/Debug configuration Environment Variables. Running Tests/Linter Locally Testing Run ./gradlew service:test to run tests Linting Run ./gradlew spotlessCheck to run linter checks Run ./gradlew :service:spotlessApply to apply fix any issues the linter finds (Optional) Install pre-commit hooks [scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit] has been provided to help ensure all submitted changes are formatted correctly. To install all hooks in [scripts/git-hooks], run: git config core.hooksPath scripts/git-hooks Running SonarQube locally SonarQube is a static analysis code that scans code for a wide range of issues, including maintainability and possible bugs. Get more information from DSP SonarQube Docs If you get a build failure due to SonarQube and want to debug the problem locally, you need to get the sonar token from vault before running the gradle task. export SONAR_TOKEN=$(vault read -field=sonar_token secret/secops/ci/sonarcloud/tsps) ./gradlew sonarqube Running this task produces no output unless your project has errors. To generate a report, run using --info : ./gradlew sonarqube --info Connecting to the database To connect to the Teaspoons database, we have a script in dsp-scripts that does all the setup for you. Clone that repo and make sure you're either on Broad Internal wifi or connected to the VPN. Then run the following command: ./

We recommend IntelliJ as an IDE. Clone the repo (if you see broken inputs build the project to get the generated sources) Run the commands in scripts/postgres-init.sql in your local postgres instance. You will need to be authenticated to access Vault. Run scripts/write-config.sh Run ./gradlew bootRun to spin up the server. Navigate to http://localhost:8080/# If this is your first time deploying to any environment, be sure to use the admin endpoint /api/admin/v1/updatePipelineWorkspaceId/{pipelineName}/{workspaceId} to set your pipeline's workspace id. Be sure to set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=config/tsps-sa.json in the Run/Debug configuration Environment Variables.
