summary: Archived Eurostat dissemination API responses and the code that reproduces every table, figure and reported number from them. The archive covers 31 European countries (EU27 with Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye) for 2014-2025 and includes income in purchasing power standards and in euros, severe material and social deprivation, financial strain by response category, housing cost overburden, income quintile shares, the Gini coefficient and household final consumption price level indices, together with Eurostat's own break-in-series flags. A manifest records the request URLs, retrieval times and SHA-256 checksums. The code uses only the Python standard library. Version 1.6.0 corrects two places where the code did not follow the rule the note states. Shares published to one decimal were being added in binary floating point, so that a combined value of 12.6 formed from one pair of components did not compare equal to a 12.6 formed from another, and fourteen country-years were therefore ranked as if they were not tied. For the same reason an annual change of exactly six points was read as slightly less and dropped at that threshold. Derived quantities are now rounded back to the precision of the published series. The headline results are unchanged. The figure module's own caption, which still described the two marked drops as the panel's largest two, now matches the note in saying they are the first and the third. The package has supported three pieces of work in turn: an earlier article on national price levels and deprivation, a measurement note on the conversion year and the response category, and a Turkish-language note on Türkiye's position in these comparisons and on the series themselves.
title: Replication package: Eurostat income, deprivation and financial strain indicators for 31 European countries, 2014-2025

summary: This is a simulated photoacoustic data set based on the Monte Carlo Method using the simulation framework SIMPA. The simulations use a literature-based forearm model (see Appendix D of Schellenberg et al., Photoacoustics 28, 2022 ) and a digital twin of the MSOT Acuity Echo (iThera Medical). The generating script performs volume generation and optical forward simulation in 3D with MCX using 10⁸ photons and a spacing of 0.1 mm for 16 wavelengths (700 - 850nm in steps of 10nm). Acoustic simulations were performed on the central slice using k-Wave. Images were reconstructed with SIMPA’s delay-and-sum reconstruction algorithm (1540 m/s speed of sound, Tukey windowed bandpass filtering (0.1 - 8 MHz), and Hilbert transform envelope detection.  It comprises 1243 multispectral images in total, each of size 200 x 400 px containing these eight channels: oxygen saturation segmentation with classes: muscle, heavy water, blood vessel, epidermis, US gel, mediprene absorption coefficient scattering coefficient scattering anisotropy fluence initial pressure distribution delay-and-sum reconstruction
title: Simulated multispectral photoacoustic forearm dataset with reference initial pressure, segmentation, and vessel oxygenation maps

summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

summary: Despite rapid progress in text-to-motion generation, existing methods are commonly designed for single-shot generation. When users are dissatisfied with specific motion details, they are often forced to regenerate the entire sequence from scratch, which is computationally inefficient and potentially destroys previously established kinematic context. A practical generation system should instead support iterative user feedback and refine only the affected spatio-temporal regions while preserving the remaining motion. Therefore, we introduce a conversational motion generation paradigm that requires the system to coordinate instruction understanding, motion generation, localized editing, and quality assessment. Recent advances in LLM-driven multi-agent systems provide a promising foundation for such role-specialized coordination. To tackle these challenges, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent RefinemenT Framework (SMART) is proposed for conversational motion generation. Within SMART, to preserve semantic consistency, we design a semantic-guided masked motion editing mechanism, which precisely grounds natural language feedback into spatiotemporal motion regions to enable localized refinements without altering unedited regions. To reduce redundant exploration, we propose a memory-based self-evolving strategy that dynamically accumulates motion editing knowledge from interaction history and reuses past successful experience. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SMART effectively supports multi-turn conversational motion generation and enables efficient motion refinement.
title: Learn to Modify: Self-evolving Multi-agent Refinement Framework for Conversational Text-to-Motion Generation

summary: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.
title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials

summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges

summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.
title: Facts Need Passports: Governing Ethics, Privacy, and Bias in Knowledge Graphs

summary: Terra Scientific Pipelines Service Overview Terra Scientific Pipelines Service, or teaspoons, facilitates running a number of defined scientific pipelines on behalf of users that users can't run themselves in Terra. The most common reason for this is that the pipeline accesses proprietary data that users are not allowed to access directly, but that may be used as e.g. a reference panel for imputation. Supported pipelines Current supported pipelines are: [in development] Imputation (TODO add link/info) Architecture WIP architecture doc Linked LucidChart Development This codebase is in initial development. Requirements This service is written in Java 17, and uses Postgres 13. To run locally, you'll also need: jq - install with brew install jq vault - see DSP's setup instructions here Note that for Step 7, "Create a GitHub Personal Access Token", you'll want to choose the "Tokens (classic)" option, not the fine-grained access token option. Java 17 - can be installed manually or through IntelliJ which will do it for you when importing the project Postgres 13 - multiple solutions here as long as you have a postgres instance running on localhost:5432 the local app will connect appropriately Postgres.app https://postgresapp.com/ Brew https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/postgresql@13 Tech stack Java 17 temurin Postgres 13.1 Gradle - build automation tool SonarQube - static code security and coverage Trivy - security scanner for docker images Jib - docker image builder for Java Local development To run locally: Make sure you have the requirements installed from above. We recommend IntelliJ as an IDE. Clone the repo (if you see broken inputs build the project to get the generated sources) Run the commands in scripts/postgres-init.sql in your local postgres instance. You will need to be authenticated to access Vault. Run scripts/write-config.sh Run ./gradlew bootRun to spin up the server. Navigate to http://localhost:8080/# If this is your first time deploying to any environment, be sure to use the admin endpoint /api/admin/v1/updatePipelineWorkspaceId/{pipelineName}/{workspaceId} to set your pipeline's workspace id. Workspace id can be found through the terra ui workspace dashboard or through the Rawls GET workspace endpoint. Local development with debugging If using Intellij (only IDE we use on the team), you can run the server with a debugger. Follow the steps above but instead of running ./gradlew bootRun to spin up the server, you can run (debug) the App.java class through intellij and set breakpoints in the code. Be sure to set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=config/tsps-sa.json in the Run/Debug configuration Environment Variables. Running Tests/Linter Locally Testing Run ./gradlew service:test to run tests Linting Run ./gradlew spotlessCheck to run linter checks Run ./gradlew :service:spotlessApply to apply fix any issues the linter finds (Optional) Install pre-commit hooks [scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit] has been provided to help ensure all submitted changes are formatted correctly. To install all hooks in [scripts/git-hooks], run: git config core.hooksPath scripts/git-hooks Running SonarQube locally SonarQube is a static analysis code that scans code for a wide range of issues, including maintainability and possible bugs. Get more information from DSP SonarQube Docs If you get a build failure due to SonarQube and want to debug the problem locally, you need to get the sonar token from vault before running the gradle task. export SONAR_TOKEN=$(vault read -field=sonar_token secret/secops/ci/sonarcloud/tsps) ./gradlew sonarqube Running this task produces no output unless your project has errors. To generate a report, run using --info : ./gradlew sonarqube --info Connecting to the database To connect to the Teaspoons database, we have a script in dsp-scripts that does all the setup for you. Clone that repo and make sure you're either on Broad Internal wifi or connected to the VPN. Then run the following command: ./

summary: Archived Eurostat dissemination API responses and the code that reproduces every table, figure and reported number from them. The archive covers 31 European countries (EU27 with Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye) for 2014-2025 and includes income in purchasing power standards and in euros, severe material and social deprivation, financial strain by response category, housing cost overburden, income quintile shares, the Gini coefficient and household final consumption price level indices, together with Eurostat's own break-in-series flags. A manifest records the request URLs, retrieval times and SHA-256 checksums. The code uses only the Python standard library. Version 1.6.0 corrects two places where the code did not follow the rule the note states. Shares published to one decimal were being added in binary floating point, so that a combined value of 12.6 formed from one pair of components did not compare equal to a 12.6 formed from another, and fourteen country-years were therefore ranked as if they were not tied. For the same reason an annual change of exactly six points was read as slightly less and dropped at that threshold. Derived quantities are now rounded back to the precision of the published series. The headline results are unchanged. The figure module's own caption, which still described the two marked drops as the panel's largest two, now matches the note in saying they are the first and the third. The package has supported three pieces of work in turn: an earlier article on national price levels and deprivation, a measurement note on the conversion year and the response category, and a Turkish-language note on Türkiye's position in these comparisons and on the series themselves.
title: Replication package: Eurostat income, deprivation and financial strain indicators for 31 European countries, 2014-2025

summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.

summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.

summary: Yield anomaly detectors in computer agriculture routinely attribute harvest shortfalls to a single dominant stressor, yet drought and pest outbreaks frequently co-occur and confound one another's signatures in remotely sensed and agronomic covariates. The framework is methodological and theoretical: it defines the attribution game, states the confounding conditions under which Shapley values are point-identified, and derives upper and lower bounds when concurrent drought and pest outbreak render the attribution non-identified. A worked illustration uses NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Accra, Ghana (5.6, -0.19) over 2000-2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 26.521 C, a standard deviation of 1.24 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, to show how a single covariate channel can be bounded before attribution is attempted. The contribution is a bound-based audit protocol that replaces point attribution with interval attribution and specifies the evidence required to narrow those intervals in operational detector pipelines.

title: Evaluation of Causal-Attribution Bounds for Computer Agriculture Yield Anomaly Detectors Under Concurrent Drought and Pest Outbreak Confounding: An Artificial Intelligence Shapley-Decomposition Audit

summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.

title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.

summary: Artificial intelligence systems that rank farmers for agricultural input subsidies are increasingly evaluated by comparing enrolled cooperative members with non-members, a design that conflates programme effect with the self-selection of farmers into cooperatives. The design is characterised analytically and by replication: between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, intraclass correlation 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The bound identifies the conditions under which an audit can separate algorithmic misranking from enrollment-driven selection, and it specifies the cluster count at which the equity contrast becomes estimable. Fifty-four clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. The contribution is a design-level audit instrument rather than a new estimator: it tells evaluators what a targeting audit can and cannot attribute, and it converts an unverifiable causal claim into a bounded, reportable quantity.
tags: subsidy targeting; instrumental variable; equity audit; cooperative enrollment; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; algorithmic fairness
title: Causal-Attribution Evaluation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Subsidy Targeting Under Endogenous Cooperative Enrollment: A Computer Instrumental-Variable Bound for Equity Audits

summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; accuracy retention; benchmark power; diagnostic safety
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmarking evaluation; diagnostic integrity
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.

summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.

summary: Vision-language foundation models adapted to weed identification in computer agriculture are typically evaluated by top-1 accuracy on held-out images, a metric that does not bound the agronomic consequence of a misclassification. The framework formalises the adaptation problem as risk minimisation over a hypothesis class of vision-language prompts, derives a PAC-Bayes bound that links few-shot sample size, prompt-space complexity and the divergence between source and target weed floras to an upper bound on the probability of herbicide misapplication, and specifies a benchmarking protocol that reports this bound alongside conventional accuracy. The bound is decomposed into a transfer term, a few-shot estimation term and a distribution-shift term, each of which corresponds to a distinct benchmarking condition that current evaluation practice omits. A worked instantiation for a four-class weed/non-weed decision problem shows how the bound responds to shot count, prompt complexity and shift magnitude, and identifies the shot count below which the bound exceeds a declared safety threshold. The contribution is a shift from accuracy benchmarking to risk-bounded benchmarking for safety-critical agricultural vision, with implications for how few-shot extension deployments should be evaluated before herbicide recommendations are issued.
tags: vision-language models; few-shot adaptation; weed identification; herbicide safety; generalization bounds; benchmarking; computer agriculture
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Vision-Language Foundation Model Adaptation for Computer Agriculture Weed Identification Under Few-Shot Extension Conditions: An Artificial Intelligence Generalization Bound for Herbicide Misapplication Safety
